2 On cloud nine 
People often just say "fluffy" or "nasty black" when talking about clouds, but meteorologists recognize over 50 types based on shape and height. Cloud number nine is the big cumulonimbus cloud, which means feeling very happy.

3 Around the rainbow

4 Mr blue sky

5 There’s life out there 
Even though we don't usually see much outside an airplane window besides clouds and other planes, the air is full of many types of bacteria—up to 1,800 kinds over cities—and they can go as high as twice a plane's cruising altitude.

6 Turbulence terror
Turbulence makes even experienced flyers uncomfortable. It causes bumps or sudden drops but has never brought down a modern airliner. However, passengers not wearing seatbelts could get injured by being thrown around or hit by loose items.

7 In-flight radiation 
Body scanners at airports create the same level of radiation as one minute in an airplane. The Earth is constantly hit with natural cosmic rays from space that have more impact higher up where planes fly.

8 You can’t cure jet lag
Jet lag happens when you travel across time zones, making your body clock mismatched to local time. Eating bland food for 24 hours before flight and staying hydrated helps lessen its effects.

9 Supersonic 747s 
You've likely traveled faster than sound in a plane due to jet streams – fast-moving air currents high up that can move as fast as 250mph, making planes reach speeds over 800mph.

10 Flying through time
Flights create an artificial journey through time zones. Special relativity means there’s actual time travel involved, though minimal—flying across the Atlantic weekly for 40 years only moves you 1/1,000th of a second into the future.

Modern tech makes it strange that planes like Malaysian flight MH370 could vanish. Planes know their location through GPS and tracking systems, but this data isn’t always shared elsewhere due to lack of regulations requiring real-time tracking.

14 Volcanic fallout
Volcanic ash can cancel flights as the glass-like particles melt in engines and cause damage on rotors. Flying into an ash cloud is dangerous.

15 The wing myth 
For years, we had a wrong idea about how wings keep planes flying. Most lift actually comes from pushing air down, which pushes the plane up due to Newton's Third Law of Motion.

16 Forget electric planes
It’s unlikely we’ll have fully electric airliners soon because batteries are much less efficient than jet fuel. To match one tonne of fuel energy, you’d need 100 tonnes of batteries—too heavy for practical use.

17 Beware the vortex 
Pilots wait to take off after another plane to allow time for air vortices created by the wings to disperse. These can make handling a plane difficult if they set off right away.

18 The doors aren’t locked
Plane doors don't need locks because once in flight, pressure builds inside that forces them closed and makes it impossible to open without overcoming this force.

In October 2012, the Taliban sent a gunman to shoot Malala Yousafzai on her way home from school. They wanted to stop her fight for girls' education. 

Nine months later and after many surgeries, Malala spoke at the United Nations on her 16th birthday. She said, “They thought the bullet would silence us, but they failed.” 

Malala Day was a big event where she sat in a main hall usually used by world leaders. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called her "our hero" and former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown wished her a happy 16th birthday.

Malala gained attention after writing about her struggles for education under the Taliban on BBC Urdu service at age 11. By 14, she was nominated for the International Children's Peace Prize by Desmond Tutu, and at 15, became the youngest person ever nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize.

The Taliban sent a gunman to attack Malala after she became famous. Multiple surgeries followed, including fitting her with a titanium plate on her forehead and a cochlear implant to help her hear better. Now living in Birmingham, England, Malala continues to go to school every day.

At the UN, Malala said she was not there for revenge against terrorists. She even expressed no hatred toward the man who shot her. “I do not hate him,” she said, adding that if he stood before her with a gun, she would not shoot back.

Malala wore a white shawl given to her by Benazir Bhutto, Pakistan’s former prime minister, who was killed by extremists.

Malala explained why the Taliban fear education and women. “The power of education frightens them,” she said. She also stated that Islam is about peace and supports children's right to an education.

A petition called "Stand with Malala" has over four million signatures, calling for all 57 million children around the world who don't go to school to have access to education. 

Malala began her speech unsure of what to say but did not need to worry.

Researchers were amazed not by how hard people found the challenge but by how far they would go to avoid it. The task was simple: sit and think.

Some found it so unbearable that they chose to give themselves mild electric shocks to break the boredom. Two-thirds of men shocked themselves at least once during a 15-minute period, while one in four women did the same. Scientists believe this difference may be because men are generally more likely to seek out new sensations than women.

Psychologists from Virginia and Harvard Universities conducted over 11 studies showing that most people dislike being left alone with their thoughts, no matter their age, education level, income, or how much time they spend on smartphones or social media. The findings suggest this is not just due to the fast pace of modern life or the popularity of mobile devices.

In one set of experiments, students were told to sit quietly in an empty room for six to 15 minutes without phones, books, or writing materials. They reported finding it unpleasant and hard to concentrate. When researchers repeated the experiment at home, people found it even more miserable and often checked their phones or got up.

The studies also included over 100 people aged 18 to 77 recruited from a church and a farmers' market. These participants also did not enjoy sitting alone with their thoughts.

To test if people would choose something bad rather than nothing, students were given the option of giving themselves an electric shock during the experiment. Despite earlier saying they would pay to avoid such shocks, some still chose to use them. Twelve out of 18 men and six out of 24 women shocked themselves at least once.

Researchers concluded that being alone with one's thoughts can be so unpleasant that it drives people to self-administer electric shocks they had said they would prefer to avoid.

Organic food has more antioxidants linked to better health than regular food and also has lower levels of toxic metals and pesticides, according to a big study led by Professor Carlo Leifert at Newcastle University. The team looked at 343 studies from around the world and found that organic food had higher levels of antioxidants between 19% and 69%. This means switching to organic fruits and vegetables could be like adding one or two more portions of the five recommended daily servings.

Antioxidants in organic food can lower the risk of chronic diseases like heart disease, certain cancers, and brain problems. However, no long-term studies have proven health benefits from eating a lot of organic food yet.

Organic crops may have higher antioxidant levels because they do not use chemical sprays to protect against pests. But other factors might also play a role, such as the types of seeds used and the lack of artificial fertilizers.

The study found that regular crops had four times more pesticide residues than organic ones. Also, conventional cereals contain less protein compared to organic ones.

Some experts say these findings are not enough to prove that organic food is better for health. Tom Sanders from King’s College London says the differences may be within normal variations and might not make a big difference nutritionally.

The research shows that organic farming can affect the quality of our food, but it also faces criticism about how the studies were chosen and whether the results show real benefits for people's health.

Emmanuel Limal, a 43-year-old actor from France who lives in Copenhagen, was tired of dating women who did not want to start a family. He had spent 20 years searching for love but found that most people he met were too busy with other activities and didn't prioritize having children.

Limal has a six-year-old daughter from a past relationship and comes from a large family; his father is one of eleven siblings. Because of this, Limal wants more children. He tried online dating sites where some women said they wanted kids someday, but their profiles showed lots of other activities that suggested they wouldn't have time for a family.

One day, he saw a profile on an online site from a woman who admitted she wanted children. This inspired him to create his own website called Babyklar.nu. The idea is simple: it's like any dating site, but users must be honest about their desire to start a family soon. Users can also say if they are okay with someone who already has kids.

When the site launched in June, there were 50 sign-ups every hour. More men than women have joined (53% to 47%). The feedback from members is very positive, and some couples met on the site and are now together.

Danish people are not having enough babies, according to a report by Rigshospitalet hospital in Copenhagen. Currently, Danish families average only 1.7 children each, which is too low to keep Denmark’s population stable. This is partly because women often wait until they are older to have kids and couples delay starting families.

Limal hopes the site will help people who want a family but haven't found the right person yet. “This is about love and children,” he says. He plans to expand Babyklar.nu to France and the UK later in 2013, though it’s currently only available for Danes. Denmark's small size means that dating doesn’t involve much travel.

Limal has also found someone who shares his desire to have a baby.

In a new study, scientists examined bacteria in the New York City subway system over 18 months. They found many types of bacteria on turnstiles, seats, ticket booths, and stations. Dr. Christopher Mason from Weill Cornell Medical College led this research. Some bacteria they found include those related to meningitis, anthrax, and bubonic plague. However, the amount of these harmful bacteria was very small, meaning people are not at risk.

The study also showed that most bacteria were harmless or helpful for breaking down waste. Bacteria linked to food like cheese and kimchi appeared around subway stations, reflecting local eating habits. For example, Swiss cheese bacteria were found in midtown Manhattan and the financial district, while kimchi-related bacteria turned up in the financial district and Bay Ridge.

Bacteria that can cause illnesses such as skin infections and urinary-tract infections were common but did not spread sickness. Out of 1,000 samples from all 466 open subway stations, they identified around 15,000 different species.

Researchers say these bacteria are normal in the city and not dangerous. Dr. Mason advises people to wash their hands regularly and live a healthy lifestyle. He feels more confident riding the subway now.

The study also found that busy stations like Grand Central had more types of bacteria compared to less used stations, such as those in Staten Island. Marine bacteria were present at South Ferry after Hurricane Sandy but included species usually found in Antarctica and fish.

Future studies will look into other cities like Paris, São Paolo, and Shanghai to see how the subway microbiome changes with seasons. This research can help health officials prevent and track diseases better.

Nelson Mandela, a key figure in Africa's fight for freedom and admired worldwide, died at age 95. He passed away at home in Johannesburg with his family present after battling health issues that kept him from public life.

South African President Jacob Zuma announced the news on TV, saying Mandela "departed" around 8:50 PM local time and was at peace. Zuma stated that South Africa lost its greatest leader, adding that people saw in Mandela what they hoped to be themselves.

Zuma said there would be a state funeral for Mandela and ordered flags to fly at half-mast. Archbishop Desmond Tutu led a memorial service in Cape Town, urging the country to become like Mandela.

US President Barack Obama called Mandela "Madiba" and praised his dedication to freedom for others over personal gain. UK Prime Minister David Cameron called him a hero of our time.

FW de Klerk, who freed Mandela and shared a Nobel Peace Prize with him, mourned the loss. Mandela was born as Rolihlahla Dalibhunga in 1918 but got his English name Nelson from his school teacher.

Mandela joined the African National Congress (ANC) youth league in 1943. He started South Africa's first black law firm with Oliver Tambo in 1952. After the Sharpeville massacre, he launched an armed struggle against apartheid and was jailed for life in 1964.

In 1990, Mandela was freed amid global joy. He became South Africa’s first black president in 1994 but left office after one term. Mandela married three times with six children, 17 grandchildren, and 14 great-grandchildren. His 91st birthday marked the first "Mandela Day."

His legacy of forgiveness and reconciliation remains a model for humanity worldwide.

In Brazil, more than 100,000 people protested against police violence, poor public services, and high costs for the World Cup. Demonstrations in major cities like Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Brasilia, Belem, Belo Horizonte, and Salvador began peacefully but later turned violent with clashes between protesters and police. The protests started after smaller ones over bus fare increases led to harsh police responses including rubber bullets, tear gas, and beatings.

The demonstrations happened as the Confederations Cup, a test event for the World Cup, was starting. People were upset about high costs, poor public services, expensive sporting events, bad healthcare, inequality, and corruption. In Rio, while most protests were peaceful, some protesters clashed with police, overturned cars, set fires, and painted walls with messages like "Revolution" and "Hate police."

Protesters had different reasons for being there. Oscar José Santos was angry at the government for not helping people. Nadia al Husin, an unemployed architect, wanted better education from the government.

In Brasilia, protesters broke through police lines to enter the national congress building. In Belo Horizonte and Porto Alegre, protests near football stadiums led to violence. Curitiba had a protest where people tried to get into the governor’s office.

Social media played an important role in organizing these demonstrations. Most protesters were young and it was their first big rally. The protests are called the "vinegar revolution" due to vinegar used against tear gas, or the "20-cent revolution" because of bus fare increases.

The president, Dilma Rousseff, said peaceful protests were okay for a democracy but faced booing at the Confederations Cup opening ceremony. With economic problems and rising social unrest, she faces political challenges ahead of the 2014 World Cup and presidential election.

Amsterdam appears liberal to tourists because the Labour Mayor recently said that marijuana-selling coffee shops will stay open even though there is a new national law about drug tourism. But Amsterdam might lose its tolerant image due to plans to send difficult neighbors to "scum villages" made from shipping containers.

The Mayor, Eberhard van der Laan, says his controversial £810,000 plan is to protect people from abuse and homophobia. The plan is to house antisocial tenants in camps for three to six months. These camps have been called “scum villages” because they are similar to what Geert Wilders, a far-right politician, suggested last year.

Bartho Boer, who speaks for the Mayor, says these plans do not go against liberal values. "We want everyone to be who they are," he says. The camps will house people who are violent and scare others repeatedly. They won't be for small problems like neighbors playing loud music on Saturday night but for serious situations where someone is being hurt or scared often.

People found guilty of causing extreme trouble will be moved out and put into basic homes, including shipping containers in industrial areas. Boer says they call these "living containers." These units have showers and kitchens and were used as student housing before. Putting them there means they won't get better homes for their bad behavior.

In the 19th century, troublemakers were sent to villages that became slums quickly. But Boer says this plan is different and will not put antisocial people together in one area. It would be more correct to call them "scum houses" than “villages” because no more than one family will live in the same area at a time.

After up to six months, these tenants will find permanent homes. The city government expects around ten families per year to enter this program starting in 2013. These temporary dwellings will be closely watched by police but also provide access to doctors, social workers, and parole officers. "We take care of them so they don’t repeat the same problems when they move into a new home," Boer says.

Male bosses in the UK get bonuses that are twice as big as those given to women doing the same job. Over a lifetime, this means men earn an extra £141,500 more than women in bonuses. In 2012, male managers earned average bonuses of £6,442 compared with £3,029 for female managers according to the Chartered Management Institute (CMI). At senior levels, female directors received £36,270 in bonuses over the past year, while male directors got £63,700.

The CMI's chief executive, Ann Francke, said it is time to address this issue in business management by promoting flexibility and fairness. Dr Ruth Sealy from Cranfield School of Management suggests making bonus payments more transparent.

While some data might be affected by women working in roles where bonuses are less common, the overall pay gap between men and women continues, with full-time male employees earning 10% more than women according to the government. Maria Miller, Minister for Women and Equalities, noted that although progress is being made, more needs to be done.

The UK government has taken steps like banning pay secrecy clauses and encouraging companies through schemes such as Think, Act, Report to improve how they recruit, promote, and pay women. Companies like Tesco and BT have joined this scheme.

However, the CMI data shows that men’s earnings are rising faster than women's for the first time in five years. Male managers' total earnings increased by 3.2%, compared with 2.8% for female managers when bonuses and salaries are combined. At senior levels, male directors saw their earnings rise by 5.3% over the last year, while female directors only saw a 1.1% increase.

Maria is sitting in a black plastic chair at a community center on a cold Tuesday afternoon. She is number 34 and waiting for her turn to get food. When it’s her turn, Maria gets a brown paper bag with essentials like pasta, eggs, and cornflakes. She also chooses between butternut squash or carrots as this week's vegetables.

Maria is the 34th person so far at East Hampton Food Pantry today. By the end of the day, over 400 families are expected to get food from the pantry to help them through the winter in Long Island.

The Hamptons are famous for being a place where rich and famous people spend their summers. But after Labor Day, when these wealthy people leave, many immigrants who live there year-round face tough times because there is no work during the winter. Maria works 14-hour days cleaning mansions during summer but has no work in winter.

Maria shares that many friends can't afford heating or medicine and rely on food pantries like East Hampton Food Pantry to eat. Vicki Littman, who runs the pantry, says they gave out more than 31,000 food bags in 2015. She explains that after Labor Day, their numbers rise to about 400 families a week because there is no work.

Larry Cantwell, East Hampton’s town supervisor, notes that housing costs are very high. Many homes are empty during winter as they belong to wealthy summer visitors only. This makes life hard for working and middle-class families who can’t afford the prices. He mentions teachers, police officers, and young professionals struggle to find affordable places.

Eddie Vallone is 22 years old and homeless in East Hampton. Churches take turns each night to house about 50 homeless people during winter. Eddie works cleaning pools and doing odd jobs but finds it hard because there’s no work from November until May or June the next year.

Robert Mysłajek finds wolf droppings between two paw prints on a muddy mountain track in Poland. He is excited because seeing wolf droppings means wolves are around, even though they are hard to spot.

There are now about 1,500 wolves in Poland, double the number from 15 years ago. Along with brown bears, lynx, and wolverines, wolves are one of Europe’s largest wild meat-eating animals. People from other countries like Britain, Germany, and the Netherlands come to learn how Poland protects these important animals.

From the wolf droppings, Mysłajek can tell that the wolf ate red deer. In his lab, he can find out more about the wolf's diet, gender, age, health, and family by studying the droppings. DNA tests show that Polish wolves travel long distances; one even went to the Netherlands but was hit by a car.

A student named Alex Entwisle asks if wolves could be brought back to Scotland. Students on a field trip in Poland discuss whether reintroducing wolves would help balance nature there, where they haven’t been since the 1700s.

Mysłajek says that while Scotland has lots of deer like Poland, it also has more sheep and roads. In Poland, he advises farmers to use electric fences, red bunting, and Tatra Mountain Sheepdogs to keep wolves away from their livestock.

Wolves help control the number of herbivores which allows trees and plants to grow better. The Polish government pays farmers if wolves kill their animals.

Poland built many bridges for wildlife after joining the European Union in 2004. This has helped wolves move around safely. However, hunting still happens in neighboring countries like Russia and Slovakia, so wolf populations can face danger there.

The new Polish government elected in October 2015 might not support protecting wolves as much as before because some politicians are hunters themselves.

Alex Entwisle thinks it’s unlikely that Scotland could have a successful wolf population due to its roads, sheep farming, and past industrial changes. He believes people in Britain prefer seeing predators on TV rather than having them nearby.

There are better things than walking along Copacabana beach in Rio while heading to watch a World Cup game. Anthony McDowell from Liverpool, an England fan, said, “The place is lovely, and the people are great. There’s a party mood.” The only thing he wished for was that the England team would play better.

McDowell and his friends joined many other supporters who turned the beachfront into a colorful area full of chants and fun. Some danced, others posed for photos, while most just walked and talked about football before watching games on big screens at FanFest nearby.

Though there were protests, transport issues, and stadium problems leading up to the tournament, visitors decided to enjoy themselves once it started. Brian Hill from Sunderland said planning was hard and costly but added, “Now that we’re here, it’s great.” His trip wasn’t perfect; he traveled over 20 hours and faced delays at the airport. His son had his sunglasses stolen on the beach, and many bars did not have big screens for games.

The tournament has been thrilling with Robin van Persie scoring a spectacular header against Spain. There were more goals in the first eight games than in South Africa in 2010. Latin-American teams won most of their early matches, making the atmosphere on the streets festive.

While there haven’t been major issues like structural problems at stadiums or big entry difficulties since the start, ticketing has still caused trouble with empty seats during some games. FIFA is looking into security lapses, including fireworks set off by Chilean fans in a game against Australia.

There were transport problems in host cities like Natal and Salvador, where traffic became chaotic due to bus strikes and delays. Some protests happened on the opening day but have since become less frequent. Security threats now are mainly petty theft and overexcited supporters blocking roads during spontaneous celebrations.

The World Cup experience varied greatly across different cities. While Manaus had full World Cup fever with decorations everywhere, São Paulo seemed almost unaffected until close to the start of the tournament.

FA chairman Greg Dyke noted a big change in mood: “We've had a warm welcome in Manaus, even though spending on the stadium seems strange given no regular games are played there. In São Paulo, we hardly felt the World Cup before the opening match.”

A girl born today in the UK can expect to live until she is about 82 years old on average, while a boy will usually live to be around 78 years old. In Andorra, they would have longer lives (about 85 for girls and 79 for boys), but in the US, their life expectancy would be slightly lower (around 81 for girls and 76 for boys). If they lived in the Central African Republic, they might not even reach middle age (49 years for girls and 44 for boys). Everywhere else, people are generally living longer now than before. Small children today have a much better chance of survival compared to four decades ago. The number of deaths among under-fives has dropped by nearly 60%, from about 16.4 million in 1970 to around 6.8 million in 2010.

This improvement is due to the work done by the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) in Seattle over five years, with almost 500 researchers involved. Knowing how many children die and why helps the world focus on keeping them alive. This work has shown that there are ways we can better care for people worldwide—like focusing more on diet or tackling alcohol use.

Seven papers published by The Lancet show a big effort to understand global health issues, though some methods are controversial. For example, in places without death registries, IHME used verbal autopsies (interviewing family members) to determine the cause of death. This method led them to say that 1.2 million people die from malaria each year—twice as many as previously thought. African doctors have noticed more adult deaths due to malaria.

Some health experts welcome this research, but some are cautious about accepting these new figures without further evidence. However, the rapid changes in leading causes of death and the rise in disabilities among older people are important findings. People are living longer but not necessarily healthier lives. Common causes of disability include mental health issues like anxiety and depression, arthritis, lower back pain, anaemia, sight and hearing loss, skin disease, and substance abuse. These conditions have not been improving over time.

In addition to this, the average age of people worldwide has increased from 26 years old in 1970 to almost 30 years old by 2010. In places like Brazil, where life expectancy was below 30 in 1970 and nearly 64 in 2010, the change is dramatic. This shift from communicable diseases to "lifestyle" illnesses such as heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and cancer has been especially noticeable in Latin America, the Middle East, south-east Asia, and even parts of southern Asia.

In Rjukan's market square stands a statue of Sam Eyde, who founded the town. Behind him is Gaustatoppen mountain, 1,800 meters high. In front is another steep mountainside. Between these mountains lies the narrow Vestfjord valley where Eyde built his factories and homes for workers in the early 1900s.

Eyde used the Rjukanfossen waterfall, which is 100 meters tall, to make electricity in what was then the world's largest power plant. However, he could not change how the sun shone on Rjukan. For half the year, from late September to mid-March, the town of 3,400 people does not get sunlight.

Recently, three big mirrors were put up high above the town to reflect sunlight into the square. Ingrid Sparbo, a retired secretary who has lived in Rjukan all her life, says it is warming both physically and mentally. Many others agree that this project brings happiness to the town.

Martin Andersen, an artist who moved to Rjukan in 2001, came up with the idea for these mirrors after noticing how hard it was to find sunlight during autumn and winter months. He thought of his child needing to go further down the valley just to feel the sun. This inspired him to create Solspeil or Sun Mirror.

Some people objected at first, worried about costs. Now even those who were against it admit that it feels nice standing in the square when the mirrors reflect sunlight. Rjukan's mayor, Steinar Bergsland, sees benefits from the project beyond just feeling warm; there are more visitors and local businesses have seen an increase in sales. The mirrors also drew a hi-tech company interested in moving to Rjukan.

The project cost 5 million kroner but with government grants and donations, Rjukan only had to pay 1 million kroner out of their annual budget of 650 million kroner. Bergsland says that although there are concerns about maintenance costs, the mirrors give them a chance to get more funding for other needs like schools and nursing care.

Fit in four minutes sounds impossible, but Dr Izumi Tabata's training plan shows it can be done. His plan involves 20 seconds of hard work followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated eight times. People often find it very tough at first, but the results can surprise them.

In the early 1990s, Tabata studied Japan’s speed skating team and found that short bursts of intense exercise worked as well as hours of steady training. He tested this with students by having one group do steady bike rides for an hour five times a week, while another group did four minutes of his intense intervals plus some easy riding.

After six weeks, the Tabata group improved their anaerobic capacity by 28% and their VO2 max (a measure of cardiovascular health) by 15%, even though they only trained for about 90 minutes a week. The steady-training group had less improvement and no change in anaerobic capacity.

Tabata’s plan requires all-out effort, like sprinting as hard as you can for short bursts. If it feels easy, you’re not doing it right. Beginners should have help from trainers to do the exercises correctly.

Soon, there will be new research showing that just two Tabata sessions a week are enough for good health benefits. Another finding is that this plan burns an extra 150 calories in the 12 hours after exercise due to something called excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC). This means it can help you get fit and burn fat.

Tabata has made a deal with Universal Studios to create more resources for trainers and DVDs. Richard Scrivener, a former Strength and Conditioning Coach, says runners and others can use Tabata training as an addition to their regular workouts, which might help reduce the risk of injuries and give joints time to rest.

The plan is tough but effective because it always demands your maximum effort every session.

In 2005, BlackBerry became popular for its instant messaging on mobile phones. At this time, BlackBerry was Canada’s biggest technology export. By 2011, riots happened in London and other cities in the UK. The BlackBerry Messenger (BBM) service helped spread information quickly during these events, leading politicians to ask for it to be shut down.

Two years later, fewer people were buying BlackBerry phones, so BBM was less popular. New apps like WhatsApp and Kik started to replace BBM because they could work on many types of phones and offer more features for free.

To keep users, BBM was made available on Android and Apple phones. More than 20 million people downloaded it, but some experts think this won’t save the service. A blogger named James Gooderson said that other apps like WhatsApp are better because they have features such as video calls and stickers which BBM lacks.

People communicate more visually now with photos and videos on services like Instagram and Snapchat. In 2011, BBM was very influential in events like the Egyptian revolution and the London riots. A young man named Jean-Pierre Moore said that during the riots, people used BBM to know where others were going next before TV news caught up.

A study shows that many young smartphone users use more than one social app regularly. Instagram has become a major network for some teenagers because it feels safer from parents than Facebook. Families with financial difficulties still find BlackBerry attractive due to its low costs, but concerns about privacy have grown after legal cases following the riots.

In better-off areas of London, students now prefer Apple phones and apps like WhatsApp over BBM. One teenager says he feels isolated because he is the only one in his group who uses a Blackberry.

A big argument between countries about drug rules happened because Bolivia wants its indigenous people to chew coca leaves. Coca leaves are used to make cocaine. Bolivia got special permission from an international agreement called the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, which sets global drug policies.

Bolivia said this agreement was against their new constitution that protects coca as part of their culture and says it's not a drug in its natural form.

For centuries, South American Indians have chewed these leaves for energy and health benefits. People who support Bolivia say they are defending the rights of indigenous people.

However, the UN’s International Narcotics Control Board said Bolivia is harming international drug laws. Many countries like the UK, US, Italy, Sweden, Netherlands, and Russia disagree with Bolivia's request.

The UK said while they respect coca leaves' cultural importance in Bolivia, they worry it could increase illegal cocaine production.

In 1964, when Bolivia was under a dictatorship, chewing of coca leaves was banned for indigenous communities. They were given 25 years to stop the practice, but that deadline passed and disagreements continued.

In 2011, Bolivia officially left this agreement and then re-joined with an exception allowing them to chew coca leaves.

This move is new in UN drug laws and worries some countries it might lead others to change rules too. The Russian government thinks it will increase illegal cocaine circulation and sets a dangerous example for other states wanting more relaxed drug control.

The UK's Home Affairs Select Committee suggested supporting Bolivia within the agreement terms. Bolivia’s re-joining can be stopped if at least one-third of 184 countries sign the convention oppose it.

Critics argue against blocking Bolivia, saying these objections aren't legally strong and ignore international rules on cultural rights.

The decision to ban coca chewing was based on a report from 1950 that opponents say wasn’t evidence-based. Growing coca leaves is legal in Bolivia under licenses, which has led to reduced cocaine production, showing promise as a model for other countries.

A few months before he died, Carl Sagan left a hopeful message for future Mars explorers. He said, "Whatever your reason for being on Mars is, I'm glad you're there. And I wish I was with you."

Seventeen years later, in 1996, a company from the Netherlands called Mars One wants to make Carl Sagan’s dream of reaching Mars come true. They plan to send four astronauts to set up a colony on Mars by 2023.

However, there are big problems:
Firstly, the astronauts will have to adapt to gravity that is only 38% of Earth's gravity. This could cause changes in their bone density, muscle strength, and circulation, making it impossible for them to return to Earth.
Secondly, they won’t be coming back because the trip home would require a very powerful rocket and life support systems for up to seven months, which is too costly and difficult.

Despite these issues, 10,000 people have applied to go. The applicants range from ages 18 to at least 62, with more men applying than women.

An applicant named Cynthia, a 32-year-old American woman, remembers asking Carl Sagan as a child if humans would land on Mars in her lifetime. He believed they would and inspired her dream of going to Mars. She sees the Mars One project as an opportunity to realize this childhood dream and be one of the first settlers on Mars.

Mars One looks for qualities like resilience, adaptability, curiosity, trustworthiness, and resourcefulness in applicants. They must also be over 18 years old.

The company says they have a plan based on current technologies and that going to Mars is possible. The website states that water can be extracted from ice in the soil of Mars and that nitrogen for breathing can be found there too. Special solar panels will power the colony, according to their plans.

Mars One has hired Paragon Space Development Corporation to develop life support systems and spacesuits needed for the mission. They expect the project to cost $6 billion. Bas Lansdorp, the founder of Mars One, believes they can raise some money by selling broadcasting rights for the mission.

The goal is to create a permanent colony on Mars. The first team will land in 2023 and more teams will arrive every two years after that.

However, many people doubt if this project can work properly because it’s very hard to get astronauts there and set up a colony with all they need for survival. Gerard’t Hooft, who won the Nobel Prize for physics in 1999 and is an ambassador of Mars One, admits there are health risks due to different types of radiation on Mars.

The mission hopes to inspire people like the Apollo Moon landings did, showing that anything can be achieved. Mars One believes it’s important to create a permanent settlement on Mars to help understand more about our solar system, life origins, and our place in the universe.

At a press conference at Leicester University, archaeologists revealed details about King Richard III's death and treatment after he died. Lead Archaeologist Richard Buckley announced they were sure they had found the remains of the last Plantagenet king, who had scoliosis of the spine. His body was buried in Grey Friars church in a hole that was too small for him.

The team used DNA tests, computer imaging technology, and genealogy to identify the bones. They also examined historical texts about Richard's death and burial.

Philippa Langley from the Richard III Society worked on this project for years despite doubts from others. Now, plans are being made to bury Richard in Leicester Cathedral near where he was found. A visitor center is also planned at an old school building nearby.

Richard died on August 22, 1485, during the Battle of Bosworth, becoming the last English king killed in battle. His skull had a deep cut likely caused by a halberd, a sharp axe blade that went into his brain, causing immediate unconsciousness and death. Another fatal blow to the head was also found.

Many injuries were inflicted after Richard died, showing he was humiliated on the battlefield and while being transported back to Leicester. One injury suggests his naked body was brought back on a horse. This wound probably came from a sharp knife or dagger rather than a weapon used in battle.

Michael Ibsen, a descendant of Richard's sister, heard this news with shock. He emphasized that many died during the battle and deaths were violent at that time.

Mathew Morris found the body during an excavation on the site of Grey Friars church. Initially, he didn’t think it was the king’s body, but further digging showed a twisted spine, suggesting it might be Richard's remains.

Some people believe Richard III was a good leader who suffered from Tudor propaganda, especially from Shakespeare. However, there are still questions about whether he killed two princes in the Tower of London.

Scientists put fake memories in mice brains to understand why people sometimes remember events that never happened. False memories can cause problems in court cases where witnesses’ memories aren't correct.

Susumu Tonegawa and his team from MIT did experiments on mice by changing brain cells using a method called optogenetics. They made certain brain cells react to blue light, which helped create the memory of getting shocked when they were actually not shocked.

In one test, the scientists put the mice in two different rooms. In the second room, the mice got an electric shock and remembered being afraid from their fake memory of the first room. When placed back in the first room, the mice froze because they falsely recalled being shocked there before.

This shows that false memories might work similarly in humans. Tonegawa said that both real and fake memories use similar brain parts, which can make it hard to tell them apart.

Chris French from Goldsmiths, University of London, says this experiment helps understand how memories form in the brain but warns human memories are more complex. Mark Stokes from Oxford University thinks these experiments are impressive but remind us that false memories created like this are not as complicated as real ones.

These studies on mice can help scientists explore questions about memories that were once just philosophical. Steve Ramirez, who works with Tonegawa at MIT, says they can now test how different conditions create false memories and whether fake memories for objects or other things can be made too.

As the technology improves, scientists must think carefully about its ethical use to avoid misuse of these techniques.

Music services like Spotify and Deezer are now earning over $1 billion worldwide. In 2013, streaming and subscription income grew more than 50%, reaching $1.1 billion. This helped European recorded music sales grow for the first time in 12 years.

Around the world, there are about 450 online music services. More people are paying to use these services because they want more choices. From 8 million in a three-year period, the number of paying users went up to 28 million, as reported by IFPI's 2014 digital music report.

People like subscription services because they can try new music easily on smartphones and tablets without buying downloads or CDs. These services are also cheaper, easy to use, and legal compared to pirated downloads.

According to Frances Moore, Chief Executive of IFPI, music streaming is now a major part of the industry. In Britain and America, streaming may soon make more money than downloading from stores like iTunes. Subscription services now account for one-third of all digital sales globally.

In the US, 23% of people use subscription or streaming services in 2014 compared to 19% in 2012. The percentage of downloaders dropped slightly from 28% to 27%. In Britain, the number of subscribers grew from 19% to 22%, while downloader numbers stayed at one-third.

Digital music now makes up 39% of all sales or nearly £5.9 billion out of £15 billion. CD and vinyl sales declined but still contribute more than half of industry income. A drop in Japanese sales led to a global decline of 3.9%.

Vinyl sales are increasing, with a 32% rise in America and a 101% increase in the UK in 2013.

The IFPI reported that One Direction was the top-selling artist of 2013 for their Midnight Memories album. Katy Perry’s Prism was the best-selling album by a female artist, sixth overall behind Eminem, Justin Timberlake, Bruno Mars, and Daft Punk.

Tech companies like Apple with iTunes Radio and Google promoting its Play Store are entering this trend as well as smaller players like Beats Music.

A thick layer of bird droppings is on the golden railing of one of Britain’s most expensive homes, The Towers. This mansion is in a part of north London known as "Billionaires’ Row." Inside, pigeon skeletons are among broken mirrors and water flows through damaged decorations.

Ten mansions along The Bishops Avenue have been mostly empty for about 25 years after being bought by members of the Saudi Arabian royal family. Greek-style columns are breaking apart, and mosaic swimming pools are filled with debris. Nature has taken over so much that owls now live there.

This area is one of Britain's most expensive streets. While house prices in London rise at a rate of 11.2% each year, making it hard for people to buy homes, many mansions on The Bishops Avenue are not being used and have padlocked gates with steel shutters over the windows.

One mansion across the street is worth £18 million but has broken windows and walls covered in paint to stop climbers. Another, sold for £20 million, has metal grilles blocking its windows.

Despite this, property prices keep going up. Dryades, a mansion previously owned by a Pakistani politician, was sold for £12 million in 2007 and is now worth around £30 million. Heath Lodge, where fashion tycoon Aristos Constantinou was murdered with a silver bullet in 1984, is worth about £13 million today after being sold for £400,000 in the late 1970s.

Seeing so many mansions fall apart while people struggle to find homes can be very upsetting. One security guard said it was frustrating to see such a large amount of property not being used.

Royals from Nigeria and Saudi Arabia were among the first to buy houses on this road near Hampstead Heath. After the shah fell in Iran, Iranians also moved here. Now, Chinese people are following Russians and Kazakhs who have spent millions for an address that estate agents say is as famous as the Champs Elysées or Rodeo Drive.

Recently, two mansions were put up for sale at £65 million and £38 million. They promise Italian marble, leather-lined lifts, and luxury panic rooms. However, in the grounds of these empty mansions, stone fountains are falling apart, lawns have become wet bogs, and inside one mansion, water drips through a huge crystal chandelier onto a carpet rotting under collapsed ceilings.

The Towers is the most dramatic example of this decay. The grand mansion has pigeons living in its halls, and algae has turned the walls bright green as water pours through three floors into an empty basement swimming pool. Unopened wooden crates marked "bullet-proof glass" show the security concerns of previous owners.

Today, very few people live on The Bishops Avenue all year round. Magdy Adib Ishak-Hannah, a private healthcare mogul from Egypt with £45 million in personal wealth, said he was among the minority who lived there permanently. He mentioned that it’s not a friendly place where you can chat over fences and that he has never seen his neighbors.

The empty mansions show how rich people see British property as investments rather than homes. For example, more than half of the flats in One Hyde Park are registered with the council as either empty or second homes.

Anil Varma, a local developer, plans to rebuild one of the most valuable sites on The Bishops Avenue into 20 apartments with services like maid service and a spa. He said it would be hard to sell large houses for £30 million to £40 million since locals won’t buy them.

But using these empty properties to solve the housing crisis seems unlikely due to their high value. Andrew Harper, a local Conservative councillor, said that very wealthy people own property there and sometimes live in them while other times they do not.

For Tua Pittman from Raratonga in the Cook Islands, a canoe is more than just transportation. "A canoe is like our island, and its crew members are like our community," says Pittman. He adds that this idea works both ways. “An island can be seen as a big canoe where politicians lead us.”

Pittman’s group recently arrived in Sydney for the World Parks Congress after starting their journey from the Cook Islands on September 25th. They sailed to Samoa, Fiji, Vanuatu, and then to the Gold Coast before heading south to Sydney. About 100 crew members took part, aiming to use only traditional navigation methods but sometimes had to rely on modern equipment.

The expedition is called the Mua Voyage. It’s a project by five Pacific Island countries—Samoa, Tonga, New Zealand, the Cook Islands, and Fiji—and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The 6,000-nautical-mile trip aimed to deliver an important message at the Congress: overfishing, loss of coral reefs, and pollution are harming the ocean.

The message also said that foreign fishing fleets were taking too many resources from their waters. Their goal was to get a higher percentage of the oceans protected in marine sanctuaries. As of 2013, only three percent of the world’s oceans were in marine protected areas, with less than one percent completely off-limits.

Marine scientist Professor Callum Roberts argued that at least 30% of each ocean habitat should be protected. The World Parks Congress delegates agreed to make it a goal to protect more ocean areas effectively by 2030, including strictly protected zones covering at least 30% of marine habitats.

Pittman was happy with this decision. He says he sees environmental problems like harder fishing and increased pollution even in his lifetime. Climate change also affects the Pacific Islands much more than larger nations.

The Mua Voyage took years to plan. Pittman believes leaders need to think like traditional navigators who understand that their vessels are small compared to the vast ocean. Politicians must find a new path to avoid environmental crises impacting island nations.

Dame Sally Davies, the Chief Medical Officer for England, says antibiotic resistance is as big a problem as terrorism. Each year, more people die from bacteria that resist antibiotics than from terrorist attacks. Tuberculosis alone causes over 150,000 deaths annually due to multi-drug resistance.

In the early 20th century, life expectancy in the UK was around 47 years for men and 50 for women, mostly because of high infant mortality rates. Today, a child born in Britain has more than a one in four chance of living to be 100 thanks to public health systems, vaccines, and antibiotics.

Intensive care units use strong antibiotics regularly, which leaves behind hardy bacteria that can resist these drugs. In the late 1990s, doctors learned about MRSA (Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus), a dangerous bacteria resistant to most penicillins. Doctors used special drugs like vancomycin as last lines of defense.

However, antibiotics were overused in both healthcare and agriculture, leading to more antibiotic-resistant bacteria. The pharmaceutical industry isn’t creating new effective antibiotics fast enough. Antibiotics become ineffective quickly due to bacterial resistance. This makes it less attractive for drug companies to develop new ones.

Since the 1940s when antibiotics became common, we started seeing bacteria resistant to them. Initially, these were rare cases but today they are widespread. In the US alone, MRSA infections cause tens of thousands of deaths each year, more than those caused by AIDS. To prevent a return to high mortality rates before antibiotics, changes in antibiotic use and stronger efforts from pharmaceutical companies are needed.

Within my career, antibiotic resistance has changed from rare cases to an epidemic problem. We must act quickly to avoid the health problems we faced before antibiotics were available.

People from Rwanda and nearby Burundi travel to Butare, a town in southern Rwanda, to visit Inzozi Nziza (Sweet Dreams), the first ice cream shop in central Africa. The flavors available are sweet cream, passion fruit, strawberry, and pineapple, with toppings like fresh fruit, honey, chocolate chips, and granola. Black tea and coffee are also sold there.

Louise Ingabire, who manages Inzozi Nziza, says that "ice cream is important" and helps change lives by introducing something new to Rwandans. The shop has given jobs to people who did not have them before. For example, a 27-year-old woman now makes money and can support her family.

Butare has about 89,600 residents and is located 135 kilometers south of the capital city Kigali. It also houses the National University of Rwanda. Many students go to Inzozi Nziza for ice cream because it's cool and different from what they usually have.

Ice cream ingredients are mostly sourced locally, with milk coming from nearby Nyanza and vanilla beans and cocoa imported. The shop was started by Odile Gakire Katese in 2010 with help from Alexis Miesen and Jennie Dundas of Blue Marble Ice Cream in New York. They set up the business as a cooperative and non-profit, transferring their shares to female employees after they showed good management skills.

Fatuma Ndangiza, deputy chief executive of the Rwanda Governance Board, says that Inzozi Nziza is an example of how women are taking on new roles in business. It's not part of Rwandan culture to eat ice cream, but Ndangiza believes it’s interesting to introduce and make this product.

Inzozi Nziza employs nine women who also practice drumming with Ingoma Nshya, Rwanda’s first female drumming troupe founded by Katese ten years ago. Some of these women are survivors of the 1994 genocide that killed almost a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

The story of Inzozi Nziza is featured in a documentary called "Sweet Dreams" made by Rob and Lisa Fruchtman, which shows how these women have built new lives after the genocide. The film has been shown in over a dozen countries and will premiere in Rwanda in 2014.

More than one-third of all women around the world—35.6%—will face physical or sexual violence during their lifetimes, usually from a male partner, according to a new report by the World Health Organization (WHO). The study also shows that 30% of women are attacked by partners and 38% of murders of women are done by intimate partners.

Dr. Margaret Chan, the director general of WHO, said, “The findings show that violence against women is a global health problem affecting millions.” She added that healthcare systems must do more to help these women.

In Africa, nearly half (45.6%) of all women will suffer physical or sexual violence. In low- and middle-income parts of Europe, 27.2% of women face this issue, while in wealthier countries, about a third (32.7%) experience violence at some point in their lives.

The report highlights that 42% of these women get hurt and may visit healthcare staff because of injuries. These visits are often the first chance for health workers to notice abuse and offer help. The effects on women’s health include broken bones, pregnancy problems, and mental illness.

Dr. Claudia Garcia-Moreno from WHO and Professor Charlotte Watts from London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine led this research. They found that violence impacts women's health by causing HIV, depression, alcohol use, unwanted pregnancies, and low-birthweight babies.

Even in high-income countries, 23.2% of women will face physical or sexual violence from a partner. The global rate for attacks by partners is 30%.

In wealthy nations, more reports of sexual assault by acquaintances or strangers are seen—12.6% compared to 11.9% in Africa.

Better-educated and employed women are less likely to suffer violence, but not everywhere. Changing social norms around the acceptability of violence against women is needed, according to Watts.

The WHO suggests training healthcare workers to recognize signs of domestic violence or sexual assault but does not recommend asking every woman if she has faced abuse. Instead, they advise being alert when treating a patient repeatedly for unexplained injuries and considering domestic violence as a possible cause.

The sale of a famous Banksy artwork called "Slave Labour" was stopped right before it happened at an auction in Florida. This artwork, which shows a child making Union Jack bunting and comments on social issues from last year's diamond jubilee, was expected to sell for about $700,000.

The owner of the art house, Frederic Thut, did not reveal the seller or how the piece came to be listed. He announced that "Slave Labour" and another Banksy artwork were withdrawn from the auction but gave no reason why.

Alan Strickland, a Haringey councillor in London where the mural originally was, expressed happiness about the withdrawal. One of his demands was that it not sell, and he is now halfway to getting it back for the community.

Claire Kober, who leads Haringey Council, tried to stop the sale by writing to Arts Council England and the Miami Mayor. The FBI did not confirm if they were investigating.

Thut said earlier in the week that the seller was a "well known collector" with legal rights to sell the piece despite accusations of dealing in stolen property. He also claimed that many emails and calls from the UK had been abusive but insisted he supported including the Banksy pieces for their preservation value.

The second Banksy artwork, "Wet Dog," removed from a wall in Bethlehem and estimated at $800,000, was withdrawn from online listings before the auction. However, "Slave Labour" remained listed until the 3 pm start time.

Thut insisted he would not disclose the seller's identity or control over the artwork after selling it.

The Poundland shop whose wall the piece came from and the building owners have not commented on who took the artwork. Banksy himself has not said anything about this, but he has spoken against others trying to sell his work before.

At Liverpool’s Anglican Cathedral, families of the 96 people who needlessly died at Sheffield Wednesday's Hillsborough football ground focused on one word: "the truth." This phrase was famously misused by The Sun newspaper to shift blame from South Yorkshire Police onto innocent victims.

Margaret Aspinall, whose son James (18) died during an FA Cup match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest, said it took 23 years to get the truth. She expressed delight at Prime Minister David Cameron's clear apology for Hillsborough's failures.

The Hillsborough Independent Panel examined 450,000 documents and produced a 395-page report that found official mistakes and supported the victims and football fans. The police tried to blame drunkenness or ticketless supporters for the disaster instead of accepting their own failings.

Professor Phil Scraton led the panel's research, finding no evidence of exceptional drunkenness, violence, or ticketlessness among Liverpool fans. Just four days after the tragedy, Chief Constable Peter Wright met with officers in a restaurant to create a strong defense story. The police also changed junior officers' statements to remove criticism and highlight fan misbehavior.

The panel found that 116 out of 164 statements were altered to remove or change comments unfavorable to the South Yorkshire Police. These changes aimed to remove any criticism of the police. Despite these efforts, the original inquiry ruled in August 1989 that claims about drunken fans were false and criticized the police.

The report also showed Hillsborough football ground was unsafe and not checked for safety by the Football Association before hosting the match. The main cause of the disaster was the mismanagement of crowds by inexperienced Chief Superintendent David Duckenfield, who opened a gate to let more people in when there was already overcrowding.

Inquest procedures excluded evidence from after 3:15 PM on the day of the tragedy and found that 41 out of 96 victims might have been saved if emergency services had acted properly. The Attorney General will decide whether to apply for a new inquest, potentially leading to prosecutions against Sheffield Wednesday, South Yorkshire Police, and Sheffield City Council.

Trevor Hicks, President of the Hillsborough Family Support Group, whose daughters Sarah and Victoria died, stated, "The truth is out today. Tomorrow is for justice."

Independent data shows Facebook has lost millions of users monthly in big markets like the US and UK as people look for new social networks. In the first three months of this year, analysts think Facebook's income will be up 36% from last year. However, studies also show that growth in places like the US and UK might have reached its peak.

According to Socialbakers, a firm that analyzes such data:
- In the past month, Facebook lost about 6 million users in the US, which is a 4% drop.
- The UK had 1.4 million fewer users in March, a fall of 4.5%.

Over six months, Facebook has seen nearly 9 million monthly visitors leave in the US and about 2 million in the UK.

The trend is similar in other countries with large followings such as Canada, Spain, France, Germany, and Japan. A Facebook spokesperson did not comment on this information.

Ian Maude from Enders Analysis notes that most people who want to sign up for Facebook have already done so. People like trying new things which makes the situation somewhat risky, even if it’s not very likely to be severe. Instagram, a photo-sharing site with 30 million users within 18 months before being bought by Facebook, is popular among younger groups.

Path, another social network created for mobile phones and limited to 150 friends per user, has grown rapidly, gaining 1 million new users weekly and reaching more than 9 million in total. In one weekend, the app was downloaded 500,000 times in Venezuela alone.

In South America, particularly Brazil, Facebook’s growth continues; monthly visitors increased by 6% to reach 70 million. India has also seen a rise of 4%, reaching 64 million users but still only a small part of the population, leaving room for more growth.

However, in developed markets, other trackers are showing declines too. Jefferies bank analysts have an algorithm that talks directly with Facebook software and suggests user levels might be lower than before. Global numbers peaked at about 1.05 billion monthly users in January but fell by 20 million in February. By April, the numbers rose again.

Nielsen reported a loss of nearly 2 million visitors since December, totaling around 27 million users in the UK, which is similar to last year’s count.

Americans are spending fewer minutes on Facebook too; it dropped from 121 billion minutes in December 2012 to 115 billion in February. This trend partly reflects a move away from personal computers toward smartphones and tablets for accessing social media sites like Facebook. While smartphone usage has doubled, this may not completely offset declining desktop use.

Facebook's upcoming report will update investors on its financial performance for the quarter. Analysts predict revenues of around $1.44 billion compared to $1.06 billion in 2012. Investors are eager to learn how fast Facebook’s mobile user base is growing and whether advertising income is keeping up with this growth.

At the end of last year, nearly a quarter of Facebook's ad revenue came from its 680 million monthly mobile users. In recent filings, the company warned it might be losing younger users to other similar services. To appeal more to smartphone users, founder Mark Zuckerberg has introduced new initiatives such as Facebook Home, an app that can be installed on certain Android phones to show news and photos directly on the phone’s home screen even when locked.

Vienna is the best city to live in, while Baghdad is the worst. London, Paris, and New York are not even in the top 35 cities for quality of life according to a study by Mercer. German-speaking cities like Zurich, Munich, Düsseldorf, and Frankfurt also rank very high.

Paris dropped ten places to number 37 because it's more at risk from terrorist attacks. London is ranked 39th.

The study looks at conditions such as health, education, housing, and the environment. Companies use this information to decide where to set up and how much they should pay their workers.

Vienna has high-quality social housing which makes living there affordable compared to other big cities. For example, a large apartment in Vienna costs around €800 per month, while an equivalent one in London would cost over £2,000.

US cities have lower rankings because of personal safety issues and crime. San Francisco is the highest-ranked US city at number 28.

Vienna has grown as a hub for companies since the fall of the Berlin Wall. It's now considered central to doing business in Central Europe.

Austria ranks high globally for GDP per person, just behind the US and ahead of Germany and Britain.

Vienna has become more popular for tourists from the UK due to an increase in budget flights. In 2015, there were 588,000 British visitors to Vienna, up by 18% compared to the previous year.

London is not in the top ten quality-of-life rankings due to air pollution, traffic congestion, and weather issues. Edinburgh comes next for Britain at number 46.

Paris has dropped because of recent terrorist attacks. Auckland, New Zealand ranks third as the highest English-speaking city in the study. Vancouver is fifth.

Cities with the lowest rankings are affected by war and political unrest. Damascus ranks better than Baghdad or several other cities like Bangui and Sana’a.

The Moroccan city of Ouarzazate is well-known for big film productions like "Lawrence of Arabia" and "Game of Thrones." Now, it’s home to another major project – four linked solar power plants. By 2020, these plants will help Morocco get nearly half its electricity from renewable sources. The first part, Noor 1, opened in November 2015.

The plants use special mirror technology that can produce power even after dark. Each plant has 500,000 mirrors spread over an area as big as the city of Rabat. All four will create enough electricity to power a million homes. Morocco’s Environment Minister Hakima el-Haite hopes solar energy will boost the country's economy like oil did for others.

Morocco spends a lot on imported fossil fuels. By using its deserts, it plans to make more renewable energy and reduce costs. By 2020, one-third of their renewable power will come from solar sources; wind and hydro will provide the rest.

The mirrors are shaped like crescents and focus sunlight onto pipes that heat a special oil solution. This heats water to create steam for generating electricity. The plants can store heat energy in molten sands for up to three hours, allowing them to work at night too.

Future plans include exporting solar power to Europe and nearby countries like Tunisia, though this will require new transmission lines. Morocco’s investments of around $9 billion into the Noor Complex are supported by international banks and local government guarantees. Subsidies from King Mohammed VI ensure that costs don’t get passed on to consumers.

The project employs over a thousand workers who put in long shifts under safety gear. The site is ready for operation, with everyone hoping it will be a big success.

Swedish prisons are known for being progressive. In November 2013, the head of Sweden’s prison service, Nils Oberg, said four Swedish prisons would close because there were fewer prisoners than before. This drop happened even though crime rates did not fall. Between 2011 and 2012, the number of prisoners in Sweden dropped by 6%, now totaling a little over 4,500.

Kenneth Gustafsson, who runs Kumla Prison, one of Sweden's most secure jails, said when he started as a prison officer in 1978, prisons focused on treating people humanely. But after some high-profile escapes in 2004, they had to focus more on security.

Sweden still uses a humane approach even for serious crimes. Prison terms are rarely over ten years and those with life sentences can apply to change their sentence to between 18 to 25 years after ten years. They also use electronic tagging of criminals and prefer community-based measures instead of short-term prison sentences as these have proven more effective at stopping people from reoffending.

The reoffending rate in Sweden over three years is between 30 and 40%, which is much lower than the UK. One reason might be that children under 15 cannot go to jail, unlike some other countries where younger children can. This means fewer young people end up in adult prisons.

A big reason for the drop in prison numbers could be the support given to prisoners after they leave jail. A probation service works with those on probation and offers treatment programs for drug, alcohol, or violence issues. Around 4,500 volunteers also help by befriending and supporting former offenders.

In Sweden’s prisons, Gustafsson says their goal is to focus on rehabilitation without being overly optimistic. They believe most prisoners want to change but recognize some will not be able to. When people leave prison, they need housing and jobs to reintegrate into society successfully.

Peter Soderlund, who served almost three years of a four-year sentence before getting out in 1998, now runs an organization called X-Cons Sweden that helps former prisoners reintegrate by providing accommodation and support networks.

The workday at the office is done. The big tasks are finished; the rest can wait until tomorrow. Most workers would want to leave.

However, many Japanese employees fear leaving early will make them look disloyal. 

For years, companies in Japan have pushed their workers very hard. Now, the government wants to change this and is thinking about making it a law for workers to take at least five days of paid vacation each year.

Japanese workers get an average of 18.5 days off with pay per year, but most only use nine days. In Britain, taking two weeks off in summer is common, while in Japan, even four nights away is seen as too much.

To improve performance, some companies now encourage short naps during work hours. The government hopes that by the end of this decade, Japanese workers will start using more vacation time like British and French workers do — about 20 to 25 days a year.

Japan's tough work culture helped it become an economic power but also led to low birth rates and health issues, including karoshi (death from overwork). About 22% of Japanese employees work more than 49 hours per week. 

Erika Sekiguchi, a 36-year-old worker at a trading company, only used eight days of her 20-day vacation in 2014. She fears taking time off will make others think she is not dedicated.

A health ministry official named Yuu Wakebe works overtime and says the pressure to match colleagues’ hours causes stress. He warns that being scared of what others think can lead to serious health problems, including suicide. Official data shows about 200 people in Japan die each year from karoshi caused by hard work schedules.

Prime Minister Shinzo Abe has spoken against unreasonable demands on workers and said the culture falsely praises long hours.

David Mitchell, an author known for his novels that often get lots of attention from critics, recently finished writing a book that won’t be seen by anyone until 2114. This is part of a project called the Future Library, created by Scottish artist Katie Paterson.

In 2014, 1,000 trees were planted in Oslo’s Nordmarka forest for this project. Every year for the next 100 years, an author will write a piece that won’t be read until these trees are used to make paper in 2114. Margaret Atwood was the first author who handed over her text called "Scribbler Moon" in 2015.

Each writer goes to a special spot high above Oslo and gives their work in a short ceremony. Mitchell says this project gives hope that our civilization can last another hundred years, even though many things seem very bad now.

Writing the book was different for Mitchell because he wouldn't be around when it's read. He felt less pressure about what others would think of his writing. Usually, he polishes his work a lot, but for this project, he had to finish quickly and couldn’t polish all parts of it.

The theme of the Future Library is imagination and time, which writers can explore in many ways. Mitchell only revealed the name of his manuscript, "From Me Flows What You Call Time," during a ceremony near the planted trees.

During the ceremony, Mitchell read a short story and a poem by William Wordsworth to children and adults under an umbrella because it was raining. The forest area with blueberry bushes will be cared for until 2114 when it is used to print all the texts.

After Mitchell handed over his manuscript in Norway, it was sealed and kept in a special room at Oslo’s new public library which opened in 2019. He says now that he has given away his book, it feels as if he dropped a coin into a river—it's gone from him forever.

An octopus named Inky escaped from the National Aquarium in New Zealand. It climbed out of its tank when the lid was not closed properly and went down a 50-meter drainpipe to the sea.

Inky, a common New Zealand octopus, left during the night when no one was around. He likely moved across the aquarium floor for three or four meters before entering the drainpipe that led to the ocean in Hawke’s Bay on New Zealand's North Island.

Rob Yarrell, who manages the National Aquarium, said octopuses often try to escape because they are curious animals. Inky probably wanted to explore outside the aquarium.

Yarrell and his staff were sad when they found out Inky was gone but did not search for him. They believe no one took Inky from the aquarium since security is very tight there.

Octopuses can fit into tiny spaces due to having no bones, and are also known to be intelligent creatures capable of using tools. One octopus at another center even opened a jar faster than any other octopus before it.

Inky was brought to the National Aquarium by a local fisherman who found him caught in a fishing pot. Inky had some scars and shortened limbs from fighting with other sea animals, but he was friendly and popular among visitors. He is about the size of a rugby ball.

The aquarium will not increase security because they believe Inky’s escape was unusual. If another octopus is found by fishermen, however, the aquarium might take it in. Yarrell hopes that one day Inky might return to them.

Why do referees do their job? Recently, there has been more criticism of referees in football matches. But many referees still support each other and work hard despite the challenges. Referees travel a lot to enforce rules that can upset some people and they hope for recognition like handshakes from players after a game.

Lee Swabey is an example of a referee who loves his job and gets satisfaction when he completes a match smoothly. He was watched by important officials during one of his matches because he has potential to advance in the profession. John Brooks, another referee with ambitions to progress, also had officials watching him, but they saw him make the tough decision to cancel a match due to frozen conditions.

Both Swabey and Brooks face situations where they need strong mental resilience. Brooks admits that when referees are criticized on TV, it can be hard, especially if he made an incorrect call himself once before. He emphasizes the importance of not stopping after making decisions but staying focused throughout the game.

Brooks has support from a coach and a sports psychologist to help him develop mentally and physically for his demanding role. In contrast, when former referees like Mike Riley started, they had fewer resources, such as books on psychology and nutrition that they had to buy themselves.

Modern technology is seen positively by these professionals since it can reduce mistakes which might affect them throughout their career.

There are cameras watching you in stores. They can tell if you try to put something in your bag without paying. Now, new technology helps stores learn more about shoppers, like their age and size. 

A report from Computer Sciences Corporation (CSC) says that around 30% of stores use facial recognition to watch customers. Facial recognition uses cameras like Intel RealSense to find out who you are by looking at your face and comparing it with a database.

Joe Jensen from Intel says the goal is not to make databases about specific people but to understand general shopping habits. For example, if a store knows that someone wearing size-10 shoes and a gold necklace usually buys socks when they walk quickly towards the sock aisle, the store can show them ads for socks.

This is like what happens online. When you look at something on Amazon, you see more ads about it later. But using cameras in stores makes people uncomfortable because they don't feel the same way as with website cookies.

Hoxton Analytics uses machine learning to guess your age and gender by looking at your shoes. They can tell if someone is a man or woman 75% to 80% of the time just from their footwear. The idea is that cameras looking down aren’t as creepy as ones watching faces.

The goal for stores using this technology is to gather information without being too intrusive. By focusing on less sensitive parts like shoes, they hope to keep shoppers comfortable while still tailoring ads and improving sales.

Some people think these practices are invasive even if no personal details are saved. Retailers say it’s about giving a better shopping experience, but others see it as creepy. Younger people may be more open to this technology because they grew up with online services that track them too.

Insects are full of protein, crunchy, and found near rocks. They have been overlooked as food in most places around the world, but now they are becoming more common on plates. In Spring 2013, there will be efforts to make eating insects less gross and put them on menus and supermarket shelves.

In April, a festival called Pestival 2013 will take place in London, where people can eat insects at an event backed by the Wellcome Trust. The Nordic Food Lab, known for its work with ants, will run a two-day restaurant. Noma, named the world’s best restaurant for three years, has chef René Redzepi who says that ants taste like lemon and a mix of fermented grasshoppers and moth larvae tastes similar to fish sauce. Bee larvae are used to make sweet mayonnaise.

In March, a BBC documentary will show Stefan Gates eating deep-fried locusts and barbecued tarantulas. There is an important environmental message behind this trend: many experts believe there is a clear benefit to the environment from people eating insects.

The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has been promoting insect farming in southeast Asia and Africa since 2011, where two billion people already eat insects regularly. In 2012, FAO published a list of 1,909 edible species of insects and plans to hold an international conference on eating insects.

Insects are plentiful worldwide – there are about 40 tons of them for every human – so they are unlikely to run out or be chemically treated. Chef René Redzepi says that eating bugs is taboo in the Western world but common elsewhere, noting that mushrooms often contain worms and honey is bee vomit.

Insects play a key role on Earth with over one million species, yet humans often kill them for no reason.
