By 2050, the global population will reach nine billion, putting more pressure on land, water, forests, fisheries, and biodiversity resources. Meat prices are rising due to rainforest destruction for cattle grazing and feed production. Cows also produce methane, contributing significantly to greenhouse gas emissions.

Eating insects is environmentally friendly: they emit fewer gases, have high-quality protein, vitamins, and amino acids, and need less food than other animals to produce the same amount of protein. They can be grown on organic waste. In China, maggot farms are successful; Zimbabwe has a thriving mapone caterpillar industry; Laos received nearly $500,000 from FAO for insect harvesting projects.

A study suggests swapping pork and beef for crickets and locusts could reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 95%. Eating insects can help the environment and even after we die, they continue to play an important role.

The world's top energy experts say coal might become as big a source of energy as oil within five years, which could be very bad for the environment. One reason coal use is going up is because the United States is using more shale gas.

A new study from the International Energy Agency (IEA) shows that people all over the world are using more coal – even in places trying to cut carbon emissions – except in the US where shale gas has replaced some of the coal. This drop in US coal use has made coal cheaper worldwide, making it more attractive to use.

Maria van der Hoeven from the IEA said: “If we don’t change our policies, coal will catch up with oil within ten years.”

Coal is easy to find and cheap to get out of the ground. In the last ten years, nearly half of new energy needs were met by coal. China and India are expected to drive world coal use in the next five years, with India possibly using more than the US.

The IEA says global coal consumption will grow by 1.2 billion tons a year by 2017, which is as much coal as Russia and the US use now combined. By 2017, people will be using about 4.3 billion tons of oil equivalent in coal compared to 4.4 billion tons for oil.

Coal produces more carbon emissions than any other major fossil fuel, contributing heavily to climate change. Old power stations without special equipment release sulfur and other pollutants that cause acid rain and health problems.

Van der Hoeven said only a high price on carbon or cheaper gas could stop coal use from growing. In the US, lots of shale gas made coal less popular. Europe, China, and others should look at this example.

In Europe, they tried to cut coal use with a special market for buying rights to release carbon dioxide. But now there are too many rights available, making it cheap to keep using coal.

If coal keeps growing like this, the risk of climate change will get worse because coal is one of the worst polluters.

Many people know they don't get enough sleep but could solve it by waking up later. Dr Paul Kelley from Oxford University suggested at a British Science Festival that schools should have different starting times to match the natural body clocks of students. This would help them do better in school and be healthier (sleeping less can cause diabetes, depression, obesity, and weak immune systems).

Kelley wrote in 2014 that children around ten naturally wake up at about 6:30am but by age sixteen this changes to around 8am. By eighteen years old, the natural waking time is even later, at 9am. Traditional school times suit younger kids but not older teenagers. Starting classes at 11am or later could be better for older teens.

Teenagers can't just go to bed earlier because their body clocks are controlled by light, which affects cells in a part of the brain called the suprachiasmatic nuclei. This means waking up early is very hard for them.

Not only students but also workers would benefit from changing work times to fit natural rhythms. Sleep loss varies: between ages 14 and 24, people lose more than two hours each night; for those aged 24 to about 30 or 35, it's around an hour and a half. By age 55, the sleep cycle balances out again.

Kelley believes that the typical workday from nine to five fits older bosses but not younger workers. He suggests different starting times based on age: people in their fifties could start at 8am, those in their thirties at 10am, and teenagers at 11am. This would improve performance, mood, and health.

Later starts could reduce accidents as drivers would be more alert. It might also end rush hour traffic if people worked different times. Kelley says this idea benefits families too because parents wouldn't have to wake up sleepy teens so early.

Dr Kelley, being 67, wakes naturally around 6:30am, like a ten-year-old does. He finds his workday easier now compared to when he was younger.

Standing above New Mexico’s deserts, Felix Baumgartner paused before jumping from a high altitude. It was a small step away from the capsule but a 24-mile drop back to Earth. Mission control wished him luck, and he jumped. 

Ten minutes later, Felix landed safely after reaching speeds of up to 725 miles per hour. He broke three world records: the highest balloon flight, the highest skydive, and becoming the first person to break the sound barrier by skydiving at Mach 1.24. His mother Ava cried with joy.

Felix wore a special suit that protected him from extreme pressure changes during his fall. Without it, he could have faced severe injuries.

He told reporters later: “When I was up there, you feel so humble and small.” He focused on coming back alive but also found the experience humbling.

This mission came after two failed attempts earlier in the week due to weather conditions. Felix rode a giant balloon, as big as 30 million square cubic feet but very thin like a sandwich bag, to reach high altitude. At the bottom was a capsule where he sat.

As he reached his goal height, Felix checked off 40 items on a list with Joe Kittinger, who held the previous record for highest balloon flight. There was concern about fogging on Felix’s visor because its heater wasn’t working well. However, they decided to continue, watched by an online audience of over eight million.

The two-and-a-half-hour journey up where Earth curved and skies turned black was followed by a fast descent captured on three cameras attached to his suit.

The success suggests astronauts might survive high-altitude emergencies by bailing out of their spacecraft. Felix’s team included Dr Jonathan Clark, whose wife Laurel died in the space shuttle Columbia accident in 2003.

Felix has done many daring acts like skydiving from buildings and mountains. He practiced for this jump with two earlier free-falls.

He aimed to break five records: being the first human to break the sound barrier by free-falling, reaching the highest altitude for a free-fall, achieving the longest free-fall time, having the highest manned balloon flight, and using the largest manned balloon ever. The mission was sponsored by Red Bull drinks.

Joe Kittinger, now 84, guided Felix during his ascent. After the jump, Felix said he wanted to inspire others and joked about a young man who wants to break his record. He felt closest to Mike Todd, the life support engineer, who helped him prepare for the suit.

This was Felix’s final big jump. He plans to enjoy his years with his girlfriend Nicole Oetl, flying helicopters on rescue missions in the US and Austria.

On Wednesday, Barack Obama returned to Washington after giving his election victory speech in Chicago. He said he wanted the country to work together with him but faced challenges from Republicans who might not agree with him. This comes at a time when there are big problems about money and spending that need solving.

Unlike 2008, Obama will not have an easy period right after winning the election because of disagreements between his party and the Republican Party. Both John Boehner (the leader of the House) and Harry Reid (a key Democratic leader in the Senate) said they wanted to work together but it might be difficult.

Obama won against Mitt Romney with more than 270 electoral college votes, a requirement for winning the election. He also received more votes from people overall. After his victory speech, which included famous lines about hope and unity, Obama began talks with Boehner about working together on issues such as taxes, spending cuts, and economic growth.

In his second term, Obama plans to work on problems like immigration reform, investing in education, dealing with climate change, and foreign policy issues involving countries like Iran and Israel. However, the economy remains a big challenge. The stock market dropped because people are worried that politicians will not agree on how to solve these problems.

Obama won several key states including Ohio, Virginia, and Colorado, showing Americans wanted him for another term despite economic struggles. He said he wants change but also reminded everyone that America is strong and united as one country.

Sweden is the best country for older people, while Afghanistan is the worst. This comes from a new global study on ageing. Sweden is first, followed by Norway, Germany, the Netherlands, and Canada. Surprisingly, the US ranks eighth and the UK at thirteenth.

This survey shows that being rich does not always mean better conditions for older adults. Sri Lanka ranks higher than Pakistan even though their economic situations are similar. Bolivia and Mauritius also do well despite not having big economies.

According to Mark Gorman from HelpAge International, "The top countries show smart choices were made in the past about pensions, education, and healthcare."

The survey covers 91 countries and includes 89% of older people worldwide. By 2050, there will be two billion people over 60 years old – more than one in five people globally.

In developing countries, the number of older adults is growing fast. Over two-thirds of older people live in poor countries now, and by 2050, this will rise to four out of five. For example, Brazil’s population aged 60+ could double from 7% to 14% in just 21 years.

The fastest ageing countries are Jordan, Laos, Mongolia, Nicaragua, and Vietnam. These countries need to plan for older populations better.

Women generally live longer than men. In 2012, there were 84 men aged 60+ for every 100 women. Older women often have less money saved, less say in family decisions, and are more at risk of violence.

The study also shows that with the right policies, population ageing doesn’t always lead to higher healthcare costs. Bolivia is an example – it’s very poor but offers free health care and universal pensions for older people. Nepal has a small pension program too.

Chile and Costa Rica show that good past investments in basic healthcare have helped their current older populations. Education is also important, as seen with the Philippines where compulsory education helps older people manage pensions.

South Korea ranks surprisingly low because it only recently introduced pensions.

The ageing index uses 13 indicators under four main areas: income security, health care, employment and education, and an enabling environment. Some measures like pension coverage and life expectancy have more weight in the scoring.

Sir Richard Jolly says this new study helps understand older people’s needs better worldwide.

Clay Cockrell works at Columbus Circle near Trump International Hotel and Tower. He leads therapy walks in Central Park for wealthy people.

Cockrell used to work on Wall Street but now helps very rich clients with their issues. He says many of the richest people, like those in the top 1%, feel guilty about being wealthy or need to hide it. They also often feel lonely because not everyone understands them.

Since the financial crisis and movements like Occupy Wall Street, life has become harder for the wealthy. Media coverage makes rich people feel they have to hide their wealth. It's difficult for the rich to talk openly about money without feeling ashamed.

Barbara Nusbaum, a money psychology expert, says it's more acceptable to say you don't have enough money than to admit having lots of it. Rich people tend to hang out with other wealthy individuals because they can understand each other’s problems better.

Oxfam reported that the richest 1% had 44% of global wealth in 2009, and by 2014, this increased to 48%. In the US, the wealthiest 0.1% owned 7% of total wealth in the past but now own 22%.

According to Spectrem Group, as of 2014, there were about 10.1 million households with more than $1 million in assets (not including their main home). In 2007, this number was around 9.2 million.

Cockrell says it's hard for rich people to trust friendships because they are unsure if others care about them or just their money. This has led to wealthier individuals feeling more isolated as the gap between the rich and poor grows wider.

The Gates Foundation worked with Boston College on a study called "The Joys and Dilemmas of Wealth," which found that wealth can create barriers in connecting with people. Many wealthy Americans prefer to keep their riches secret out of fear of negative judgment.

Cockrell advises his clients not to let money define them because other parts of life can still cause problems. He says their issues are real and important, no matter how much they have financially.

Takahito Iguchi thinks Google Glasses are not fashionable. Many people think they look silly or smug when wearing them. Google first gave these glasses to software developers instead of celebrities like Scarlett Johansson, which wasn’t a smart move. As a result, there are pictures that show the glasses looking strange.

Iguchi, who is from Japan, wants to make a better version of Google Glasses. His product is called Telepathy One and it looks more stylish and futuristic. He showed these at a festival in Texas and got $5 million for his business idea.

Telepathy One is simpler than Google Glass. While Google Glass lets you do many things like surfing the internet, sending emails, or taking photos, Iguchi’s glasses focus on sharing visual and audio information with friends and family. You can use them to share your view through Facebook or email, or talk to a friend who appears as a floating image.

Iguchi believes his product will help people understand each other better. He thinks when you see things from someone else's point of view, you'll feel closer to them. His company is small compared to Google but he’s confident it can succeed. The hardware for Telepathy One will be made in Japan, and the software team will work in San Francisco.

Iguchi left Tokyo because he believes Silicon Valley offers more global connections than his home city. He hopes that by sharing stories about people through his product, he can help others learn from different viewpoints around the world.

Google’s vice-president, Vint Cerf, warned that digital information could be lost forever because the software needed to view it will become outdated. He spoke at a meeting in San Jose, California, and said this loss could mean future historians might miss out on important details from our history.

Cerf calls for creating “digital vellum,” which would help preserve old software and hardware so that files can be recovered no matter how old they are. Our emails, tweets, and even websites could disappear if we don't take action soon.

“Bit rot” is the term used to describe when old computer files become useless because the programs needed to open them are outdated or unavailable. Cerf warns that this issue might cause a “forgotten generation.”

To explain bit rot further, in ancient times, people wrote on clay tablets and papyrus scrolls which could be read for centuries. Today, however, our digital documents like PDFs and Word files can only be opened with specific software programs.

This problem already exists. In the 1980s, people saved documents on floppy disks or uploaded games from cassettes to computers like the ZX Spectrum. Even if these disks and cassettes are still in good condition today, the equipment needed to run them is mostly found only in museums now.

Historian Doris Kearns Goodwin wrote a book about Abraham Lincoln using letters she found in libraries. Cerf says that if those were emails today, they would probably be lost in 100 years. He also points out that important documents often gain significance over time and might not be recognized as important until much later.

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University are working on a solution called Olive, which can read defunct files by mimicking the original computer systems. However, getting legal permission to copy and store software before it becomes outdated can be difficult when companies go out of business or stop supporting their products. Cerf suggests that preservation rights might need to be included in laws about copyright, patents, and licensing.

A day started with police raids at a hotel in Zurich and ended with the U.S. charging 16 football officials with corruption, including five from FIFA’s executive committee. Among those charged were Ricardo Teixeira and Marco Polo Del Nero.

The U.S. Department of Justice accused these individuals of fraud and other crimes through kickback schemes detailed in a new 240-page report. This increases the total number of defendants to 27, plus 24 unnamed co-conspirators. The Attorney General, Loretta Lynch, called the betrayal by these officials outrageous.

On this day, when FIFA hoped to introduce reforms during an ongoing corruption crisis, Swiss police arrested Juan Ángel Napout and Alfredo Hawit. Napout is the president of the South American football confederation, and Hawit heads North and Central American and Caribbean football bodies. The Swiss Federal Office of Justice said they were being held pending extradition.

The investigation now includes 11 current or former FIFA executive committee members accused of taking over $200 million in bribes from TV and marketing contracts. Lynch stated that eight individuals, including five unnamed earlier, had pleaded guilty since May.

Lynch warned those still hiding: "You will not escape our focus." She noted the U.S. Department of Justice's commitment to end corruption within international football leadership due to its impact on principles.

Issa Hayatou, acting FIFA President, refused to comment on the arrests but insisted that neither he nor FIFA is corrupt. He claimed only a few individuals showed negative behavior and did not generalize the situation.

How long can you hold your breath? I tried it myself. The first 30 seconds were easy. By 45 seconds, I wanted to stop but pushed through. As the second hand passed one minute, my heart was pounding. I let out a tiny bit of air and felt better for a moment. Finally, after one minute and twelve seconds, I gave up and took a huge breath.

Holding your breath is important in some sports like freediving. In 2006, while making a BBC show called "Don't Die Young," I met Sam Amps from the UK freedive team. She taught me how to hold my breath longer underwater. By the end of our session, I held my breath for 90 seconds, enough to swim one width in a pool. Sam could easily swim three widths and hold her breath for five minutes.

Sam said she breathed slowly before each dive and took a deep breath before diving. She also trained herself to resist breathing longer than most people do.

Some say humans have the ability to lower their heart rate and metabolic rate to hold their breath longer because of an ancient aquatic phase in human evolution, but this idea is not scientifically proven.

Voluntarily holding your breath isn’t unique to humans or non-aquatic mammals. Experiments show that on land, heart rates don't drop during breath-holding, though they do slow down when submerged in cold water. This slower heart rate applies to many air-breathing animals and doesn't prove an aquatic phase of human evolution.

Holding your breath is now useful in medicine for breast cancer radiotherapy. Normally, radiation treatment takes several minutes but requires the patient to hold their breath between bursts because moving can cause the radiation to miss its target. Doctors at University Hospital Birmingham found that patients can hold their breath for five and a half minutes by breathing oxygen-rich air before holding their breath.

The trick is not about fooling the body’s sensors of low oxygen or high carbon dioxide levels but in delaying diaphragm fatigue. The diaphragm, which helps you breathe, contracts when you inhale and holds this position during breath-holding. By raising oxygen levels and lowering carbon dioxide levels before holding your breath, doctors can delay the point at which the diaphragm gets tired.

Eventually, though, even if you fool it for a while, the diaphragm sends strong signals that force you to breathe again.

On Tuesday, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge won a round in their fight to protect their privacy when a French magazine was told it couldn't sell or use photos taken at their private chateau in Provence. However, this isn’t over; French officials still need to decide if they will start criminal charges against the magazine editor and photographer.

The Tribunal de Grande Instance in Paris ordered the gossip magazine Closer to hand over all digital files of the pictures within 24 hours and stop sharing them online or on their app. The ruling only affects Mondadori Magazines France, which publishes Closer. They must pay €2,000 for legal costs, and a fine of €10,000 per day if they don’t follow the order.

The judge said these photos were intrusive because the couple was sunbathing partially naked in their private area, far from any public road. The magazine might face an additional €10,000 fine for every photo published after this ruling by Mondadori, owned by former Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi.

The Duke and Duchess welcomed the judge’s decision. A lawyer for them said it was “a wonderful decision.” However, they still want a criminal case against those responsible for taking and publishing the photos, including the editor of Closer.

French law says that breaking privacy rules can lead to one year in jail and a fine of €45,000. The couple hopes this action will stop paparazzi from intruding on their private life in the future.

The magazine's editor said it was not fair to respond so strongly to publishing these photos. However, copies of Closer were selling for high prices on eBay until they were removed after complaints.

Galina Zaglumyonova woke up in her apartment in Chelyabinsk due to a big explosion. The explosion broke her balcony windows and her houseplants’ pots. She saw a large trail of smoke in the sky and heard car alarms from below. “I didn’t know what was happening,” she said, “There were explosions one after another. I thought it was an airplane crash.”

In fact, she had seen a ten-ton meteorite hitting Earth with fireballs just as the sun rose. About 1,200 people got hurt, and over 40 needed hospital care due to flying glass from the sonic boom made by the falling meteorite. No one died.

The meteorite entered Earth’s atmosphere at least at 33,000 miles per hour and split into pieces between 18 and 32 miles above ground, according to Russian scientists.

This event caused fear in Chelyabinsk, a city of over a million people south of Russia's Ural mountains. Cell networks were overloaded with calls. Videos showed the meteorite glowing brighter as it neared Earth. The trail was visible for hundreds of miles and even in Kazakhstan.

Tatyana Bets, at work in a hospital clinic’s reception area, noticed a bright light and smoke in the sky before hearing explosions. At least three craters were found by officials, with one over six meters wide and another meteorite fragment going through an icy lake. Radiation levels at impact areas were normal according to military checks.

Schools and universities closed in Chelyabinsk, and many other workers went home early. Around 200 children got hurt. The clinic where Bets worked saw many people with cuts from glass. A student dormitory was badly affected; several frightened students were treated there. 

More than 100,000 square meters of glass broke and 3,000 buildings were damaged. The total cost of damage in the city might exceed one billion roubles (£20 million).

The meteorite arrived less than a day before asteroid 2012 DA14 was expected to fly by Earth at about 17,510 miles away. Experts said these two events weren't connected.

Afterwards, rumors spread. Some Russian media suggested local air defense units blew up the meteorite above 15 miles in altitude. Vladimir Zhirinovsky, a political leader, said it was not a meteor but an American test weapon.

Some people quickly tried to sell parts of the meteorite online after the event. President Putin and Prime Minister Medvedev were told about this incident. Rogozin, another official, suggested creating an international warning system for space objects and noted neither the US nor Russia could stop such objects.

Glastonbury Festival plans to reduce plastic water bottle use to become more environmentally friendly. Each year at this event in Somerset, around one million plastic bottles are used on a site covering 900 acres.

To help, organizers will give stainless-steel reusable bottles to 2,000 road crew and band members. They also plan to sell thousands of these bottles to festival-goers so they won’t use plastic ones. The 140,000 people attending the festival are encouraged to bring their own reusable bottles that can be filled at 400 water taps spread across the site.

Lucy Smith, who handles green issues for Glastonbury, said the UK has good quality tap water but everyone likes bottled water. The next plan is to replace all plastic beer glasses and cutlery with reusable items in 2015.

Environmentalists say there are about 150 million tonnes of plastic waste around the world, which harms ecosystems and wildlife. Glastonbury wants to be the greenest festival by copying America’s Burning Man event where people must take away what they bring.

Festival-goers are encouraged to use public transport or carpool. Plastic bottles can take hundreds or thousands of years to break down, and their production and transportation add to carbon emissions. In the UK, about 13 billion plastic water bottles are sold yearly, but only one in five is recycled.

Smith says festival-goers should drink tap water from underground reservoirs instead of buying bottled water. WaterAid will set up water kiosks for reusable bottles and free refills around the site. These kiosks, similar to those used in Africa, will also be DJ booths at night.

Almost half of all rubbish was recycled in 2013, and there will be 15,000 recycling bins available in 2014. Some critics say Glastonbury is becoming more corporate. Iron Maiden’s Bruce Dickinson won’t bring his band back because he thinks the festival has become too bourgeois.

The weather forecast for this year's event predicts sunny and dry conditions, unlike previous stormy or muddy years.

The world shares him, but London claims him as their own. However, Stratford-upon-Avon plans to celebrate William Shakespeare in 2016, marking the 400th anniversary of his death. Paul Edmondson from the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust argues that Stratford was important throughout Shakespeare’s life.

"People have seen Shakespeare as someone who left Stratford behind and went to London just for money," he said. "But Stratford is where he bought land, kept his library, lived, read, and thought."

John Aubrey, a diarist born 11 years after Shakespeare died, believed there was nothing special about him. However, the world disagrees with Aubrey.

In Singapore, Macbeth will be performed, while Romeo and Juliet will be shown in Brussels. The Shakespeare Globe is touring almost every country with Hamlet. In London, they are setting up a pop-up cinema along the South Bank that has 37 screens, one for each of Shakespeare’s plays.

The National Theatre and Royal Shakespeare Company are marking this anniversary too. There will also be lectures, recitals, conferences, films, concerts, operas, and exhibitions. 

There is not much documentary evidence about Shakespeare’s life. His friends gathered every play they could find into a First Folio published in 1623. This book includes drafts, prompt scripts, actors’ parts, and 17 plays never seen before.

Actor Mark Rylance calls it his favorite book. Most surviving copies of the First Folio will be displayed, including those from British and Bodleian libraries and a copy found recently in France. The National Archives and King’s College London are organizing an exhibition at Somerset House with four of Shakespeare’s six known signatures and other important documents like his will.

Dominic Dromgoole, former Globe director, joked that Shakespeare was a true Londoner but acknowledged "some spurious claim" by Stratford-upon-Avon. However, Stratford insists it educated Shakespeare. His old school room is being restored with £1.4m Heritage Lottery grant and will open as a permanent visitor attraction.

Shakespeare bought New Place, one of the best houses in town, where he died on St George’s Day, 23 April, his birthday. Edmondson believes that after buying this house in 1597, Shakespeare did most of his thinking there, including planning late plays like The Tempest.

The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust says New Place is the "jewel" for the anniversary celebrations but it’s just a hole now. His home was demolished 300 years ago and replaced by another house that was flattened in 1759 due to a tax dispute with an irascible clergyman, Francis Gastrell.

The site of Shakespeare's kitchen was recently found and the whole area is being redisplayed for the anniversary, marking foundations and restoring the garden. “Without Stratford,” Edmondson said, “there would have been no Shakespeare.”

On one August day, about 1 billion people used Facebook, according to Mark Zuckerberg. In ten years, the social network changed how people connect, do business, get news, and even use words.

Zuckerberg said that being more open and connected makes the world better. It helps you have stronger relationships with loved ones, creates a strong economy with more jobs, and builds a society that shows our values.

1 Facebook has changed what “friend” means.
“To friend” someone is now a verb. Unlike in real life, where ending a friendship can be hard, it’s easy to "unfriend" on Facebook. The words "share" and "like" have taken on new meanings too. School reunions are less surprising because you already see updates about your old classmates’ lives online.

But unlike in real life, all friends on Facebook are equal. Whether someone is a close friend or just an acquaintance from work, they’re treated the same way on the site. Researcher Robin Dunbar thinks that even though people can only have around 150 strong friendships, it might become easier to avoid learning how to get along because unfriending is so simple.

2 We care less about privacy.
The saying "if you're not paying for it, you’re the product" applies well to Facebook. Users know they are sharing information but still do it willingly. Pew Research Center found that most young people post their photos and other details online. They share a lot of personal info because they can create an image for themselves.

3 Facebook has created many jobs.
Facebook changed how businesses market. Marketers understand customers better than ever before thanks to the data available on the platform. Brands pay a lot for ads, with Facebook's ad revenue reaching $3.32 billion, up by 46%.

4 Facebook helped organize revolutions.
Though called the Twitter revolution, the Arab Spring used Facebook heavily for organizing protests in places like Ukraine. Facebook was key for spreading information and rallying people to action.

5 Facebook makes news.
Many people get their news from social media. About a third of users post about politics on Facebook. For young adults, the internet is often the main source of news. Facebook allows news companies to earn money from ads around articles posted on the site.

6 Users are changing Facebook.
Facebook started as a student network but now 56% of older internet users have accounts. The platform has changed over time, like how people share photos and connect with others.

We might need to get used to Facebook’s influence because it is likely to stay around for some time.

Low-income countries will face big problems from climate change over the next hundred years. They will see rising sea levels, stronger storms, hotter days and nights, unpredictable rain, and longer heat waves.

A UN report from 2007 said temperatures might rise by up to 6°C by the end of this century. Scientists now think that is unlikely but expect average land and sea temperatures to keep going up, possibly reaching 4°C higher than today. This could damage crops and make life very hot in many cities.

As it gets warmer and oceans heat up, tropical and subtropical areas will see big changes in rain. East Africa may get more short rains while West Africa can expect heavier monsoons. Burma, Bangladesh, and India might face stronger cyclones; southern Asia should expect more heavy summer rains. Indonesia could have less rainfall from July to October, but coastal regions around the South China Sea and Gulf of Thailand can expect extreme rain during cyclones.

The report says that high latitude countries like those in Europe or North America will receive more rain, while many dry and semi-dry subtropical areas will get less precipitation. In wet tropical regions, heavy rain events will become stronger and happen more often when it’s warmer.

Monsoons may begin earlier but end later, making the season longer.

Scientists and commentators from developing countries have welcomed this report, saying it backs up what they are already observing in places like Bangladesh where climate change is affecting them now.

Sea levels are projected to rise an average of 40–62 cm by the year 2100. This threatens millions living in big cities like Lagos and Calcutta.

Warmer temperatures could cause more weather disasters, with stronger storms that have higher winds and rain even though there might be fewer cyclones overall. Urban areas will likely get very hot; this can reduce growing periods for crops by up to 20% in some parts of Africa.

Dr. Camilla Toulmin from the International Institute for Environment and Development says everyone is at risk, but climate models are not yet good enough to predict exactly what will happen in specific places.

Oxfam predicts that world hunger could worsen as crop production and incomes get hurt by changing climates. By 2050, the number of people at risk of hunger might rise by 10% to 20%, with fewer daily calories available worldwide.

"The changing climate is already making it harder to fight hunger, and this looks set to get worse," said Oxfam. "A hot world means a hungry world."

Sometimes, middle-aged men feel sad and buy expensive cars. This feeling of sadness can be called a "midlife crisis." Now, scientists say that chimpanzees and orangutans might also experience this midlife crisis.

In a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, an international team of researchers found that these apes have lower well-being in middle age. The scientists asked zookeepers and caretakers about the mood and happiness of more than 500 apes from different places around the world. 

The results showed that chimpanzees and orangutans are less happy at around 30 years old, which is their midlife. For chimpanzees, this low point in well-being happens between ages 28 and 27 years. Orangutans feel this way at about age 35.

Alex Weiss from Edinburgh University said that the findings suggest the midlife crisis may be a shared experience with our closest animal relatives due to similar biology. However, Robin Dunbar from Oxford University is not sure if apes can really have such feelings because they do not think far into the future like humans do. Alexandra Freund from the University of Zurich also thinks there's little proof that a midlife crisis exists in people.

Weiss believes studying these animals might help understand why some men feel sad during middle age.

When you hear "Amazon," what do you think about first—the big forest, the long river, or the online store? These thoughts are now part of a big discussion about changing internet addresses. Brazil and Peru don't like that Amazon the company wants ".amazon" as its new web address.

The company from Seattle asked to have this special address, but Brazil and Peru say it should not belong only to one business. They think it could be used for things like saving nature or supporting local people’s rights.

Other groups also disagree with names like “.patagonia” and “.shangrila.” This issue is very important because it talks about who controls the internet and how we use it.

Until now, web addresses were easy to understand: ".com" for businesses, ".gov" for governments, etc. But now there will be many more types of addresses. The group that decides on these rules, ICANN, got lots of requests for new names, each costing nearly $200,000.

Amazon asked for several new domain names like “.shop,” “.song,” and “.book.” But the one causing trouble is ".amazon." Brazil and Peru want Amazon to give up this name because it’s a place that includes parts of their countries and other areas too. They say allowing companies to use places as names doesn't help everyone.

Argentina also disagrees with Patagonia, a clothing company, wanting “.patagonia.” Argentina says Patagonia is an important area for natural resources like oil and agriculture and has its own government.

China didn’t agree with a hotel group using “.shangrila,” but this case isn't as strong because the name was given in 2001 to attract visitors based on a story’s famous place.

ICANN's team of government advisors suggested pausing decisions about these names until they meet again in July. The first new domain names could be used by late 2013.

He is not the first person to doubt Mars One, a very ambitious private plan aiming to settle humans on Mars starting from 2025. But Joseph Roche is different from most critics as he is among the astronauts shortlisted for this mission.

Roche, an astrophysicist at Trinity College Dublin and one of the 100 people selected in February, wrote for The Guardian about his doubts regarding the feasibility of Mars One. He states that their selection process “was not strict enough to reach the high standard set by traditional astronaut programs.” Roche also believes that the Dutch Mars One team is too naive in thinking they can achieve this supposed $6 billion mission alone and it’s very unlikely to happen.

Roche suggests: "More openness would be good for Mars One, but I think their selection process was not strong enough. They do not work with other scientists, so maybe it's time for them to accept that this plan is too hard and focus on supporting other space missions."

He also mentions concerns about how the mission organizers promoted a list of top ten candidates. The ranking did not show who were the most likely astronauts but was based on "supporter points" earned through actions like buying official merchandise.

The mission timeline says Mars One plans to send a lander and satellite in 2018, followed by a rover in 2020, cargo missions from 2022, and humans arriving starting in 2025. Each crew of four would go every two years and not return to Earth.

Gerard’t Hooft, a Dutch Nobel prize winner for physics who supports the project, also doubts this timeline is realistic. He said: "It will take longer and cost more."

Roche told Medium that at first they promised in-person regional interviews over several days but later changed it to ten-minute Skype calls after making candidates sign a non-disclosure agreement.

He says he does not want to be too negative about space travel as he is excited by new ideas for the future of space exploration. He would volunteer if a one-way mission ever became possible, though he thinks such a mission will not happen in his lifetime.

The small room looks like a classroom with walls made of corrugated iron, decorated with charts showing letters and a map of Bangladesh. But, it is hard to focus because of the sound of hammering and chemicals in the air that irritate the eyes and throat.

Children learning here are lucky as they do not have to work in nearby factories. For 14 years, SOHAY, an organization supported by the Global Fund for Children and Comic Relief, has been working in poor areas of Dhaka to help child workers go back to school. They focus on children who work in dangerous places like aluminum, plastic factories, and leather tanneries.

This classroom is one of 23 centers SOHAY set up to prepare kids for primary school. Children can also do homework at these centers with help from peers.

Alamin, a ten-year-old boy who used to work in a plastic factory, now attends one such center. His father sells things on the street and his mother works part-time as a housekeeper. They are happy he is in school instead of working. Rabi, Alamin's friend, also likes going to school.

SOHAY’s manager, Mohammed Abdullah al-Mamun, says these centers aim to make education easier for children and change how people think about kids’ education in the community. SOHAY also holds sessions for parents and employers to discourage child labor and offers training to help families earn more money.

Mamun explains that getting working children into school is very hard because their physical and mental conditions are different from other children, making it difficult for them to make friends or adjust to school life. It’s also a challenge to keep them in school as dropout rates are high. Schools need to be sensitive and care about these children.

Zhorna Akter Sumayya, a seven-year-old girl whose brothers work, now goes to a government primary school after getting introduced to education at SOHAY's center. Her parents, who struggle with income from her father’s job at a rickshaw garage and mother’s work as a housekeeper, are glad she is in school.

In 2015, SOHAY helped 1,540 children leave dangerous jobs and got 2,125 kids at risk of working into schools. About 780 more are preparing to start school in 2017. The organization also helps around 635 working children learn about their rights under Bangladesh’s 2010 child labor elimination code.

Bangladesh's Labor Law bans children under 14 from work, but according to UNICEF, over 4.7 million kids below this age are employed informally and 1.3 million between five to seventeen years old work in dangerous industries.

Sadia Nasrin of Sonjag, another local organization, explains that getting kids into school without compensating for lost income is tough. To solve this, Sonjag works with the community to explain why education is important. They form groups with social workers, leaders, mothers, young volunteers, and government members who motivate employers to let children attend school.

Community people are key in making these changes. People living in slums face threats like eviction and displacement. Nasrin says that national plans do not consider street children's needs well enough and legislative measures are limited.

It is critical to get kids into school early or else they might end up working without an education, which Mamun finds hard to prevent once they grow older. SOHAY works to stop children from entering hazardous jobs by providing educational opportunities.

A senior US researcher warns that people might miss the natural sounds like birds singing or water flowing because they listen to music on earphones. Kurt Fristrup, a scientist at the US National Park Service, says high levels of background noise make it hard for people to enjoy these sounds.

He explains that people are ignoring nature’s sounds and getting used to loud noises instead. This is causing them to lose their ability to hear well. The US National Park Service recorded sound levels in over 600 areas across the US and found human activity makes noise everywhere, even in parks like Yosemite, Yellowstone, and Denali.

Fristrup predicts that noise pollution grows faster than the population, doubling every thirty years. This makes it hard for people to hear natural sounds clearly. He says using headphones or noise-canceling headphones can help create a quieter environment.

When background noise increases, it affects hearing in the same way fog affects vision. People can only focus on sounds close by instead of hearing everything around them.

Fristrup fears that if quiet places become rare, many children will grow up without knowing what peace and quiet feel like. Other scientists say listening to natural sounds can help people relax after stressful events.

In experiments, participants listened to recordings of nature or mixed with traffic and other noises after giving a stressful talk. Those who heard only nature recordings calmed down faster than those who did not. Taff suggests visiting protected areas to enjoy the natural sounds before they become harder to find. Over time, humans may have learned that quiet places mean safety, which makes them feel calm today.

A race engineer works between drivers and mechanics. New graduates can start earning £25,000 to £30,000 and quickly move up to junior roles making over £40,000 in a few years. Senior engineers earn £50,000 to £90,000 with the chance of six-figure salaries as they advance. The job involves taking driver feedback, analyzing data for best performance settings, then telling mechanics what to do. A degree in automotive/mechanical engineering or motorsport technology is needed along with hands-on experience. You must handle stress well. Long hours are a downside.

An ethical hacker tests company computer security by trying to break into systems. New hires can earn £35,000 to £50,000 while team leaders get £60,000 to £90,000. You don't need a specific degree but should have tech passion and strong problem-solving skills. A tough moment is finding that the network you are testing has already been hacked.

A bomb-disposal diver earns up to £100,000 working for two months out of every three in the private sector. The job involves diving to find unexploded weapons like bombs or grenades and either safely recovering them or disposing of them properly. You need diving inspection and medical technician qualifications along with explosive ordnance disposal training and lots of experience. Staying calm under stress is key as you work alone underwater with poor visibility in small spaces. Being away from home for at least six months a year can be difficult.

A social engineer tries to trick company employees into giving up confidential information, allowing access to sensitive data or computer networks. The pay ranges from £50,000 to £80,000 on average with graduates starting around £25,000 and increasing quickly with experience. A degree in IT is common but psychology or marketing backgrounds can also be useful. You must be able to lie convincingly, fit into different environments, and have a strong sense of ethics and legal understanding. People often misunderstand your job as being that of a spy.

A power-line helicopter pilot flies close to high-voltage lines to inspect them with cameras for the power company. The salary is around £65,000. You need a private helicopter pilot license, commercial pilot’s license, and about 2,000 hours flying at low levels. Flying very close to power lines can be nerve-wracking but there are no negatives according to Robin Tutcher from Western Power Distribution.

A private butler handles various tasks like wardrobe management, chauffeuring, pet care, managing staff, serving meals, running errands, booking restaurants, house security, and more for employers. They earn £60,000 to £90,000. Formal qualifications are not required but courses at the British Butler Academy or Institute can help. Being dedicated to caring for others is crucial. Long hours and an unpredictable schedule make it hard to have a family life. Butlers also face isolation, cultural differences with employers, and may work for unpleasant people.

They call it the Richie Rich Club, and it's about to get even richer. In India, the wealthiest people will make four times as much money by 2018. This report comes from talking to 150 very rich people. It shows that more business leaders and new inheritors are becoming multimillionaires.

In recent years, India had slow growth, higher food prices, and a weaker currency. But in May 2014, the Bharatiya Janata Party won big by promising to make the economy better. Now, there are almost one-sixth more Indians worth over $3.75 million than in 2013.

Murali Balaraman, who wrote part of the report, says cities are growing quickly and the middle class is getting bigger. There are many new chances for business. India's rich people have around a trillion dollars, which is one-fifth of all the wealth in the country. By 2018, this could be $4 trillion.

Rich people like to show off their money with luxury goods. Abhay Gupta from Luxury Connect says there will be more demand for high-end things because many people want what rich people have.

Cars are a favorite purchase. In 2009, wealthy Indians showed off locally made SUVs, but now only foreign cars impress others. Mercedes sales in India rose by 47% in 2013, and BMW launched a $200,000 model in Delhi. Lamborghini makes two models: the Gallardo and Aventador. But traffic and bad roads make it hard to enjoy these cars.

The most popular investments are real estate within India and jewelry. Mukesh Ambani, India's richest man, built a 27-story home worth $1 billion. Lakshmi Mittal’s niece had a wedding in Barcelona that cost around $80 million.

Luxury buyers want unique things. One person bought nine cases of expensive Japanese whisky for a wedding. Another cut up half of identical Louis Vuitton bags to match accessories. Traditional wedding gifts like silver plates are being replaced by luxury brands like Rolex watches and Louis Vuitton bags.

Almost half the new rich people live in smaller cities, and many give money to charity. But the growth in giving isn't as big as their wealth growth. Balaraman says that while there's a wide gap between rich and poor, it’s accepted in India. People know who is rich and who is poor but continue with their lives normally.

Margaret Thatcher, one of Britain's strongest leaders since Winston Churchill, has passed away at age 87. She had been dealing with health issues due to dementia for years. The British government plans a special funeral for her at St Paul’s Cathedral.

British Prime Minister David Cameron said she was a great leader who helped save the country. President Obama from America remembered her as someone who worked closely with President Reagan and shaped history with strong beliefs and determination.

Thatcher was Britain's first woman prime minister and served the longest since 1827, for 11 years. She made many changes in Britain by selling state-owned businesses to private companies and dealing with powerful trade unions.

During her time as leader, she also worked well with U.S. President Ronald Reagan against the Soviet Union. This earned her respect from people in former Soviet countries who saw her as a champion for freedom.

Thatcher became famous after winning leadership of the Conservative Party in 1975 and then leading Britain through big changes like selling government businesses to private companies and controlling unions, which many workers did not like.

She was known for strongly defending British interests in Europe, even when it caused problems with other European leaders. While she gained respect from some, others disagreed with her policies. After a long career, she retired but kept working on promoting her ideas through the Thatcher Foundation.

At one school in Stirling, when kids hear "daily mile," they stop writing and go outside to run laps around the field. For over three years, all students at St Ninian’s Primary have walked or run a mile every day. They do this at different times during the day and seem happy about it. None of the children at the school are overweight.

The daily mile has helped improve these kids’ fitness, behavior, and focus in class so much that many other schools across Britain are copying this idea. Children walk or run around their school or a nearby park for 15 minutes.

Elaine Wyllie, who leads St Ninian’s, said: “I get at least two emails daily from other schools asking how we do it. It's amazing to think kids all over the country might be running because of what we started.”

One in ten children are overweight when they start school at four or five years old. In 2015, a study found that English students were less fit than ever before. So primary schools quickly noticed how good the daily mile could be.

The daily mile has been added to many schools in London, Gateshead, Wales, and other parts of Scotland. Others are planning to start it during the 2015-6 school year. In Stirling alone, 30 schools have already started or plan to start the daily mile.

Elaine Wyllie said: “It’s a simple way for children to be more active. It doesn’t cost anything and is easy to do. The most important thing is that kids enjoy it. They return to class energized and happy, just like how children used to look.”

At St Ninian’s, teachers take students out of lessons whenever they can fit it into the day for their daily mile around a special path on the school field. Only heavy rain or ice stops them.

The benefits are still being studied. Researchers from Stirling University are looking at how the daily mile affects kids’ physical health, thinking skills, and feelings.

Kevin Clelland, a teacher from Leeds who visited St Ninian’s before starting it in his own school, said: “It’s so simple but seems to have big effects. We really want to help our pupils be more fit.”

Active Cheshire is sending people to Scotland to see how the daily mile works and plans to start it in 450 schools if a test run succeeds.

Tanni Grey-Thompson, chair of ukactive, said: “All children should get 60 minutes of activity every day. It’s great to see the daily mile helping students be healthier and do better in class.”

The Scottish government also supports this idea. A spokesperson said: “Initiatives like the daily mile can help parents teach their kids healthy habits from a young age. We are happy many schools in Scotland are taking part or plan to.”

The Canadian tennis player Frank Dancevic criticized the Australian Open organizers for forcing players to compete in very hot conditions after he collapsed during his match when temperatures reached 41°C.

Dancevic fainted for about a minute during the second set of his first-round game against Benoît Paire. He said it was too dangerous for the players and mentioned that the heat made him see things that weren’t there, like Snoopy.

He added, “Players should not be collapsing or leaving matches because of the heat. It’s not normal to get heat stroke after playing only a set and a half.”

Dancevic also pointed out that many other players complained about how hot it was but the tournament kept going until someone gets seriously hurt or worse.

Other famous players agreed with Dancevic. Andy Murray said, “The conditions are very tough and look bad for tennis when people collapse.” Caroline Wozniacki mentioned her water bottle melted on the court from the heat.

John Isner and Victoria Azarenka also complained about how hot it was during their matches.

The tournament had a plan to help with extreme heat by giving players extra breaks between sets. However, they decided whether to stop play based on more than just temperature readings, including humidity and wind.

Dancevic got medical help but still lost his match 7–6, 6–3, 6–4. He said he felt close to stopping completely because of how hot it was.

A ball boy also needed medical care after collapsing during another player’s game. Peng Shuai from China had to be helped off the court due to heat and cramps.

The tournament's chief medical officer, Tim Wood, said most players finished their matches without needing major medical help despite a few having issues with the heat.

Most players agreed that while conditions were tough, both players faced the same difficulties. Roger Federer said if you train hard enough, you can handle it.

Dancevic disagreed and said some players are naturally better at handling heat than others and playing in such dangerous temperatures is very risky. He also mentioned he still couldn’t urinate an hour and a half after his match due to dehydration from the heat.

Sir Alex Ferguson will stop being Manchester United's manager at the end of this season after 27 years. During his time, he has become the most successful football manager in Britain. He won 13 English Premier League titles, two Champions Leagues, one Cup Winners’ Cup, five FA Cups, and four League Cups.

Ferguson explained why he is retiring: “I thought about this a lot and decided it’s the right time to go. I want to leave Manchester United strong, and I believe I have done that with a good squad of players and a great youth system. The club's training places are some of the best in sports, and Old Trafford, our home stadium, is one of the best in the world.”

He thanked his family, especially his wife Cathy, for supporting him throughout his career. He also praised the players and staff for their hard work and dedication over the years.

Ferguson surprised everyone by announcing his retirement suddenly during a meeting with first-team players on Wednesday morning. Then he talked to the backroom staff and other club employees about it.

Joel Glazer, who owns Manchester United with his brother Avie, said Ferguson is not only a great manager but also an amazing person whose dedication to the club has been outstanding.

Avie Glazer added that Ferguson will continue as a director of the club. He praised Ferguson for all he did in 27 years at Manchester United and wanted him to stay involved with the team's future.

David Gill, who worked closely with Ferguson for 16 years, said they knew this day would come but kept planning to ensure everything was ready for when Ferguson retired. He mentioned how much respect he has for Ferguson’s care for the club and everyone in football.

First-team coach René Meulensteen shared that Ferguson told his backroom staff about retiring on Wednesday morning. He believed it was a hard decision made after careful thought and wished Ferguson all the best.

Lego made a lot more money in the first half of 2014 because their movie, "The Lego Movie," was very popular. The movie did well at box offices in the US and UK. In the US, it earned over $250 million by April, and in the UK, it brought in £31 million. It cost about $60 million to make.

Lego's sales went up across Europe, the Americas, and Asia because children liked products linked to the movie. Lego’s finance director, John Goodwin, said that the success of "The Lego Movie" helped their sales a lot during this time. He also mentioned they are waiting to see how well it will do when the DVD comes out later in 2014.

In the first six months, Lego's profits went up by 12% to $630 million and sales increased by 11%, which is more than three times what they made six years ago. Jørgen Vig Knudstorp, Lego’s chief executive, said that these results are very good in tough economic times.

Lego started making plastic bricks in 1949 and became a popular toy worldwide by the 1970s. In 2003, they were almost out of business but Jørgen Vig Knudstorp changed things around to focus on their main products. They also opened their first factory in China and an office in Shanghai to grow more in that big market.

He lived like a rich person but didn't actually have much money in the bank, which made Spanish authorities curious. This Chinese businessman named Gao Ping had lots of expensive things and ran several businesses in Spain, but he might not be paying taxes on the goods he brought from China.

In 2012, when police searched his warehouses, they found a lot of cash: €12 million in small stacks of €100, €200, and €500 bills. The money was tied with rubber bands. Gao is said to have laundered up to €300 million yearly, sold fake goods, and toys without safety marks. His business hurt Spain's other companies.

The police worry about €500 notes because they are easy to carry and hide. Criminals use them for tax evasion, money laundering, and drug dealing. The UK stopped using these big bills in 2010 as they were mostly used for illegal things. Italy warned that the mafia often used these notes.

Experts like Peter Sands want to stop making high-value bills because it makes life easier for criminals. They argue that without these large notes, criminals would use smaller bills or gold and diamonds, which are bulkier and easier to catch. Europol asked the European Central Bank (ECB) to think about stopping €500 notes.

Germany and Austria like using cash a lot, more than half of their transactions are in paper money. Some people say limiting cash goes against individual freedom, but law enforcement is worried because they find many suspicious bundles of cash often linked to crime.

The ECB says it doesn’t have proof that the €500 note is used for illegal things, but EU ministers want to look into making restrictions on these big bills by May 2016.

McDonald's is a big burger chain and symbol of American business around the world. But now, its golden arches are looking bad. Sales worldwide dropped by 3.3% in results that were called very poor.

In China, sales went down by 23% after a food scandal where workers at a supplier said they used old meat for McDonald’s and KFC. In Europe, sales decreased by 4%, mostly because of problems in Ukraine and Russia's negative view towards Western countries. About 200 out of 450 restaurants in Russia are being checked for safety issues, and ten have been closed.

In the US, where there are about 40% of McDonald’s restaurants, sales have fallen for 12 straight months. Sales went down by 4.1% recently. Young people are choosing to eat at other places like Chipotle instead of McDonald's. The number of visits from young adults between 19 and 21 years old dropped by 13% since 2011.

In a survey with over 32,000 American diners, McDonald’s burgers were voted the worst in America. People prefer burgers from Five Guys or Smashburger instead. Chick-fil-A was rated best for chicken meals. Many see McDonald's as less healthy than other restaurants like Chipotle which uses antibiotic-free meat and local produce.

McDonald's tried to reach out to customers by answering questions about its food. Some asked if it used "pink slime" (a controversial filler made from beef gristle and fat) or if there were worms in the beef. McDonald’s says pink slime was dropped in 2012, but doubts still exist among consumers.

McDonald's is also losing customers who want faster service at lower prices. Even though its items have become more expensive since adding $2 menu items, they are still less costly than other fast-food chains. However, longer waiting times due to a bigger and more complex menu are causing complaints from customers.

In the UK, McDonald’s business has improved with better breakfast menus, coffee, and free Wi-Fi, making it popular among British adults.

McDonald's plans to address food misconceptions in its home market by offering organic food and custom-made burgers. They also want a simpler menu but more choices for filling customization. This idea is challenging and needs further detail before implementation.

Despite the drop in sales, McDonald’s continues expanding globally, planning to open 1,400 new restaurants by the end of 2014. Analysts think its market share will keep shrinking but they still believe McDonald's will remain a major player for years or even decades.

How close are we to having drones deliver packages? Amazon says it’s not far away. But others think more work needs to be done for public safety.

Paul Misener, an important person at Amazon, told a meeting that his company will be ready as soon as all the rules are set up. He made a joke about sending fruit to show how easy it could be.

By June 2016, the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) plans to have new rules for commercial drones. Only drones weighing up to 25kg can fly under these rules. The FAA says that all drones should use different radio frequencies so they cannot be hijacked or jammed.

Professor Sajiv Singh from Carnegie Mellon University runs a delivery company called NearEarth. He said current drones need simple instructions like "go here, do this task, and come back." Even short flights can have problems if the drone is landing in an area with new obstacles it hasn’t seen before.

The main issue is keeping radio contact with the drone and planning for when that link breaks. Daniel Huber, a roboticist, said off-the-shelf drones just crash without guidance.

Jay McConville from Lockheed Martin MST said bigger drones are needed for heavy deliveries. Making pilot controls easier to use is also important.

Huber thinks most technology needed for drone delivery already exists but says safety remains a concern. Commercial aircraft have very low failure rates, and drones need to reach similar standards.

Singh explained that air travel is dangerous, so high safety standards exist. He said plans must be made if something goes wrong with the drone.

Waiters are asking people to help them keep their tips. PizzaExpress workers will protest at some restaurants because the company takes 8p from every £1 of tips paid by card. This costs the waiters about £3 a night. The union, Unite, says this is unfair and has started an online petition.

PizzaExpress makes around £1 million a year from this fee. Chantal Chegrinec from Unite believes that if the company values its workers, they should get all of their tips. Unite began the campaign after PizzaExpress was bought by Hony Capital in 2014.

Protests started at the British Museum branch in London. An employee who works there for 15 years and gets paid only the minimum wage says she relies on tips to make up her low wages.

Other restaurants like Ask and Zizzi also take an 8% fee from card tips, while some like Café Rouge and Bella Italia deduct 10%.

PizzaExpress defends this charge by saying it covers the cost of running a tronc system which distributes tips among staff. But other chains such as Wagamama and Pizza Hut do not take any admin fees.

Unite has distributed leaflets to customers in ten south London restaurants, and almost 6,000 people have signed their petition. A waiter from another restaurant says at least a third of his income comes from tips, which are very important for him since he earns only £6.50 an hour.

Conservative MP Andrew Percy wants to change the law so that staff can control their tips better and plans to raise this issue in parliament after summer break.

The National Security Agency (NSA) has access to systems of big US tech companies like Google, Facebook, Apple, and others through a secret program called PRISM. This lets them gather things like search history, emails, file transfers, and live chats.

A top-secret PowerPoint document that The Guardian verified shows how the NSA collects information directly from these companies' servers. While the slide show says the tech firms are involved, all of them say they don't know about such a program.

Google said it does not have any special way for the government to access private user data without following the law carefully. Executives at other tech firms also denied knowledge of PRISM or similar plans.

This NSA access is possible because of changes in US surveillance laws from 2007, under Presidents Bush and Obama. The program can watch communications live and stored information. It allows targeting any customers outside the US and some Americans who communicate with people abroad, without needing warrants for all cases.

The PRISM program began in 2007 with Microsoft and has expanded to include other tech giants like Yahoo, Google, Facebook, PalTalk, YouTube, Skype, AOL, and Apple by 2012. These companies cover most online emails, searches, videos, and communication networks.

Companies must follow requests for users' communications under US law. But PRISM lets the NSA directly access these company servers without needing their permission first. 

A recent leak of this information is rare since the NSA usually keeps its operations secret. The PRISM program means the NSA can gather targeted communications from tech companies’ servers directly, avoiding individual court orders.

A senior official stated that the PRISM program collects communications under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA). This law does not allow targeting US citizens or people in the US and is overseen by several bodies to protect Americans' privacy. Congress recently reauthorized this program after discussions, and it provides crucial intelligence for protecting against threats.

Do you want your child to be good at sports and maybe compete on the world stage? Try to make sure they are born in November or October. A study by Dr. Gavin Sandercock from Essex University found that children born in those months are fitter than others.

The research included 8,550 boys and girls aged ten to sixteen from 26 schools in Essex. The children were tested on stamina, handgrip strength, and lower-body power between 2007 and 2010. Children born in November had the most stamina and power and were second strongest overall. Those born in October were nearly as fit, with higher strength scores.

A boy born in November can run at least 10% faster, jump 12% higher, and be 15% more powerful than a child of the same age born in April. This difference could help decide who becomes a top-level athlete because small differences matter when selecting elite athletes.

Children born in April were found to be the least fit overall, followed by those born in June. This might mean they are less likely to make school sports teams and perform well.

The study suggests that children born early in the school year have an advantage both academically and physically. The authors believe vitamin D exposure during pregnancy could explain this difference since autumn-born children get more sun while their mothers are pregnant.

John Steele from the Youth Sport Trust says a good first experience with sports at school can greatly improve physical literacy, agility, balance, coordination, and enjoyment of physical activity. 

UK Sport said that among elite adult athletes, the month of birth does not seem to be a key factor for success.

Thirty-five years ago, when Kate Bush first performed, mobile phones were new. Now, she wants her fans to put their phones away during her shows at the Hammersmith Apollo in London. She wrote on her website that she prefers direct contact with the audience instead of them using their devices.

Bush asks fans not to take photos or videos so everyone can share the moment together. This could also keep the show a surprise for the thousands who have tickets for her 22 shows.

Many artists feel the same way as Bush. Roger Daltrey from The Who said it’s strange when people focus on their screens instead of enjoying the concert. Beyoncé has asked fans to stop filming and enjoy the performance directly.

The issue isn’t just in music; sports fans also protest against using phones at games. For example, Manchester United asks fans not to film with tablets during matches.

Johnny Marr believes that looking through a phone screen means missing out on the full experience of live music. Some venues have even put up signs asking people not to use their devices during shows.

However, Sam Watt from Vyclone says filming at concerts can add to the experience by creating shared videos later. He thinks artists like Kate Bush might change their minds if they saw how it works.

Leading water experts warn that by 2050, the world's population may need to switch almost completely to a vegetarian diet to avoid serious food shortages. People now get about 20% of their protein from animal products, but this might drop to just 5% to feed the extra two billion people expected by 2050.

A report by Malik Falkenmark and his team at the Stockholm International Water Institute states that there won't be enough water on current farmlands to produce food for nine billion people in 2050 if we follow current trends. But there will be just enough water if only 5% of total calories come from animal-based foods.

The price of staple foods like corn and wheat has risen almost 50% since June, caused by severe droughts in the US and Russia, and weak monsoon rains in Asia. This could lead to a second food crisis within five years. More than 18 million people are facing serious food shortages across the Sahel.

The scientists say that adopting a vegetarian diet can help increase water available for growing more food. Feeding animals requires five to ten times more water than feeding humans directly with plant foods. One third of all cropland is used to grow food for livestock.

Other ways to feed people include cutting down on waste and increasing trade between countries with extra food and those that don’t have enough. Right now, 900 million people are hungry even though the amount of food per person has been growing. With 70% of all available water used in agriculture, feeding two billion more people by 2050 will put a lot more pressure on water and land.

The report is being released at the start of a major world water conference in Stockholm, Sweden, where around 2,500 people from 120 countries are meeting to talk about global water supply problems.

A different report says that helping farmers in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia invest in small pumps and easy technology is better than big irrigation projects. This can increase yields up to three times and add tens of billions of US dollars to household income.

Cities usually don't move, but Kiruna, a town in northern Sweden, has to relocate because of a mine beneath it. The mine is causing the ground to sink, threatening to swallow the town.

The mining company LK founded Kiruna in 1900 and made it rich through iron ore, but now this same mine could destroy the town. Kiruna’s mayor says, "Without the mine, no one would build a city here."

Kiruna is located 145 km inside the Arctic Circle with harsh winters where temperatures drop below -15°C. Despite this, people stay for the mining jobs.

In 2004, LK told Kiruna that digging was causing the ground to sink and could destroy buildings in ten years. Now cracks are appearing closer to town.

The city is planning to move by 2033, like a millipede walking eastward along new streets. A new town square with a circular town hall will be built 3 km away from where Kiruna is now. Important buildings will be moved piece by piece and reconstructed in the new location.

People are worried about losing their identity as some places with special memories won't move. The mining company has given £320 million to build new facilities like schools and libraries. 

The plan is to build multi-story apartment blocks around courtyards on straight boulevards, which will be very different from the current town of houses with gardens. New residents might come for cultural facilities such as a cable car over the main street, but it's unclear if existing residents can afford living there.

Residents are also concerned about their homes' new locations and values. The company has agreed to pay 25% more than home values, but many think this is not enough at market rates. To help with valuations, architects have studied housing in nearby cities and noted the features of Kiruna’s houses.

US researchers found that government programs collecting telephone records threaten people's privacy. Using just call and text logs, scientists from Stanford University could figure out names, addresses, and partners' names. They also uncovered private information like one person owning a rifle, another having an irregular heartbeat, and someone else being pregnant or having multiple sclerosis.

The study used "metadata," which includes numbers called, when calls happened, and call lengths. This data is not protected by law in the same way as the content of messages. A former official at the US National Security Agency (NSA) said that metadata can reveal everything about someone's life.

For their research, Stanford scientists signed up 823 people who allowed them to collect phone data through an app and shared Facebook information. They collected over 250,000 calls and more than 1.2 million texts. The researchers found names for 82% of the participants by analyzing call patterns. They also figured out where people lived based on businesses they called.

The study showed that metadata can reveal personal details like relationships and health issues. For example, one person was identified as owning a rifle because of calls to gun stores. Another had health problems revealed through calls to cardiology centers and pharmacies.

Patrick Mutchler, who led the research at Stanford, said this work shows how rich phone data is but that most people do not know about its potential. The findings suggest policymakers need to think carefully before supporting mass surveillance programs.

Angela Erdmann never met her grandfather because he died in 1946, six years before she was born. On April 8, 2014, she learned about a message in a bottle that her grandfather had thrown into the Baltic Sea 101 years earlier. The museum exhibiting it gave the message to Erdmann.

"I was very surprised," said Erdmann, who is now 62. A genealogical researcher came to her home in Berlin and told her he had something from her grandfather. He explained that a fisherman named Konrad Fischer found the bottle with a message inside. The name on the card matched her grandfather's.

The brown beer bottle was in good condition after being in water for 101 years. Holger von Neuhoff, who works at the International Maritime Museum in Hamburg, said this is likely the oldest known message in a bottle.

Researchers think Erdmann’s grandfather, Richard Platz, threw it into the sea while on a hike with friends in 1913 when he was 20 years old. Most of the postcard inside could not be read, but the address in Berlin and a request to send it there were clear. He included two stamps so that the finder would not have to pay for postage.

Erdmann learned more about her grandfather this way even though she never met him because he died at 54 years old when she was not yet born. She found out that he was a writer who valued freedom and respect between people. “My mother taught me what my grandfather had taught his two daughters, including my mom,” said Erdmann.

Erdmann likes culture and traveling like her grandfather did. Even though she is happy about the message in the bottle, she hopes no one else will throw more bottles into the sea because it can cause pollution. The museum plans to display the bottle until May 2014 before trying to read more of the text.

Erdmann wants to add photos so visitors can see who threw the bottle into the water.

The person next to you in the store queue looks normal, but she might be carrying notes about the store's appearance and cleanliness instead of a shopping list.
