She could also be timing how long the line moves or have a tiny camera hidden somewhere. These signs suggest she may be a mystery shopper.

In the UK, there are around 50,000 mystery shopping visits each month according to an association that handles this work. More people shop online now, but physical stores still want to provide a better experience than what is available on the internet. Companies hire mystery shoppers to check how well their stores meet these expectations.

Jill Spencer from ABa, a company that hires mystery shoppers, explains that each shopper visits different locations and never returns to the same store within three months. A typical day involves visiting five to ten stores for up to eight hours, with an additional one or two hours spent writing detailed reports about their visit. Mystery shoppers can earn up to £155 a day plus money back for travel and stays, as well as car depreciation costs.

Video mystery shoppers, who film their visits secretly, might make even more – around £300 a day.

Laura, a 50-year-old from Devon who has been a mystery shopper since 2001, usually gets between £5 to £20 to spend at each store. She buys items related to what the retailer wants her to check and can keep those products. Laura earns about £30,000 to £40,000 yearly from this work.

However, regular paid mystery shopping jobs are rare now. Over 500,000 people have signed up as mystery shoppers in the UK, but less than 10% get consistent work and pay has dropped.

Some companies now offer free products instead of money to motivate their workers. Laura says she would do a cruise for free but thinks paying a small fee for meals or trips is unfair.

Hannah, a 41-year-old lawyer, does mystery dining without payment. She gets expensive meals and stays at fancy hotels as part of her job. However, she has to spend hours writing detailed reports about the experience afterward, which can be tough while also trying to enjoy her meal.

New figures show that over a million British workers are employed under zero-hours contracts. This means the use of these contracts by businesses is much more widespread than previously thought.

The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD) conducted a survey of over 1,000 employers to get this figure. The findings led to calls for the government to look into how widely used these contracts are.

Zero-hours contract workers often do not get paid time off or sick pay and must ask permission before getting another job. According to the CIPD, about one-third of those on zero-hours contracts work full-time hours, usually 30 hours per week or more. One-third of charities and one in four public organizations use these contracts.

This new number makes experts doubt official data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The ONS recently raised its estimate to around 250,000 people working under zero-hours contracts.

Peter Cheese, the head of the CIPD, says there needs to be more clarity about what zero-hours contracts are and how they should be used. He believes both good and bad practices need to be examined for businesses and workers alike.

Retailer Sports Direct employs around 20,000 out of its 23,000 staff on these terms. Other companies like Cineworld cinemas and Buckingham Palace also use them for their employees, especially in the summer months.

Vidhya Alakeson from an independent think tank called Resolution Foundation says if there are a million workers on zero-hours contracts, it is no longer a small issue that can be ignored. She thinks the government needs to review these contracts thoroughly and consider how they affect employment rights, pay, and personal well-being.

Trade unions say employers sometimes force staff into signing these contracts to avoid giving them benefits. Dave Prentis from Unison states most workers are only on these contracts because they have no other choice.

Zero-hours contract workers often find out their working hours at the last minute but must be ready for more work if needed. They should get holiday pay based on how many hours they work, but they do not qualify for sick pay.

The National Trust charity employs many seasonal staff under zero-hours contracts and says it offers the same pay and benefits as full-time workers. However, the trust believes that flexibility is important due to unpredictable weather conditions.

Politician Chuka Umunna argues that these contracts should be rare exceptions rather than a common practice because they can leave workers insecure about when they will work.

Some people argue that zero-hours contracts might have helped reduce unemployment during tough economic times. The CIPD found that only 16% of those on the contracts reported their employers frequently not giving them enough hours each week.

The private sector uses these contracts less, with only 17% making use of them compared to 34% in charities and 24% in public organizations.

Industries where zero-hours contracts are more common include hotels (48%), education (35%), and healthcare (27%).

A new count shows that there are more tigers in Nepal now than at any time since the 1970s. This gives hope to people who work to protect animals because tiger numbers have been going down for 100 years across South Asia.

The number of wild Bengal tigers in Nepal has gone up to 198, which is a rise of 63.6% over five years. Maheshwar Dhakal, an ecologist with the Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation in Nepal, said this was very encouraging.

To count the tigers, more than 500 cameras were placed in five protected areas and three wildlife corridors. Over 250 experts worked on the survey, which cost about £250,000.

Dhakal also mentioned that a similar survey was done in India. In India, there are now around 1,300 tigers across many large protected areas.

Nepal has promised to double its tiger population from 121 by the year 2022. Tiger skins and body parts used for traditional medicine have become more expensive because Asia is getting richer. Criminal groups pay local people in Nepal a lot of money to kill tigers, then trade their skin and bones through India.

A big problem is that some high-ranking officials work with criminal networks involved in the tiger trade. The increase in tiger numbers is due to better protection in national parks, stronger anti-poaching efforts, and improved management of tiger habitats, where forests cover 29% of Nepal's land. But there is a need for more measures to protect both tigers’ habitat and prey.

As the number of tigers has grown, conflicts with villagers have also increased. In 2012, seven people were killed by tigers near national parks compared to four in 2011. Villagers want better protection from attacks. Krishna Bhurtel, a village headman in Chitwan, said the government should come up with plans to protect people from tigers.

Chitwan National Park has the most adult tigers with 120, followed by Bardiya National Park (50) and Shukla Phanta Wildlife Reserve (17). In Nepal, some rich people display tiger skins or heads as decoration. Tiger bones are used in traditional Chinese medicine. The illegal trade of tiger parts is very profitable and threatens tigers.

Diwakar Chapagain from the World Wildlife Fund said that well-off Tibetans use tiger skins for festival costumes.

Louise Haggerty, a 56-year-old hairdresser and waitress, went shopping late at night for Black Friday deals. She said it was very chaotic inside the store. “It was crazy. It was really messy,” she added.

Haggerty went to Sainsbury’s with her friend hoping to buy a cheap flat-screen TV but couldn’t because many people pushed in line. A woman who was second in line got pushed out by young people and didn't get anything. Haggerty said, “People were acting badly – it was terrible.”

Frustrated from not getting the Blaupunkt 40” TV that went down to £149.99 (originally £299.99), she bought a Dyson Animal Vac for £159.99 (originally £319.99). Haggerty said, “I don’t even know if I want it.”

Andy Blackett, 30, an estate agent, had more luck and got two coffee makers, two tablets, two TVs, and a stereo for good prices. His friend Henry Fischer, a 19-year-old student, didn’t get anything because someone took his TV.

Blackett and friends first went to Tesco but found it too chaotic, so they moved to Sainsbury’s. At Tesco, more than a dozen police officers had to handle scuffles between shoppers. Shoppers tore down barriers put up for the midnight sale. The store delayed selling TVs until the situation was under control.

Police also intervened at other stores like Willesden and Surrey Quays just before midnight when sales began. In Manchester, two people were arrested. South Wales Police said staff at Tesco called them because they were worried about so many people coming to the sale.

James Alled, a 30-year-old businessman, was one of the first to buy TVs for £250 each and planned to sell one for more money. Christine Ball, 62, came early but couldn’t move forward in line. She wanted to get her grandson a cheap TV for Christmas.

Mel Mehmet, 23, went shopping last year too, but this time she felt scared by how people behaved. “It’s crazy having sales at midnight,” she said. She planned to go to PC World later since their sale starts at 8 am.

Barack Obama told young people to be hopeful and talk to those who think differently if they want to make changes in the world. During his last visit as president to Britain, he spoke with 500 youth leaders in London and said that problems can be solved by people. He mentioned tools like social media help make a difference.

Obama acknowledged that young people face challenges from events like 9/11 and dealing with bad news on the internet. But he encouraged them to keep pushing for progress, which needs effort and belief.

He talked about healthcare changes, education policies, and diplomatic deals with Iran as important parts of his legacy. Obama said it's okay if big issues aren't solved quickly because change takes time.

When asked about TTIP, a trade agreement, Obama said we shouldn’t avoid globalization but must focus on workers' rights.

Before the meeting, some young people were excited to hear Obama speak and ask questions like how to get more voting rights. A young Sikh Londoner asked Obama about racial profiling at airports, which he addressed by talking about America’s diversity and supporting American Muslims who integrate well into society.

Obama later met Jeremy Corbyn for a long talk about technology, global corporations, and challenges facing industrial societies. He also briefly discussed Britain's EU membership debate with Corbyn. The day ended with Obama playing golf with Cameron and having dinner with the prime minister and US ambassador in Hertfordshire.

Millennials use technology a lot. More than eight in ten sleep with their mobile phones near them, and almost two thirds admit to texting while driving. One in five has posted a video of themselves online, and three quarters have made a profile on social media.

Compared to other groups, millennials are the most active on social media. In 2010, 75% had at least one social media account, compared to only 50% of Generation X, 30% of baby boomers, and 6% aged 65 and older.

Here are some millennials who don't use social media:

Celan Beausoleil is a social worker from Oakland. She deactivated her Facebook in December 2015 because she found it overwhelming to see personal details from others on top of her work demands. Though she likes how social media connects people worldwide, the overload made her consider spending that time doing other things.

Mathias works for Baltimore City government and deleted his Facebook and Twitter accounts in November 2012. He enjoys having more free time and prefers calling friends rather than checking their online profiles.

Lauren Raskauskas from Naples is private about her life and deactivated her social media due to privacy concerns. She likes the control it gives her, especially during break-ups when she doesn’t have to worry about changing status updates or profile photos.

Rajagopalan at Boston College says he hasn't seen any negative effects of not using social media. He only signed up for Facebook to contact his new roommate but rarely uses it and has avoided other social accounts even though as a sports fan, Twitter is where most news breaks out.

A new study shows that large predators like brown bears, wolves, and lynx are doing well across Europe, even where there are many people. Scientists found these animals in almost one-third of mainland Europe. There are around 17,000 brown bears, 12,000 wolves, 9,000 Eurasian lynx, and 1,250 wolverines, mostly outside nature reserves.

Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, and Britain do not have any breeding populations of these large carnivores. But scientists think that even in places like Britain, it could be possible to bring back big predators.

Wolves can live in areas with up to 3,050 people per square kilometer, more than the population density of cities like Cambridge or Newcastle. On average, wolves live where there are about 37 people per sq km, lynx where there are 21 people per sq km, and bears among 19 people per sq km.

The success in Europe is partly because of a "land-sharing" model that lets predators and people live together rather than separating them. This approach works with political stability, support for protecting prey animals like deer, and helping farmers with non-lethal ways to protect their livestock, such as electric fences. The EU Habitats Directive has been very important in this success.

George Monbiot, who is starting a new charity called Rewilding Britain, said it’s great that these species are returning but noted that Britain has lost more large mammals than most other countries and needs to do more to bring them back. He thinks the reintroduction of lynx into Scotland could be successful if it works in other parts of Europe.

The view from Doñana National Park in southern Spain is amazing for bird lovers. This park covers 200,000 hectares of salt marshes and is very important for birds migrating between Africa and Western Europe. The park also has rare birds like the Spanish imperial eagle and endangered animals like the Iberian lynx.

In 1998, a dam burst at Los Frailes mine, 45km north of Doñana, causing almost two billion gallons of toxic water to flow into the river that runs through the park. The water was acidic and full of waste metals, which killed more than 25,000 kilos of fish and nearly 2,000 birds.

Cleaning up after this disaster cost €90 million. Spain then spent an additional €360 million to restore parts of Doñana that were drained for rice and cotton fields back into wetlands.

However, the park still faces threats like plans for a new oil pipeline through it and more tourist development, which could harm water supplies. The Andalucían government has also decided to reopen the Los Frailes mine that caused the 1998 disaster.

Laurence Rose from the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) says reopening the mine is very worrying because Doñana already faces many threats as Europe's most important bird sanctuary. But local authorities want mining jobs to help the economy after Spain’s financial crash in 2008, which caused high unemployment.

The government promises modern mining techniques will be used at Los Frailes that won't make toxic waste water. Still, some people like Carlos Dávila from the Spanish Ornithological Society fear it could harm eco-tourism, an important business for Doñana where tourists come to see birds nesting in trees and flying around.

Laurence Rose warns Spain doesn’t have enough resources now to deal with another disaster as harmful as the one in 1998. Carlos Dávila says people are forgetting how important it is to protect this unique place.

In the UK, there's no law that forces restaurants to give tips to workers. This was found in a government study from May 2016 where customers, employers, and employees shared their thoughts on tipping. The government plans to change rules so low-paid staff get the money left for them.

Some waiters are charged up to 15% of card tips as an admin fee. There's also evidence that waiters might have to pay extra if they don’t make enough in tips to cover these fees. The government wants to stop restaurants from taking any fees or making deductions from tips.

The government also wants to make tipping more clear for customers by asking restaurants to show their tip rules openly.

We asked some UK waiters about the tipping process and how it could be better:

1. Rodri, 37, London: 
- Around half of a waiter’s pay comes from tips.
- He gets an average of £60 in tips per eight-hour shift but can make more than £100 on good nights or less than £40 on bad ones.
- After a tipping scandal in 2015, things improved for many workers. However, some still face unfair treatment like having to pay part of their tips toward admin fees.

2. Elle, 22, Edinburgh:
- She gets around £20 in tips per eight-hour shift.
- At her main restaurant job, she doesn't get the tips but makes minimum wage plus extra money.
- In France, waiting tables is seen as a secure and well-paying job without relying on tips.

3. Ashley, 22, London:
- He averages £10-£15 in tips per eight-hour shift after sharing with others.
- Tips are also used to cover broken items by customers or staff.
- In Australia, waiters get paid better wages and don’t depend as much on tips.

4. Tom, Manchester: 
- His tips average around £40 a night, helping him pay expenses like rent.
- He thinks Italy does tipping right; people round up their bills instead of adding extra charges.

In Britain, tea, baked beans on toast, and fish and chips have been popular for a long time. But tastes are changing, according to a study by the government that started in 1940 because of health concerns.

Even though Britons love tea, they drink much less now than before. In the 1970s, people drank about 68g of tea per week, but now it is only 25g. That means today’s average person drinks just eight cups a week compared to 23 in 1974.

The study has data from 150,000 homes over the years and shows that some eating habits are getting healthier. People drink more low-calorie sodas and less whole milk. They also eat more fresh fruit. However, they consume a lot more chips, pizza, crisps, and ready meals now.

There’s been a big change from white bread to brown, but people are eating fewer slices overall — about 15 per week compared with 25 in the past. Baked beans have dropped by one-fifth. Adults now eat around 75g of pizza each week, while pasta consumption has almost tripled.

The study also shows that fresh potatoes have become less important in people’s diets, decreasing by 67%. Other vegetables like cucumbers and mushrooms are eaten more often now. Takeaway food has nearly doubled from 80g per person a week to 150g, with chips and meat being popular choices.

Fruit consumption is up by 50% since the 1970s. In 2014, UK adults ate an average of 157g of fruit daily — almost two of the five portions recommended by the government. Bananas are the most favored, with each adult eating about 221g per week.

The study also shows that Britons spend less on food now, at just 11% of their pay compared to 24% in 1974.

Elizabeth Truss, the UK Environment Secretary, says this data highlights how culture has changed what people eat and can help predict future trends.

Agios Efstratios is a remote island that is largely ignored by banks and the government. There are no ATMs or credit-card machines on the island. Before Greece's financial crisis, residents managed well by banking at the post office. Visitors booked rooms every summer for its beaches, clear seas, and fresh seafood.

Now, because everything runs on cash, closing banks have made life hard. People must travel nine hours round trip to get money, and tourists say they can’t gather enough funds to visit. Mayor Maria Kakali says tourist numbers are down 80%. Even people from Athens who own homes here aren't coming.

Kakali is trying to get a bank or ATM installed but thinks it may come too late for this season. Tourism is the main source of income, along with fishing and agriculture. There are almost no reservations in August when usually many ask for rooms.

A bigger problem is that the government plans to end a tax break for islands. This lower sales tax was meant to help island communities survive as everything had to be imported, making living costs high and tourism more affordable. Mayor Kakali says if they have to pay 23% tax, life will become very difficult because food and fuel are already expensive.

Agios Efstratios has only three shops and two restaurants in summer, with no official hotels. Lemnos, a nearby island, also faces problems. In 2015, the government hired a new ferry company that brought many visitors but then bank controls hit.

For Agios Efstratios and Lemnos, this crisis timing is tough as they were just starting to attract more visitors. Mayor Dimitris Marinakis of Lemnos says recent economic struggles will worsen with tax increases. He believes reduced spending will harm the economy.

The crisis hits young people hard who often work multiple jobs but still can't afford families. They fear leaving like their grandparents did years ago. If taxes rise, even more young people may leave.

Mayor Kakali hopes to prevent this by improving education on Agios Efstratios and possibly traveling to Athens with school children to remind the government about island needs. She says the government doesn’t pay much attention to northern Aegean islands.

Scientists have connected the brains of two rats, allowing them to share sensory information. This is a step towards what they call an "organic computer." The team from Duke University and Brazil used devices called brain-to-brain interfaces that let the rats work together on tasks to get rewards like water.

In one test, when the first rat pressed a lever after seeing a light, its brain signals were sent to the second rat's brain. The second rat then pressed the right lever 70% of the time without seeing any light.

The scientists also connected rats in different places using the internet. One rat was in North Carolina and another in Brazil. They still managed to share information.

Miguel Nicolelis, who leads this research, says they can connect multiple brains to share data. This could help solve more complex tasks that one brain cannot do alone.

Anders Sandberg from Oxford University thinks sharing sensory information is important but does not mean the rats will plan together or become smarter than usual. He says there's no risk of "rat multiborgs" taking over, and thoughts are hard to transmit accurately anyway.

Thousands of people protested against killing sharks on Australia’s beaches. They asked the state's leader to stop it. Richard Branson, who owns Virgin Atlantic, and RSPCA Australia did not like this plan either.

The government started catching and killing sharks longer than three meters after many shark attacks in Western Australia. A surfer, 35 years old, died in November 2013, becoming the sixth person to die from a shark attack in two years.

However, across all of Australia, there is only one shark-related death per year on average over the last fifty years. Kate Faehrmann, from Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, said at a protest in Perth: “Drumlines used to catch sharks can also hurt dolphins and turtles.”

People protested in cities like Perth, Sydney, Adelaide, and at beaches in Victoria and Queensland. Surfer Anthony Joyce said killing some sharks would not make much difference.

The state government does not say how many sharks they have killed but some think smaller sharks were released after being caught on drumlines. Conservationists claim there is no proof that the cull will reduce shark attacks because no other culls only used drumlines before.

Researchers at the University of Western Australia say more shark attacks may be due to Western Australia having a fast-growing population, not an increase in sharks.

Richard Peirce from the Shark Trust charity said the cull could bring more predators close to the coast. “It is sad that the government chose this ineffective and counterproductive method.”

In 2012, there were 80 shark attacks worldwide with seven being fatal. Humans kill nearly 100 million sharks each year.

RSPCA Australia thinks the rise in attacks is due to more people in the water, not more sharks. Richard Branson said killing sharks will scare tourists and hurt tourism.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) asked Washington to fix its money issues after the US almost had a debt default. Also, federal workers came back to work after 16 days without pay due to the government shutdown. President Barack Obama said the country should stop dealing with problems at the last minute.

Christine Lagarde, who leads the IMF, wanted more stability in financial decisions. She suggested raising the debt limit for a longer time and encouraged approving a budget for 2014 and replacing cuts that could hurt economic growth. 

The Senate made a deal to avoid another crisis which passed through the House of Representatives just before a deadline to extend the US debt limit.

Jim Yong Kim, who leads the World Bank, was relieved but asked policymakers worldwide to focus on promoting economic growth and jobs.

Stock markets showed some relief in Asia, but there were expectations for more battles over money in Washington at the start of 2014. The shutdown cost the US about $24 billion according to Standard & Poor’s. China, the biggest lender to the US government, was upset that this crisis could put their investments at risk.

Obama signed a bill just before midnight on Thursday which avoided default and had wide support in the Senate. This deal only fixes issues until January 15th for funding and February 7th for raising debt limits.

Obama hoped this agreement would end uncertainty but indicated he did not want more budget fights next year. He said, "We have to stop governing by crisis." 

Republican Senator Mike Lee was still defiant, saying they will keep trying the right thing even if it leads to more trouble ahead. However, polls showed that voters blamed Republicans for causing the crisis and none of their goals were achieved with this deal.

What does it feel like to see something that will soon disappear forever? Sudan is the last male northern white rhino on Earth. If he doesn’t mate with one of two female rhinos at Ol Pejeta Conservancy in Kenya, there won't be any more northern white rhinos left. At 42 years old, Sudan's chances are slim. There are only two other northern white rhinos in the world, both females and kept in zoos.

Sudan is protected by armed guards who watch over him carefully. However, poachers still threaten to kill him for his horn to sell on the Asian medicine market, even though his horn has been cut off to stop them.

Sudan doesn’t know how special he is. He looks sad as he wanders around with his guards. His head is strong and made of bone and tough skin, a symbol of great strength. But this powerful head is also very vulnerable. Sudan holds his head low under the dark sky, like it’s weighed down by his fate.

His legs look short compared to his big body, similar to rhinos from long ago. In 1515, an artist named Albrecht Dürer drew a rhino that looked much like Sudan. People have been fascinated by these animals for thousands of years.

People have been killing the things they love since ancient times. Beautiful pictures of woolly rhinos were painted in French caves up to 30,000 years ago. As the climate changed at the end of the Ice Age, human hunting likely led to their extinction.

Today, despite people’s efforts to protect them, rhinos are being killed for their horns more than ever before. In South Africa alone, from 13 poached rhinos in 2007, the number rose to over 1,200 in 2014 and continues to rise.

The northern white rhino is almost extinct because of this hunting. Other types of African rhinos are also being killed by poachers. The Javan rhinoceros is nearly gone too. Even though India has protected its rhinos from British hunters, poaching remains a serious problem there as well. It’s sad to see such great creatures threatened by human actions.

Have we learned nothing since the Ice Age?

James Bond is in one of the world’s longest-running movie series with 23 films earning over $6 billion globally. The character shows no signs of slowing down. Skyfall, released in 2012, became the highest-grossing film at the UK box office and earned a total of $1.1 billion, ranking ninth all-time.

The announcement for the 24th Bond movie, titled Spectre, has created great interest. People wonder if Spectre can match Skyfall's success.

Charles Gant from Heat magazine says that Skyfall was smart because it appealed to both new and old fans by mixing modern elements with nostalgic ones. The title "Spectre" seems promising as it aims to keep the diverse Bond fan base interested.

Eon Productions, the company behind all official Bonds since Dr No in 1961, is working hard to make Spectre successful like Skyfall was. They kept key creative people from Skyfall on board for Spectre, including director Sam Mendes and writers.

Skyfall almost doubled Quantum of Solace’s earnings, which made $586 million in 2008. While no one expects Spectre to earn as much, Eon is not being careless about the film's success.

The Bond series had some dull moments before Daniel Craig and Sam Mendes joined. The films lost excitement towards Pierce Brosnan's end but recovered with new energy under Craig and Mendes.

Bond has gone through changes since Sean Connery first played him. Each lead actor brought a different style, and some worked better than others. Roger Moore’s later movies did not excite audiences much, while Brosnan had commercial success and Craig took the series to new heights.

Skyfall's earnings are huge compared to other Bond films, but when adjusted for inflation, older Bonds like Thunderball, Goldfinger, and You Only Live Twice performed almost as well. Licence to Kill is still considered the least successful Bond film.

The Bond brand has stayed powerful over decades despite legal battles with rival companies trying to use the series’ popularity. Two movies, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again (Thunderball) in 1983, were made outside Eon Productions due to rights issues. MGM and Sony settled these disputes by 2013.

Goldeneye, with Pierce Brosnan as Bond, marked a big renewal after Licence to Kill’s poor performance. Director Martin Campbell helped modernize the series with impressive stunts in Goldeneye's opening scene and a successful video game spin-off that reached a new audience.

An agreement to improve safety in Bangladesh’s clothing factories might face legal action because factory owners want money for closing their factories and doing repairs. Some repairs are expected to take months, and owners say they can’t afford to pay workers during this time or cover the cost of major repairs needed to make buildings safe.

This comes after a building called Rana Plaza collapsed in Dhaka, Bangladesh’s capital city, in 2013, killing 1,138 people. Now, hundreds of factories are being checked each month for fire and structural safety under an agreement called the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh. This accord is supported by over 170 international brands like Primark and Marks & Spencer, along with trade unions such as IndustriALL.

One factory owner from Dhaka, Softex Cotton, has threatened legal action against the Accord after his factory was closed due to structural issues. He wants $100 million in compensation. Another unnamed owner said closing a factory for even a few months would result in losing orders and permanently shutting down: “There is no such thing as temporary closure.” The owner argued that the Accord did not clearly state who would pay for closures.

Jenny Holdcroft, policy director at IndustriALL, said that brands have agreed to keep ordering from factories during their closures. So far, 12 factories need major work, but many can continue operating on other floors while repairs are done. The Accord also ensures workers get paid during factory closures. Holdcroft explained that the details about who pays for what were left open so that owners could contribute if they could afford it.

Shaidullah Azim from the Bangladeshi Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association said another group called the Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety, supported by US retailers like Walmart and Gap, has set aside $5 million to pay workers while repairs are done. This pressure makes factory owners demand more support from the Accord to help their workers during closures.

Oxfam says the huge wealth of the richest 100 billionaires is making inequality worse and making it harder to fight poverty. These rich people often get richer at the expense of low-wage workers who do not have secure jobs or decent pay. 

If these 100 richest people gave away their $240 billion income from 2012, they could help end extreme poverty four times over. But very few billionaires are sharing this wealth.

In a report called "The Cost of Inequality: How Wealth and Income Extremes Hurt Us All," Oxfam says world leaders should reduce inequality to levels seen in 1990. The richest 1% have increased their incomes by 60% over the past 20 years, and this trend has sped up since the financial crisis.

Barbara Stocking from Oxfam said extreme wealth can hurt economies, politics, society, and the environment. In the UK, inequality is getting worse like it was in Charles Dickens' time. In China, the top 10% earn almost 60% of income, which makes it one of the most unequal countries on Earth.

In the US, the richest 1% now get twice as much national income compared to 1980. The report says reducing inequality could help growth and investment. World leaders should close tax havens where up to $31 trillion is hidden, which could raise $189 billion in taxes.

David Cameron stated that there is a “clear result” from the Scottish independence referendum. The vote showed that Scotland decided not to separate from England and Wales by 10.6 points. Cameron promised big changes, including letting English MPs vote on issues affecting only England. He said, "We have heard the settled will of the Scottish people."

Alex Salmond, Scotland’s first minister, accepted that Scotland had voted against independence for now. However, he said he would work with Westminster to push for more power for Scotland.

The yes campaign won in Glasgow, Dundee, and North Lanarkshire but lost overall. The no campaign got 2,001,926 votes (55.3%) compared to the yes campaign's 1,617,989 votes (44.7%).

Cameron stated that changes would start after the general election. He said they need to listen to people in England too.

Ed Miliband promised stronger powers for Scotland and change across the UK. Nick Clegg agreed with this view, saying the referendum showed a need for more power for Scotland while also wanting wider reforms.

However, some Conservative MPs might disagree with Cameron’s plan to give more power to Scotland quickly.

Nigel Farage of the UK Independence Party said that England needs better representation too since Scottish MPs can vote on English issues. He believes there should be a fair settlement.

Cameron and Queen Elizabeth II will make statements to calm any tensions after the referendum result.

Ministers want to act fast to avoid problems like those in Québec, where behavior after a similar vote led to more support for separation later.

The no campaign was relieved that they won because recent polls showed the result could have gone either way.

Brazilian singer Anitta is famous for bringing favela music into mainstream music. However, there’s a debate about her skin color change since becoming popular.

Some people say she had to look less black to become successful in the white middle-class market. This was seen when old photos showed her with darker skin compared to recent images where she looks lighter. People wonder if this is because of products or changes made using Photoshop.

Jarid Arraes, a psychology student and blogger, wrote that media often discriminates against dark-skinned people. He says the lightening of Anitta’s image shows how Brazilian society favors white people over black ones.

Anitta started her career in Rio de Janeiro's baile funk scene as a dancer and singer. Now she is well-known for songs like "Show das Poderosas" which has 52 million YouTube views. She tries to connect the mostly black and mixed-race favelas with richer white communities below.

Critics ask if Anitta or her marketing team changed her image too much to attract more paying customers. This topic is sensitive in Brazil because it’s a mixed-raced nation, but there’s still inequality based on skin color.

White workers make about twice as much money as those of African descent. Black and mixed-race people often have fewer years of education than white Brazilians. Most high positions are held by white people while black and mixed-race individuals tend to do lower-paying jobs.

Anitta changed her style from the rebellious favela sound to something more acceptable for everyone. This change came with her move from a favela to mainstream music, not necessarily because of racial reasons but due to different tastes in various social groups.

Some believe Anitta’s image shift is about makeup and styling rather than changing her skin color. Leandro Silva de Souza, an activist, says the public still enjoys dark-skinned artists like Ellen Oléria who won a talent show recently.

Anitta says everyone should be able to define their own identity and that people can be powerful without needing to look beautiful but through attitude.

In 2005, Pope Benedict XVI came as a humble worker for God. On a cold February Monday in 2013, he left like an old laborer who can no longer ignore his back pain and weakening strength. He spoke to cardinals in Latin about quitting.

He said on February 28, 2013 at 8:00 PM, the seat of Rome would be empty, and a new pope needed to be chosen.

Monsignor Oscar Sanchéz Barba from Mexico was there for a different meeting. He described the room being silent after Benedict’s announcement. The cardinals were shocked and speechless.

Angelo Sodano, who knew about this decision beforehand, spoke briefly saying he and others had listened with disbelief. After his address, the Pope blessed everyone and left in silence.

John Thavis, a Vatican reporter, guessed that Benedict might resign but was wrong on the date. He thought Benedict would do it if he felt unable to manage the job due to health reasons.

The Vatican said this decision was brave because it faced reality about aging and managing a large organization. Some wonder if there were other reasons for his resignation, like unknown health issues or other concerns from his past. However, such ideas are not officially supported by the Vatican.

People are thinking about what it means when God’s representative decides to stop being chosen. Benedict felt he was no longer fit to lead and said somewhere in eight years, he stopped believing that God could work with him as a tool.

The Chemin des Dunes school has a plastic roof held up by a crooked tree trunk and desks made from old chairs. But the students study with great focus. They hope to start new lives in France.

Kamal, a 29-year-old electrical engineer from Sudan's Darfur region, attends three or four hours of classes daily. He says, "The French language is very hard, but we try our best. If we keep coming every day, maybe we can achieve our dreams." Kamal believes learning keeps his mind active.

Kamal and other refugees are frustrated because media only talk about people trying to sneak into the UK at night from the camp outside Calais. He says, "I need to tell people in the UK that not everyone wants to go there. Many of us want to stay in France."

France has more than 250,000 refugees, according to the United Nations. This is twice as many as the UK even though both countries have similar populations.

There are also 56,000 asylum seekers waiting for their claims to be processed in France and 36,000 in the UK. While waiting, France does not give financial support or allow refugees to work. The process can take months, so many stay at the camp where they get a free meal and shelter every day.

Zimarco Jones started the school this summer because students were bored of waiting and nervous about starting life in France without knowing the language. It opened on July 11th with French classes as well as English, art, and t'ai chi. The Nigerian founder is now planning to build another classroom.

George, a refugee from Darfur who wanted to cross to the UK because he speaks fluent English, says that after two weeks of classes he decided to stay in France instead. He says, "Anywhere there is peace, I can live."

Local teachers are volunteering at the school during their summer holidays. Jenny Flahaut, 33, a worker from a children’s home, joined after seeing an advertisement on Facebook. She wants to help people in Calais and disagrees with how migrants are shown by media and politicians.

The volunteers plan to set up a separate classroom for around 200 women and two dozen children as there are ten times more men than women at the camp and many women feel uncomfortable studying with male students they don’t know. Zimarco dreams of making the camp a place where people can live, not just survive. He wants to start a football team and change its name from "the jungle" because he says it implies that residents aren't human.

"We have a disco, a house, a mosque, a school, and shops," Zimarco explains. "We are not animals."

In Canada’s Arctic, summers have almost 24 hours of sunlight every day. For Muslims in Iqaluit, Nunavut, this makes fasting during Ramadan very hard because they must fast from sunrise to sunset.

Abdul Karim, a 29-year-old man who moved from Ottawa to Iqaluit in 2011, has been fasting for over 20 hours each day. This year, he eats at about 1:30 AM and breaks his fast around 11 PM. He will stop only if it harms his health.

In Iqaluit, most Muslims follow the timetable of Ottawa or Mecca to manage their fasting during Ramadan. Atif Jilani, who moved from Toronto in 2015, says this means fasting for about 18 hours daily but is more manageable than following the local sunrise and sunset.

The small Muslim community in Iqaluit usually gathers at the city's new mosque for nightly suppers during Ramadan. They eat traditional foods like dates and curries even though it’s still bright outside.

Nazim Awan, president of the Yellowknife Islamic Centre, says Muslims in Yellowknife have several choices for fasting times. Most follow Edmonton's timetable, which is about 15 hours daily. Ahmad Alkhalaf, who moved from Toronto to Inuvik, follows Edmonton's schedule because there’s no sunset or sunrise.

The Muslim community in Iqaluit and other northern areas adjusts their Ramadan practices due to the unique daylight conditions. They strive for balance between religious observance and local traditions, sometimes including local game like reindeer in their meals.

Abdul Karim says that despite the current challenges, he will continue his practice because one day Ramadan will occur during winter when days are shorter.

The Senate Intelligence Committee approved a bill that lets the National Security Agency (NSA) keep collecting Americans' phone records but adds some transparency. Sponsored by Dianne Feinstein, it allows NSA to collect and store metadata in 90-day periods. Some lawmakers want phone companies to hold this data instead. The bill passed with an 11-4 vote.

The bill lets analysts look at the data if they think there is a 'reasonable suspicion' of ties to international terrorism. It also allows surveillance on foreigners entering the US for up to 72 hours.

Senator Patrick Leahy proposed another bill that would stop the collection of domestic phone records, but it was opposed by Mark Udall and Ron Wyden who said it doesn’t change enough.

Feinstein defended the NSA’s collection program as legal and useful for national security. She stated the new bill will make several improvements to oversight such as requiring an annual public report on how many times the data leads to FBI investigations, limiting who can query the database, imposing criminal penalties for unauthorized access, and restricting the number of contacts from a query.

Feinstein told reporters that the NSA program is vital for protecting the country. However, independent experts think this bill may clash with another one introduced by Leahy and Jim Sensenbrenner called the USA Freedom Act. The Freedom Act would stop the bulk collection of Americans’ phone records.

Wyden noted that concerns about foreign spying have overshadowed domestic surveillance in the US. Wyden emphasized his main goal is to end mass surveillance on millions of law-abiding Americans, stating that people do not want to give up their rights for security.

Feinstein said she opposes NSA spying on foreign leaders like Angela Merkel but supports collecting American phone records. She also mentioned James Clapper agreed to write her about a report claiming the NSA intercepted data between Google and Yahoo centers. Wyden thinks this has implications for Americans' privacy, as global communications make it harder to spy on foreigners without affecting US citizens.

Noise from passing ships can greatly disturb animals like killer whales and dolphins more than we thought before. New research shows that this noise might make it harder for these animals to communicate with each other and find food. The low rumble of ships was already known to bother large whales, but now scientists have found that the noise is also happening at higher frequencies, where killer whales hear best.

This kind of disturbance could prevent killer whales from communicating and using echolocation, a way they use sound to locate objects like prey. Dolphins and porpoises might face similar issues since they also use high-frequency sounds. The research suggests this noise may affect the endangered population of 84 killer whales that live near shipping lanes along the US west coast.

Scott Veirs from Beamreach, who led the study, said even a small increase in sound could make it more difficult for killer whales to use echolocation. He explained this is concerning because their main food source, chinook salmon, is already rare. Hearing a click off a fish is very hard for these animals, and noise makes it harder.

The scientists measured underwater sounds from about 1,600 ships passing through Haro Strait in Washington State over two years. They recorded the noise made by different types of ships that pass through the area around 20 times each day.

On average, the noise next to all these ships was very loud at 173 underwater decibels, which is similar to a loud rock concert when heard through air. However, whales are usually farther from ships and would experience sounds more like a lawnmower or vacuum cleaner around 60 to 90 decibels.

Veirs mentioned that scientists know noise affects baleen whales but pointed out the new research highlights risks for smaller whales, dolphins, and porpoises. He said while ships were known as low-frequency noise sources, their study found increased high-frequency noise too.

Noise can cause problems like making whales group closer to hear each other or use up fat stores more quickly if they have trouble finding food. This is dangerous because the fat contains manmade toxins that are harmful when released into their bodies.

Veirs suggested ways to reduce ship noise, such as slowing down ships and using quieter technologies from military vessels on commercial ones. Slowing a ship by six knots can cut noise intensity in half.

While some whale species like humpbacks have improved with less whaling, others still face threats including ship noise. The US government has protected large areas of the Atlantic to help endangered North Atlantic right whales.

In Europe, killer whales carry high levels of banned PCB chemicals, and scientists are investigating whether pollutants caused the deaths of stranded sperm whales in Britain. In Australia, whales face risks from ships, oil drilling, and Japan's plans to resume whaling in Antarctic waters.

The balls have fallen into place and matched all six numbers, meaning it's time to celebrate big by buying a car like an Audi, planning a trip to the US, or looking for new homes. This is what many lottery winners do, based on how they spend their money.

Since starting in 1994, the UK Lottery has made around 3,000 millionaires who have won more than £8.5 billion total, with each winning about £2.8 million. These winners have also helped create an additional 3,780 millionaires among their family and friends.

Most winners (59%) stop working right away after they win, while some (19%) continue to work, and others (31%) volunteer. The study by Oxford Economics shows that 98% of the spending by lottery winners stays in the UK. Each winner keeps six people employed full-time for a year through their purchases.

The winners have added almost £750 million to the UK's GDP and given more than £500 million in taxes. They spent most on homes, with about £2.72 billion on main properties and £170 million paying off debts. About £2.125 billion went into investments, £1.17 billion were gifts to family and friends, and £680 million was for cars and vacations.

This study by Camelot, the company that runs the UK Lottery, looked at 100 winners who each won more than £1 million. The findings show that over 3,000 winners have bought 7,958 homes in the UK, or around 2.7 per winner, spending about £3.3 billion.

Most winners (82%) changed their main home, on average spending about £900,000 each. Many winners put things like a hot tub (29%), walk-in wardrobes (28%), electric gates (24%), and games rooms (22%) into their new homes. A small number of winners also hired beauticians.

Winners tend to buy Audis the most (16%), followed by Range Rovers, BMWs, Mercedes, and Land Rovers. They have spent £463 million on 17,190 cars, with an average car costing around £46,116.

For holidays, about 27% of winners chose the US as their favorite destination, followed by the Caribbean (9%). However, some UK caravan sales also got a boost from winners; over 18 years, 10% bought a caravan worth about £7.4 million in total.

Some winners started businesses themselves (15%), helped others start businesses (9%), or invested in other businesses (6%). These business activities have created jobs for around 3,195 people.

Andy Logan, who wrote the report, said that winning lottery money changes not only the winner's life but also those of friends and family. It has a big effect on the UK economy because most winners spend their money in the UK.

DNA from a wisdom tooth of a European hunter-gatherer has given scientists an important look at early humans before farming began. This Mesolithic man, who lived around 7,000 years ago in Spain, had blue eyes, black or brown hair, and dark skin according to his genes.

He likely could not digest milk well and had trouble with starchy foods compared to farmers who started the first agricultural revolution. With farming, humans got closer to animals and needed stronger immune systems to avoid diseases from these animals. However, tests on this hunter-gatherer’s DNA show he already had genetic changes that helped boost his immune system against infections.

Carles Lalueza-Fox of the Institute of Evolutionary Biology in Barcelona led the study. He said most of his initial ideas about what they would find were wrong.

In 2006, a group of cavers found two skeletons in a cave in northwest Spain. The remains belonged to two men aged around thirty and were well preserved by the cool conditions in the cave. Carbon dating placed them at around 7,000 years old, before farming came from the Middle East.

The scientists focused on one skeleton that was better preserved and managed to reconstruct the man’s whole genome using DNA from a wisdom tooth. This is the first time researchers have obtained the complete genome of a modern European who lived before the Neolithic revolution.

Surprisingly, the man had dark skin despite having blue eyes, which suggests blue eye color appeared in Europe earlier than lighter skin. The scientists also noted that artists often show Mesolithic people with light skin instead of dark skin and blue eyes.

Comparing this hunter-gatherer’s genome to modern Europeans showed his DNA most closely matched people from northern Europe like Sweden and Finland. This indicates some genetic changes related to immune system function existed before the shift to farming cultures in Neolithic times.

Martin Jones, a professor at Cambridge University, noted that while moving from hunting and gathering to settled farming likely had negative health effects due to living closer with animals and water crowding, this study highlights the role of pathogens even before agriculture.

Modern chemists often wait a long time for new elements but recently four were discovered at once by researchers from Japan, Russia, and the US. These new elements complete the seventh row on the periodic table and make many science textbooks outdated. They are very short-lived and highly radioactive.

The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), which makes rules about chemical names, confirmed these four elements on December 30, 2015. Scientists now need to give them official names instead of the current placeholder names: ununtrium, ununpentium, ununseptium, and ununoctium. These placeholders show their atomic numbers which are 113, 115, 117, and 118.

The elements were found by teams in Japan, Russia, and the US. The Japanese team will name element 113, making Japan the first Asian country to do so. Elements can be named after mythological concepts, minerals, places or countries, or scientists.

Scientists hope that understanding these new elements better could help with dealing with nuclear waste and lead to new technologies. They must also suggest two-letter symbols for the elements before IUPAC reviews them.

To find these elements, researchers combined lighter nuclei and looked for signs of radioactive decay. The properties of the new elements are not fully known because only a few atoms have been made. 

Paul Karol from IUPAC said that understanding these heavy elements could help nuclear theorists learn more about very heavy nuclei. Any practical use of these new elements is far away due to how hard they are to make.

Prince Harry flew out of Afghanistan after completing a four-month mission. During this time, he admitted to killing insurgents while flying his Apache helicopter and talked about the stress of being part of the royal family.

Harry also expressed frustration with some media outlets and mentioned how his father often reminded him to behave more like a member of the royal family. He piloted an Apache helicopter that helped protect soldiers on the ground but said it mostly served as a deterrent against enemy attacks.

In interviews, Prince Harry talked about managing three different roles: his army life, social time, and duties with his family. Sometimes he would act in ways that were not expected of a prince because he wanted more privacy.

Harry criticized newspapers like the Sun, Daily Mail, and Daily Telegraph for articles comparing him to World War II pilots, which he felt was unfair. He also mentioned how reading about himself in the media made him upset, even though his father advised him not to read it.

The prince began his Afghanistan mission in September of last year, operating a £45 million Apache helicopter that supported NATO troops and helped rescue wounded soldiers. During an earlier tour, he had to leave quickly after a magazine broke news about his presence there.

Harry was asked if he felt more comfortable as Captain Wales than Prince Harry. He said yes because it was easier to forget his royal status when in the army with other soldiers who wore the same uniform.

Before leaving for Afghanistan, Prince Harry faced criticism over party pictures that showed him naked in Las Vegas. He admitted this behavior let him down but also blamed a lack of privacy expected by the media.

Harry and his brother were interested in helicopters because they could avoid too much attention, unlike with other modes of transport where more people might follow them.

A new study shows that Earth's temperature could rise by a minimum of 4 degrees Celsius (7.2 degrees Fahrenheit) by the year 2100 if greenhouse gas emissions are not reduced. This increase is twice what world governments think is dangerous.

Professor Steven Sherwood from the University of New South Wales in Australia led this research. He explained that as Earth gets warmer, fewer clouds form, which means less sunlight is reflected back into space and temperatures rise even more.

Sherwood said that a 4-degree Celsius temperature increase would likely be very bad for life on Earth. It could make living conditions difficult or impossible in many tropical areas and cause the Greenland ice sheet to melt completely along with parts of Antarctica's ice sheets, leading to significant rises in sea levels.

The study also shows that clouds play a big role in climate change. Before this research, scientists weren't sure how much warming would happen from increases in carbon emissions. This new information helps narrow down those estimates and suggests the temperature increase will be on the higher side of previous projections.

When water evaporates from oceans, it can rise high enough to form rain clouds that reflect sunlight or not rise far enough to form no clouds at all. Computer models now show that both processes happen in reality, leading to predictions of significantly higher temperatures than before.

Sherwood noted that while some people doubt climate change predictions, the new study suggests these doubts are unfounded because they rely on models predicting less warming, which may be incorrect.

Global average air temperatures have increased more slowly since 1998 due to an ocean phenomenon called El Niño. However, heat is still being trapped by greenhouse gases and mostly absorbed into the oceans.

A November 2013 study suggested that the recent pause in temperature rises might not be real but could result from a lack of temperature readings in polar regions where warming is greatest.

Sherwood acknowledged his team's work on clouds does not completely rule out lower temperature increases. However, for this to happen, there would need to be new information showing something significant we don't know yet about the climate system. 

He concluded that if global average temperatures rise by at least 4 degrees Celsius by 2100 and no action is taken to reduce emissions, it will have big impacts on the world and the economies of many countries.

From glow-in-the-dark trees to underground bike storage and solar-powered trash cans, we explore some unique ideas that could make our cities better places to live. City life often brings pollution, traffic jams, and loss of green spaces. Inventors are trying new things to solve these problems.

1 Pop-up parks: Instead of car parks, people can turn empty parking spots into small parks with plants and trees. This idea started in San Francisco as an art project and has spread globally.

2 Subterranean storage: To keep bikes safe, a Tokyo firm designed an underground bike park that holds 204 bikes in a cylinder seven meters wide. It is anti-seismic and retrieves bikes within 13 seconds with the touch of a button.

3 Glow-in-the-dark trees: Dutch designer Daan Roosegaarde created plants that glow using DNA from marine bacteria mixed with plant genes, aiming to eventually replace street lights.

4 Footfall harvesting: Special tiles in pedestrian walkways capture energy from people's steps and convert it into electricity. This technology powers streetlights and has been installed at London’s Heathrow Airport.

5 Supertrees: In Singapore, large steel trees up to 50 meters high have flowers and ferns growing on them. They absorb and disperse heat, collect rainwater, and provide air ventilation for nearby conservatories. Some supertrees also have solar panels.

6 Water-producing billboard: A special billboard in Lima traps humidity from the air and turns it into drinking water using condensers and filters. It produces about 96 liters of water each day that people can drink for free.

7 Neo-walled gardens: Walls are now being used to grow plants without soil, improving aesthetics and air quality. British firm Biotecture installs these "living walls" on buildings like the Taj Hotel in London.

8 Algae-powered building: In Hamburg, an apartment complex uses algae growing on its south-facing facades to produce energy through photosynthesis. The harvested algae is used for electricity production.

9 Smart rubbish bins: Solar-powered trash compactors can hold up to 150 gallons of waste and use solar panels on their lids for power. They send notifications when full, reducing the need for frequent garbage collection.

10 Spray paint: In China’s city Chengdu, authorities spray yellowing grass green to keep the city looking bright. This non-toxic method is now used in other cities as well.

The 1985 film "Back to the Future II" predicted flying cars, but today smartphones and other new technologies are making life exciting. Changes in economics, demographics, technology, and the environment are changing how people travel.

Robert Puentes from the Brookings Institution says it's a fast-changing time for transportation. As Americans spend more time commuting and old infrastructure gets worse, cities need to rethink their transport systems. Old models that focus only on cars aren't enough anymore because of growing populations and carbon emissions. Now, transportation is important for making cities sustainable.

Cities like Los Angeles, Seattle, and Chicago are adding bus lanes, walkways, and rail options. They're also working with companies to create self-driving cars and smart technology that lets vehicles talk to each other and the roads around them.

A study from UCLA found that people born between 1980 and 2000 make fewer car trips and drive less than previous generations did at their age. Younger drivers use apps like Waze, which helps find faster routes but can also cause more traffic in neighborhoods.

The rise of ride-sharing services such as Uber and Lyft is changing how people move around cities. Experts say that communication between vehicles and infrastructure will improve transport even more. Right now, traffic lights only know a car is approaching, but future technology could let cars tell traffic systems where they are going and how fast they're moving.

Driverless cars have been tested since 2012, but it's not clear when they'll be common. Partial automation of cars is already happening, like automated buses or trucks in specific areas. Driverless cars can improve safety by reducing human errors and make driving more efficient. However, because the average car on the road is about 11 years old, it will take time for driverless technology to become widespread.

As countries try to avoid serious climate change, new policies could lead to fewer-emission vehicles and apps that encourage biking or carpooling. In the future, people might use a single transit pass to access different kinds of transport in one day.

People travel for work, family visits, or shopping. Technologies like virtual meetings can reduce the need for trips. While flying cars were once seen as high-tech, new technologies are even more advanced and could help deal with future social and environmental issues.

Every morning before it gets hot in Delhi, some old friends meet near the India Gate monument. They stretch, breathe deeply, and meditate on the dry grass.

Arvind Singh, a 42-year-old salesman, says, “Doing yoga is the best way to start the day instead of eating breakfast.”

Many other people do yoga across crowded cities in India too.

On June 21st, which is the new International Day of Yoga, Prime Minister Narendra Modi hopes many people will join in. In Delhi, up to 45,000 people might gather near India Gate for a big yoga event that lasts 35 minutes.

The participants will include Prime Minister Modi himself and other famous people from different countries.

Modi has been encouraging more Indians to do yoga since he won the election in 2014. In May 2015, schools were told to make sure students attended yoga events on a Sunday. There are also plans for police officers and civil servants to have free yoga lessons. Air India says it will teach trainee pilots how to do yoga.

Some politicians think more people doing yoga could help reduce sexual violence in the country.

Modi suggested an international day of yoga when he spoke at the United Nations in New York in 2014, saying that yoga is a gift from ancient Indian tradition and can help with health and climate change. Yoga is between 3,000 to 6,000 years old and began on the Indian subcontinent.

Some people think Modi’s focus on yoga might not be fair to other traditions in India. But others say that yoga does not have to be tied to any one religion. Suneel Singh, a guru from south Delhi, adds, “Yoga is for everyone and it keeps you healthy at little cost.”

Harvey Goldsmith, a famous music promoter in Britain who has worked with major artists like the Rolling Stones and Madonna, says the large summer music festivals, such as Glastonbury, might end soon. He said at the Hay Festival in Wales that there are too many festivals but not enough big bands to perform.

In 2014, about 900 music festivals happened between May and September in the UK. Goldsmith thinks most of them cannot continue because new big acts aren’t emerging. He says young people now prefer individual songs rather than full albums, which makes it hard for rock bands to build a reputation.

Goldsmith also talked about his plans with Robin de Levita to open a new 1,100-seat theater in Wembley that will stage the first adaptation of "The Hunger Games" series in June 2016. They plan to use an innovative concept called SceneAround where the audience can rotate around different scenes.

During his talk at Hay, Goldsmith shared some stories from his career. He mentioned Keith Moon putting dynamite down a hotel toilet and John Lennon’s stage fright before performing at Madison Square Garden in 1974. He also revealed why Elvis Presley never performed outside North America—it was due to the uncertain immigration status of his manager.

Goldsmith believes Freddie Mercury is one of the best live performers ever, but he says there are no new big acts forming that could headline major festivals like Glastonbury. According to him, the music festival era might be coming to an end and a rise in mixed events with poetry or magic shows may occur instead.

When two islanders found a small boat on a Pacific atoll, they went to check it out. Inside was a man named José Ivan who said he had been drifting for 16 months from Mexico, more than 12,500km away. He was very thin and only wearing old underpants.

José said he left Mexico in September 2012 with someone else who died at sea. He told Ola Fjeldstad, a student on the Marshall Islands, that he survived by catching turtles and birds without fishing equipment. The boat was damaged and missing its propellers.

The islanders took José to meet the mayor, Ione de Brum, who called officials in Majuro. They plan to send a boat or plane to pick him up once it is ready. Right now, José is staying at the local council house where he’s getting food and water. He has low blood pressure but can walk with help.

Fraser Christian teaches survival skills and says catching turtles by hand is possible since they come close to small boats. The biggest challenges are lack of water and exposure. Some people handle these conditions better than others.

In 2006, three Mexicans survived nine months at sea near the Marshall Islands on rainwater, fish, and birds. Poon Lim stayed alive for 133 days on a raft in the Atlantic before being rescued by Brazilian fishermen. Dougal Robertson and his family were saved after 38 days at sea when their boat sank.

In another case, three Mexican fishermen drifted nine months near the Marshall Islands before US coastguard helped them. A Panamanian fisherman survived 28 days alone but his friends died of thirst.

SeaWorld has seen an 84% drop in profits as fewer people visit the park. This happened after a documentary called Blackfish said SeaWorld mistreated orca whales, which made many people upset and led to three deaths. Even though SeaWorld tried to improve its image by spending $10 million on ads and lowering ticket prices, attendance still went down from 6.58 million in 2014 to 6.48 million in 2015.

SeaWorld's CEO Joel Manby says the company needs more time to recover and is working hard to change its image. The company plans new attractions like a shark exhibit and a place for swimming with dolphins, but it still faces problems, including a spying scandal where an employee joined animal rights protests against SeaWorld.

People who care about animals say families don't want to see orcas in small tanks anymore, so SeaWorld won't make more money until the whales are better treated. In August 2015, SeaWorld’s shares were worth less than half of what they were in 2013.

It was a nice summer evening and I went for a swim off Doolin Pier in County Clare, Ireland, where I moved in 2012. There was a woman swimming with Dusty, a dolphin who is very friendly with people who often swim with her.

Dusty came to Doolin around 2008, and many have swum with her since then, thinking she's completely tame. She even appeared in an Irish tourism ad where a girl wanted to touch a dolphin.

That evening, the woman was tickling Dusty’s tummy, which looked very inviting. About 20 tourists and locals were watching this from the pier. After I got into the water, Dusty left the woman she was with and became very aggressive – later, I found out she is very protective of her space when with someone else. Her tail was moving wildly at first, but then I realized she might be angry. Knowing I had to leave the water quickly, I swam towards the pier, but in a split second Dusty hit me with her snout. It was powerful and painful, pushing me forward very fast.

People on the pier were shocked as they watched this happen. The sight of Dusty’s tail flapping next to me made me fear she might hit me again, causing me to go under and possibly drown.

I reached the pier but couldn’t get out because I was hurt. Feeling terrified, I shouted for help. A man extended his arm to pull me onto the steps. Then another man came over saying he was an orthopedic surgeon with expertise in marine-related injuries. He had seen what happened on the pier as he drove into Doolin. Cold and worried about my condition, especially internal bleeding, he checked me and said I likely had broken bones but no signs of internal bleeding. Later, it turned out that I had six spinal fractures, three broken ribs, and a damaged lung.

I stayed in the hospital for five days, wore a back brace for several weeks, and was off work for five months with limited mobility, stiffness, and pain. Post-traumatic stress followed this close call; I felt anxious about everything and overreacted to situations more than before. I had trouble coping with loud noises and suffered memory loss. Three months earlier, I opened a health-food shop but had to give it up due to my injuries. That year was very tough, but now I'm recovering through craniosacral therapy, osteopathy, and massage. Today, I’m building my own osteopathy practice, which has given me new empathy for patients.

I am thankful to be healthy again and want to stop others from getting hurt. People often see dolphins as friendly creatures, so the idea of a dolphin attacking someone is surprising. Even though Dusty looked like she was smiling, she can be dangerous if provoked.

I don’t blame Dusty; I respect her. She’s wild and unpredictable, and people need to know this. Many come here to swim with her but may not understand how risky it can be. That summer reportedly saw several injuries like mine.

After the man pulled me out of the water, Dusty swam away but came back, floating next to me vertically as if she was sorry. The people on the pier were amazed when Dusty and I locked eyes, and her anger seemed gone. That moment helped end my fear, and I made peace with her.

Seeing coworkers and friends use e-cigarettes has become very common. But, have we reached the peak of vaping? Data suggests that vaping may be on the decline among smokers and recent ex-smokers who make up most vapers. This information will be closely watched by major e-cigarette companies which have invested millions in promoting e-cigarettes.

In 2014, a health charity called Action on Smoking and Health (ASH) reported that electronic cigarette usage in Britain grew from around 700,000 users in 2012 to about 2.1 million by 2014.

However, the Smoking Toolkit Study, backed by the Department of Health, shows vaping may be losing popularity. The study showed that vaping rates among smokers and ex-smokers increased until late 2013 when around 22% were using e-cigarettes. By the end of 2014, this rate dropped to about 19%, with early signs showing it continued into 2015.

Professor Robert West from UCL’s Department of Epidemiology and Public Health said that the number of smokers who use e-cigarettes while still smoking is going down. He noted that there hasn’t been much growth in long-term ex-smokers or non-smokers using e-cigarettes.

While vaping may not be growing in popularity in the UK, it seems to be increasing in the US where it has been aggressively promoted. However, West questions how accurate this data is as it does not clearly differentiate between those who have tried an e-cigarette once and those who use them regularly.

Experts say concerns about young non-smokers taking up vaping are unfounded. Only 1.8% of children regularly use e-cigarettes according to ASH research. E-cigarettes seem mostly popular among adults trying to quit smoking.

James Dunworth, director of ecigarettedirect.co.uk, pointed out that while the growth in vaping has slowed down, there was a significant increase since May 2011. He added that product improvements are helping customers switch from traditional cigarettes.

West said e-cigarettes act like an advanced nicotine patch and are more popular than patches. They are used in about one-third of quit attempts, making them the most common method for quitting smoking.

Hazel Cheeseman from ASH believes it is too early to say if vaping has peaked. Although growth seems to have slowed in the UK over the past year, there is no decline in people using e-cigarettes to stop smoking. She stated that vaping is safer than smoking and can be helpful for some people trying to quit.

Recently, the European Commission (EC) plans to increase taxes on e-cigarettes which could affect their popularity. Starting in 2016, a new EC tobacco directive will lower nicotine levels in e-cigarettes. This might make vapers use more to get the same effect and make e-cigarettes more expensive.

West suggested policymakers should view e-cigarettes as a tool for quitting smoking rather than regular cigarettes. He noted that some local authorities and organizations treat them like regular cigarettes and ban their use in public places and outdoors.

Scarlett Johansson is suing French novelist Grégoire Delacourt for €50,000 because she says his book makes false claims about her personal life.

Delacourt's novel "The First Thing We Look At" features a model who looks just like Johansson. In the story, this model goes through different adventures until it is found out that she isn't really Johansson, and then she dies in a car crash.

Johansson’s lawyer Vincent Toledano said Delacourt's book illegally uses her name, reputation, and image. He says the novel has false information about her private life. Toledano wants to stop the book from being translated or made into a movie.

Delacourt says he chose Johansson as an example of beauty today but that his character is not really her. He thinks it’s sad that she is suing him and believes judges should not be involved in such matters.

The author is known for other successful novels, like "My List of Desires," which was translated into 47 languages. Delacourt feels shocked by the lawsuit because he thought Johansson would contact him to talk instead of taking legal action.

Delacourt argues that if authors cannot mention real things in fiction, it will be hard to write stories. He believes his book is about love and beauty, not just about Scarlett Johansson.

The publisher's spokeswoman Emmanuelle Allibert says the lawsuit is crazy because the novel is about a woman who looks like Johansson but is not her. Delacourt’s lawyer Anne Veil also argues that using Johansson in this way is not commercial.

In the United States, such a case would be unlikely due to freedom of speech protections under the First Amendment. However, in France, personality rights are more strictly protected.

Delacourt was expecting flowers from Johansson as a sign of appreciation but instead got sued.

Young people in Cuba are excited about a new free internet service at a cultural center in Havana. The famous Cuban artist Kcho offers this service, which has been approved by Etecsa, the state-owned telecommunications company. Although the internet is slow and sometimes crowded, it's a big deal because only around 5% of Cubans have unrestricted access to the internet.

People can now use websites like Facebook and Twitter and talk with family abroad. Adonis Ortiz, who is 20 years old, says he comes as often as he can to video chat with his father in the United States, whom he hasn’t seen for nine years.

As relations between Cuba and the U.S. improve, American tech companies like Google and Apple may enter the Cuban market soon. Meanwhile, Cuba has installed a high-speed cable from Venezuela and uses some Chinese equipment.

About one-quarter of Cubans have internet access, but mostly through a restricted domestic network with limited websites and email. Kcho lets people use his own internet connection for free. He says he wants to help Cubans learn about the internet even though it costs him $900 per month. 

Kcho’s real name is Alexis Leiva Machado, and he became internationally famous after winning a grand prize at an art biennial in South Korea. His artwork often has rustic, seaside, and patriotic themes.

The center's courtyard is busy with young people using laptops, tablets, or smartphones throughout the day. In Cuba, home broadband is rare and expensive. At Kcho’s studio, internet speeds are around 2mbps, which can be very fast when there aren’t many users at night.

Scott Kelly spent 340 days in space on the International Space Station (ISS) and says it felt like forever. He took pictures of Earth and did lots of work to help NASA learn about living in space.
