Kelly and his Russian partner, Mikhail Kornienko, studied how weightlessness affects humans. When he returned to Earth, Kelly's body hurt more than usual because of gravity.

NASA will keep testing Kelly's health with his twin brother, Mark, who is a retired astronaut. This helps NASA understand the effects of space on the human body better.

Kelly noticed that after returning, he had trouble throwing objects onto tables because he underestimated gravity’s force. The fresh air and sweet smell from the capsule upon landing in Kazakhstan made him feel amazed again after his long mission.

The ISS, as big as a football field with rooms like a six-bedroom house, relies on solar power. Kelly stressed that there are many things to learn about living in space, comparing it to early computer research at NASA.

From space, Kelly saw beautiful views but also pollution. He said the thin atmosphere looks fragile and he became more aware of environmental issues. He thinks people need to protect air and water because we affect these environments and can change them for better or worse.

Kelly kept busy during his mission by focusing on tasks like welcoming new crew members, spacewalks, robotics work, and science experiments. Being back on Earth hasn’t fully felt real yet, as he experienced culture shock after seeing crowds again.

Though a NASA scientist said Kelly could be ideal for a Mars mission, Kelly doesn't think he will fly with NASA again but keeps an open mind about private spaceflight companies like SpaceX.

Junior Smart knows a lot about gangs. He's 36 now and has had two different parts of his life. When he was in his late teens, after his mom died, he joined a gang in south London. At first, it seemed like fun, but later it became serious about making money through criminal activities.

Smart did not pass his GCSEs at school but later passed them in college. He had a full-time job and also worked as a DJ. However, on the side, he was involved with illegal gang activities. Eventually, he was arrested for drug-related crimes and spent 12 years in prison.

In prison, Smart realized he needed to change his life. Now, he runs a team of 12 workers and six volunteers who help young people leave gangs and crime behind. He saw how the prison system did not work well for inmates with drug problems, which motivated him to start helping others in prison.

After serving five years, Smart was released early and put into action his plan to help ex-offenders avoid going back to prison. He believes that arresting gang leaders does not solve the problem; instead, it can make things worse by creating fights within gangs for leadership positions. This often leads to more violence on the streets as new members join to fill gaps.

Gangs are recruiting very young children now, even from primary schools. These kids are called “tinies” and can be as young as eight years old. They do tasks that keep their senior gang members safe, like selling drugs or committing crimes.

Smart says it is hard to convince young people to leave crime when they earn a lot of money illegally, especially with high unemployment rates. However, his project has helped over 1,000 clients and only about 20% reoffend. He believes in giving everyone a chance to change.

Wales will become the first country in the UK where people are assumed to have agreed to donate their organs after death unless they choose to say no.

The Welsh Assembly voted for this new rule, which means hospitals can assume that someone wanted to give their organs unless the person said otherwise while alive. The final part of the bill passed with 43 votes, eight against, and two abstentions. Some religious groups are not happy about it because they think it is not moral, and others worry it could make things harder for grieving families.

Mark Drakeford, the Welsh Health Minister, said this was an important day for Wales and devolution. He added that 226 people in Wales are waiting for organ transplants. This new law aims to respect what the deceased wanted and increase the number of organs available by making sure family members know the person's wishes.

Opponents fear that the need for more organs could override a dead person’s or their family’s wishes, but ministers say there will be safeguards in place.

The Welsh government says families can still object if they think organ donation goes against what the deceased would have wanted. Wales is taking this step because there are not enough organs for those who need them. About one person dies each week while waiting for a transplant.

Around a third of people in Wales are on the organ donor register, but surveys show that over two-thirds say they support organ donation. The new law will apply to anyone over 18 who has lived in Wales for at least a year before death. Organs donated can go to people anywhere in the UK.

Doctors are happy with this move because it could help more people needing transplants. Some religious groups, however, think that taking organs without explicit consent is not loving or generous and could upset grieving families.

For John Lewis’s 2015 Christmas advertisement, they focus on an old man living alone in a crater on the moon. This story aims to support Age UK and collect hundreds of thousands of pounds for charity. The campaign costs £7 million and includes a TV ad, smartphone game, glow-in-the-dark pajamas, and moon-themed decorations in 11 stores.

In the ad, a girl named Lily sees an old man on the moon through her telescope and tries to reach out to him by sending letters and gifts until they make contact. The message of the ad is “Show someone they’re loved this Christmas,” which matches Age UK’s campaign: "No one should have no one at Christmas."

John Lewis will give profits from a mug, gift tag, and card to Age UK. Rachel Swift, head of marketing at John Lewis, says the ad makes people think about those who might be alone during the holidays.

The moon scenes were filmed at Warner Bros Studios where Harry Potter films were made. The set was built by someone who worked on Star Wars: The Force Awakens. The ad cost £1 million to make and features a song called "Half the World Away" performed by Norwegian artist Aurora.

In 2014, John Lewis's penguin ad had over 22 million YouTube views by early January, making it one of the most popular ads that year. This campaign focuses on thoughtful gifts for loved ones during Christmas.

Sarah Vizard from Marketing Week says even though more brands are doing Christmas ads, John Lewis still does emotional stories best. Other stores like Waitrose and Burberry also launched their Christmas ads in November.

Europe is going to become the first place to make car makers do real-world emissions tests. These tests show how much pollution cars really create on roads, not just in labs as they are tested now. European Commission Vice President Frans Timmermans approved these new rules. The tests will check if cars release no more than 80 mg of nitrogen oxide per kilometer, but only one out of sixteen cars met this limit in tests.

Pollution from diesel engines like nitrogen oxide and particulates is thought to cause at least a quarter of the 29,000 deaths each year due to air pollution in the UK. This number may go up when new medical research comes out later this year.

The current lab test for measuring these emissions is very old. It’s easy to cheat by using tricks like taping windows and doors to reduce air resistance or testing cars on smooth roads with high temperatures.

A Commission spokesperson said they are working on a plan that will properly measure car pollution in real driving conditions. They expect no big problems in getting approval for this new test.

Campaigners say car makers often cheat the current tests, causing much more pollution than allowed when cars are driven on actual roads. The new real-world emissions test is an important step to fight urban air pollution. States should support these new rules and ignore car makers who complain that they are too strict.

In 2014 research showed that actual nitrogen oxide emissions from cars were seven times higher than the standard of 80 mg/km, with some models being 22 times over the limit. Around one third of all nitrogen oxide pollution comes from road transport, mostly diesel vehicles. In cities, this can reach up to 64%.

The car industry tried to delay changes in testing rules but say they need more time for technical and economic reasons. They suggested their own draft regulation that would cover fewer pollutants and start later, but their proposal was rejected.

After the Commission approves it, member states will make final changes before introducing the new tests by September 2017. Other countries like China and Korea are watching how this goes.

Some cities have pigeons, but Lima has black vultures called gallinazos. They fly around and sit on old buildings like churches from long ago.

These birds look a bit scary with their wrinkled heads and small eyes. Many people think they remind them of the problems in Lima like poverty and trash.

But now, environmental groups are using these birds to help solve a big problem: illegal dumping of trash. They put cameras and GPS trackers on ten vultures that don't have any diseases. The vultures fly around and find where people throw away garbage illegally. 

One of the trained vultures is named Samuel. He wears a tracker and flies over Lima to spot hidden dumps and record their locations.

His trainer at Lima’s Huachipa Zoo, Alfredo Correa, says these birds have strong stomachs that protect them from germs when they eat dead animals.

The project is run by USAID and Peru's Environment Ministry to fight trash problems. Other vultures are named things like Capitan Huggin and Capitana Aella.

There’s a funny video showing the vultures as brave heroes fighting against dirt and sickness, while people ignore the problem.

Lima has four landfills for nearly ten million people, so lots of illegal dumps exist. About one-fifth of all trash goes to these dumps, which pollute Lima's rivers with runoff.

The most fly-tipped areas are three poorer neighborhoods: Villa Maria del Triunfo (39.4%), Villa El Salvador (25.3%), and El Agustino (18.3%).

Some residents don’t pay taxes, so the local governments can't afford to pick up trash. The project hopes that by sharing GPS data from vultures with city officials, they will clean up the messes.

The goal is also to get people to act like "vultures on the ground" and report illegal dumping and recycle more. This idea came from a 2014 United Nations meeting in Lima about climate change. 

An artist named Cristina Planas put big vulture sculptures on dead trees, which helped raise awareness of conservation and recycling.

People are scared by how vultures look but really they help us by cleaning up trash where we left it.

A major report warns that up to a billion people will still be in extreme poverty by 2030 unless countries deal with inequalities and factors that push people back into poverty. The Chronic Poverty Advisory Network (CPAN) says many who rise above the poverty line of $1.25 a day can fall back due to issues like drought, illness, insecurity, or conflict.

In rural Kenya and South Africa, 30 to 40% of those escaping poverty have fallen back in. In Ethiopia between 1999 and 2009, this number rose to 60%. Even countries like Indonesia and Vietnam see about 20% falling back into poverty.

The report gives examples of individuals who slipped back into poverty. Amin from Bangladesh lost income due to his and his wife's illnesses, the cost of his son’s marriage, his father's death, and loss of fishing nets. Lovemore from Zimbabwe became one of the poorest in his village after losing his job due to illness and taking care of his grandchildren.

Andrew Shepherd, a research fellow at the Overseas Development Institute who wrote the report, says governments need to ensure people permanently stay above the poverty line. He notes that many families face setbacks and have difficulty recovering.

While it's possible to end extreme poverty by 2030, the report argues current methods won't work. Despite dropping from 1.9 billion in 1990 to 1.2 billion in 2010, progress will be harder due to climate-related issues and deep poverty in parts of Africa.

The report calls for a focus on chronically poor people – those who are poor for many years or their entire lives. Policymakers must tackle chronic poverty, prevent impoverishment, and sustain escapes from poverty.

Policies include social assistance like safety nets, education, and economic growth policies to help the poorest benefit from national prosperity. The report suggests stronger tax systems and aid will be needed, as many developing countries spend less than $500 per person annually on development.

The report urges governments to reduce conflict risks, establish inclusive peace settlements, and address inequalities affecting the poorest people. It also calls for challenging social norms like dowries that contribute to extreme poverty.

The top book on Amazon in the U.S. isn't Harper Lee's new novel "Go Set a Watchman" or George R.R. Martin’s fantasy series, nor is it Zoella’s young adult book “Girl Online.” Instead, Johanna Basford’s coloring books for adults are at the top of the bestseller lists.

Basford’s book "Secret Garden," with its detailed pictures of plants and animals, has sold 1.4 million copies worldwide. Her new book, "Enchanted Forest," has already sold just under 226,000 copies. Fans include Zooey Deschanel, who shared the link on Facebook, and South Korean pop star Kim Ki-Bum, who posted an image for his followers.

Eleanor Blatherwick from the publisher Laurence King said, "The last few weeks have been crazy since 'Enchanted Forest' came out. We knew the books would be beautiful but didn’t expect such success."

In the UK, coloring books are very popular too. Richard Merritt’s "Art Therapy Colouring Book" is in fourth place on Amazon's bestseller list, Millie Marotta’s "Animal Kingdom" is seventh, and a mindfulness coloring book is ninth.

Ana McLaughlin from publisher Michael O’Mara says that coloring helps people relax. They first released "Creative Colouring for Grown-Ups" in 2012 but the trend really took off with their book "Art Therapy" in 2014, selling many copies because it was marketed as a way to reduce stress.

Basford believes coloring books are relaxing and creative. She says she drew her first book for grown-ups who might have enjoyed coloring when they were young but didn’t feel it was okay before.

Since Basford released "Secret Garden" in 2013, the response has been amazing. Her publisher thought the idea was good right away.

Basford is working on a third book and Michael O’Mara plans to release more adult coloring books by May. The trend shows no signs of slowing down, with people sharing their pictures widely online and framing them proudly.

People are excited about these intricate designs, even though they don't need artistic talent to color in the lines.

Margaret Allen runs a special exercise class for older people. She lets them take a tea break halfway through the workout. After warming up and doing some exercises that raise their heart rate, they can drink tea and sit down.

The 93-year-old great-grandmother herself barely sweats during her classes despite having a painful trapped nerve in one leg and a knee that needs to be replaced. Some of her eight students look like they need the break more than others.

On the day I visited at a church hall near Middlesbrough, everyone was eating slices of fruitcake for Margaret’s birthday. Her 89-year-old sister Joan made it. After finishing their cake, Margaret leads them in a Scottish dance with lots of toe pointing and leg kicking.

Margaret has run classes in this seaside town for 45 years. She started playing piano for a fitness class during World War II to pass the time during blackouts. When she was about 40, she took over after the previous instructor retired. At one point, there were more than 18 regulars paying £1 each.

Now, her group is shrinking. They recently attended a funeral for one of their younger members who died at age 68 from motor neurone disease. The youngest in the class now is Jean Cunion at 60 years old. Jean found support here after losing her mother and admits she’s maybe not as fit.

Ruth Steere, 76, says Margaret always notices when they make mistakes even though her back is to them while playing piano. 

Margaret has never had formal training but choreographs moves based on five tapes from fitness guru Eileen Fowler who lived to 93. She believes staying active and busy keeps her healthy after her husband died in 1997.

One of her students, Winnie Robertson, an 84-year-old former teacher, says the key to fitness is never giving up: "Use it or lose it." Margaret still plays piano, gives speeches, and participates in a Scrabble club for over-90s. She took computer classes at age 88 but didn’t enjoy using them.

Margaret admits aging isn't easy and jokes about her doctor's shock when he saw her and guessed she was only 78. She has a straightforward view on weight gain: "People shouldn’t eat too much."

In 2013, Margaret watched the news where another fitness instructor claimed to be the oldest in the country at age 80. But Margaret didn't correct her publicly.

Margaret thinks staying busy and active is key to good health and happiness despite aging challenges.

It started with a fake scallop dish, but now some top hotels and stores in Japan are having big problems because they lied about their food. This could hurt how people see Japanese cooking around the world.

The trouble began when Hankyu-Hanshin, an Osaka-based hotel chain, said it had given wrong information about many menu items from 2006 to October 2013. About 78,000 people were affected. For example, they sold flying fish eggs as red salmon caviar.

Hankyu-Hanshin's president, Hiroshi Desaki, tried to fix the problem by cutting his pay and the pay of other leaders, but customers were still angry. Later, Desaki resigned because he said the company had betrayed its customers. One head chef even gave back a medal from the government.

The hotel chain has given refunds to over 10,000 people so far for about 20 million yen, with an expected total cost of around 110 million yen.

Since then, other big restaurants and hotels in Japan have had similar problems. People paid high prices thinking they were eating expensive foods like kuruma shrimp or wagyu beef but got cheaper versions instead.

The scandal began when a customer wrote on their blog that the scallop at Tokyo’s Prince Hotel was actually a different, cheaper type of shellfish. The hotel looked into it and found over 50 menu items needed correcting. This made other hotels admit they had also misled customers about food ingredients.

For example, another chain called Hotel Okura said they added fat to beef to make it juicier and incorrectly labeled tomatoes as organic.

The government spokesman, Yoshihide Suga, said these incidents caused a loss of trust among consumers because they were cover-ups.

This scandal happened at a bad time for Japan. They are trying to get South Korea and other countries to lift bans on food imports from after the Fukushima nuclear accident. Also, UNESCO is considering adding Japanese cuisine to its list of cultural treasures. This scandal could hurt how safe and trustworthy people think Japanese food is.

One newspaper said it was “astonished by the industry’s lack of morals.” They are worried this might hurt Japan's reputation for safety in foods and services.

Experts say that after the 2008 financial crisis, hotels tried to cut costs but still wanted to attract customers with detailed menu descriptions. This led them to use different ingredients than they listed on menus.

The new food labeling law coming in 2015 will not cover menus, so there is no legal action against these hotels and restaurants. However, Japanese consumers care a lot about where their food comes from and are upset by this scandal. In a poll, 72% of people said the origin of ingredients was most important when choosing dishes.

In summary, top hotels and stores in Japan have admitted to mislabeling food on their menus, which could harm how Japanese cuisine is seen around the world and cost them millions of yen in refunds and lost trust.

Author Philip Pullman says that illegal downloading is like stealing someone's wallet. In an article for Index on Censorship, he defends copyright laws and criticizes people who download music or books without paying.

Pullman states, "The technical brilliance of the internet makes it hard to see how wrong it is to steal artists' work." He adds, “It’s theft just like taking money from someone’s pocket.”

He wrote this article after a meeting between British Prime Minister David Cameron and music industry leaders at Downing Street where they discussed web piracy. Pullman says that authors and musicians often struggle for years before getting noticed, but as soon as their work becomes popular, people can easily steal it.

Pullman argues simply: “If we want to enjoy someone’s work, we should pay for it.”

However, Cathy Casserly, the CEO of Creative Commons, disagrees. She believes that copyright laws created in an older time prevent artists from sharing and building upon each other's work in new ways. Artists need to find creative ways to distribute their work, she says.

Rachael Jolley, editor of Index on Censorship, agrees with Casserly. The current laws do not fit the digital age and might make consumers criminals. New models are needed for artists to earn a living from their work.

According to Ofcom data between November 2012 and January 2013 in the UK, about 280 million music tracks, 52 million TV shows, 29 million films, 18 million ebooks, and 7 million software or games were pirated. About 18% of internet users over 12 admit to piracy, with 9% fearing they might get caught.

At the Downing Street meeting, Cameron appointed Conservative MP Mike Weatherley as his adviser on this issue. The BPI spokesperson said that Weatherley is a strong supporter of copyright and artists' rights.

When Larry Pizzi, who has worked in the bicycle business for many years, first heard about electric bikes almost 20 years ago, he wondered why anyone would want to add a motor and batteries to a bike. Even today, some traditional bike lovers are still unsure about e-bikes.

Bike shops have been slow to sell e-bikes even though they've existed since the late 1990s. Sales in the US have been small. Pizzi, who now runs Currie Technologies, the top e-bike seller in the US, thinks that this will soon change. Major bike brands like Trek, Raleigh, and Specialized are starting to make electric bikes too.

Pizzi believes that "we're close to widespread acceptance of electric bikes." More companies are entering the market each month.

The US is different from other countries when it comes to e-bikes. In 2014, almost 32 million e-bikes were sold worldwide, mostly in China where they are used for transportation. They are popular in Europe too, especially in the Netherlands and Switzerland. German postal workers use them, and BMW makes one that costs about $3,000.

Electric bikes are not motorcycles or mopeds; they have an electric motor to help you pedal but can also be ridden without power. Riding feels like having a tailwind, making it easier to go fast or climb hills. Unlike mopeds, e-bikes usually can use bike paths and cannot go over 20 mph.

There's no official number of how many e-bikes are sold in the US each year, but estimates range from about 50,000 to 175,000. This is similar to electric car sales, which reached 118,000 in 2014.

To succeed in the US, e-bike companies need to overcome legal, cultural, and financial challenges. E-bikes are banned in some states like New York, even if the law isn't always enforced strictly. Traditional bike shop owners don’t like adding motors because of added weight; some e-bikes weigh almost 30 kg.

E-bikes can be expensive too. Basic models cost around $700, but Court Rye from ElectricBikeReview.com says a good quality e-bike with a reliable battery costs at least $1,500. High-end bikes are even more expensive.

The companies that make and sell e-bikes say they can solve these problems. E-bike technology, especially batteries, is getting better. "Batteries are becoming smaller, lighter, more dependable, and lasting longer," says Don DiCostanza from Pedego, an electric bike company.

Big electronics firms like Bosch and Shimano are entering the market, which should help change how traditional bike shops view e-bikes. Companies like Pedego and ElectroBike are opening their own stores rather than waiting for bike shops to start selling them. They also support efforts to make e-bikes legal everywhere.

Electric bikes become more practical as cities build better cycling infrastructure with dedicated lanes. In 2014, the US Census Bureau reported that bike commuting grew from about 488,000 in 2000 to 786,000 in 2012. E-bikes make commuting easier by helping with hills and reducing sweat.

Don DiCostanza says most of Pedego's customers are baby boomers wanting to enjoy biking again without worrying about hills. Pedego has almost 60 stores in the US and sells bikes to tour companies in San Francisco and Washington, DC.

ElectroBike, which operates 30 stores in Mexico, opened its first store in California in autumn 2014 with plans to expand to 25 US stores within a year. CEO Craig Anderson wants to reduce traffic and pollution while promoting healthy living. He tells customers, "Ride this once and try not to smile."

Startups like Pedego will compete against larger companies like Trek and Currie Technologies, which was bought by Accell Group in 2012. Currie’s Larry Pizzi says that while baby boomers are important, many younger people use e-bikes for commuting instead of cars.

Accell also sells a cargo bike with a stronger motor and rear rack called the Yuba brand. This can carry two children or up to 45 kg of shopping, making it an alternative to a minivan.

Is streaming music about to become really popular? In 2014, only 41 million people used music streaming services worldwide. This is a small number compared to how many could use them. Many users came from deals with phone companies, so they may not be very active.

Apple has made products like iTunes and the iPod that were popular. They want to reach 100 million subscribers for their new Apple Music service, which would make $12 billion a year. In 2014, all recorded music was worth about $15 billion globally.

Will downloading end? Downloads started in 2003 and grew big under iTunes, but the income from downloads is decreasing. In the UK, it fell from £283 million to £249 million between 2013 and 2014. Most people only buy a few songs each year, spending around £39 on music.

Is Apple Music friendlier for artists? Unlike Spotify, which has been criticized by many artists, Apple is seen as more supportive of artists. This could help attract them to the platform.

Will Apple get exclusive deals with big artists? Exclusive albums can bring in new users. For example, Spotify paid a lot to have Led Zeppelin and Metallica exclusively on their service. It’s not clear if Apple can convince major acts like AC/DC or Adele to do exclusives for streaming.

Is Apple Music going to beat other services? Even though Apple has lots of money, they are just starting in the music streaming market. Others like Spotify have more experience but lose a lot of money too. If Apple loses money on their service, they may stop it unless they can beat competitors first.

When talking about climate change, people usually focus on the problem but forget there are many solutions. These solutions include recycling faster, reducing emissions, and finding sustainable replacements for plastic, air conditioning, smartphones, and fast fashion.

Recently, experts at a meeting in Copenhagen showed how climate change is affecting all continents and said we need to work harder to reduce emissions. They also talked about the solutions.

Arnold Schwarzenegger chairs the Sustainia Award, which honors ten top sustainability projects used in 84 countries. These projects cover areas like food, fashion, energy, transportation, education, and health. For example:

- In California, plastics can now be made from greenhouse gases at a competitive price.
- In Switzerland, an effective system recycles clothes and shoes in over 60 countries.
- In Canada, smartphones help make bike-sharing more convenient.

The Sustainia Award 2014 went to Wecyclers, a Nigerian project. Wecyclers uses bicycles to collect waste from low-income areas in Lagos. Families can exchange their garbage for points that they can use to buy goods. Companies then buy the sorted waste and turn it into items like mattresses, pillows, and trash bags.

Wecyclers helps solve local waste problems since only 40% of Lagos's rubbish is collected. In Africa overall, only 46% of municipal waste is picked up. So far, more than 5,000 families have joined the project, with plans to expand it to other Nigerian cities.

While many climate change solutions focus on high-tech ways to reduce emissions or improve efficiency, we also need low-tech ideas that can make big impacts in communities. With a variety of solutions tackling different challenges, we should concentrate more on the parts of these stories that inspire action and create momentum for real change.

Although BB King mainly played blues music, he was open to different musical styles and cultures. It's hard to think of another blues artist who influenced so many musicians and fans over a career lasting 65 years. 

Riley B King was born near Itta Bena, Mississippi, and learned guitar from a family friend while singing with gospel singers. In his early 20s, he moved to Memphis. He started playing at bars in West Memphis, Arkansas, and became a disc jockey on a Memphis radio station. His name "The Beale Street Blues Boy" was shortened to "Blues Boy King," then to "BB."

King had his first hit in 1952 with "Three O’Clock Blues." This song stayed at the top of the R&B chart for 15 weeks. He wrote and recorded many songs like “Please Love Me,” “You Upset Me Baby,” and “Sweet Sixteen.” King developed a unique guitar style that was innovative yet rooted in blues history. He admired T-Bone Walker, Blind Lemon Jefferson, Lonnie Johnson, Charlie Christian, and Django Reinhardt.

King toured constantly during the 1950s, playing over 342 shows in one year. In 1965, his album "Live at the Regal" became famous. He had R&B hits with songs like “How Blue Can You Get” and “Paying the Cost to Be the Boss.” His song “The Thrill Is Gone” reached high on pop charts in 1969.

King gained popularity among rock fans through collaborations with artists like Mike Bloomfield, Eric Clapton, Carole King, and Joe Walsh. He traveled internationally for concerts but also played at prisons, which led to his involvement in rehabilitation programs.

In 1990, King was diagnosed with diabetes but continued touring less frequently. For his 80th birthday in 2005, he released a Grammy award-winning album with collaborations including Eric Clapton and Mark Knopfler. In 2009, he won another Grammy for "One Kind Favor," and in 2012 performed at the White House.

King was married twice and had 11 children who survived him; four others passed away before him.

Kenton Cool usually likes to talk a lot, but now his voice is just a low growl because he worked hard at high altitude. He is in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital city, after flying down from Everest base camp that morning. Over the weekend, he did some amazing climbs. On Saturday, he climbed to the top of Nuptse, then reached the summit of Mount Everest early Sunday. On Monday, he topped Lhotse. 

“It was a lucky chance,” Cool says. “For the first time since the late 1990s, there were fixed ropes on all three mountains.” But he thinks someone will do it without ropes or extra oxygen in the future.

Cool talks about Ueli Steck, a Swiss climber who wanted to climb Everest’s west ridge and Lhotse with no fixed ropes. He left the mountain after an argument with Sherpas at Camp 2.

Helicopter rescues are becoming more common on Everest. Recently, Simone Moro used a helicopter to rescue someone at 7,800 meters high. This shows how much helicopters are being used now for rescue and transportation.

Environmental problems affect tourism in the Everest region. Alton Byers says that climate change and tourism put stress on Sherpa areas. Glaciers are retreating or disappearing, causing less water for agriculture and new lodges. In Namche Bazaar, a pipeline is being laid to provide more water because the stream is polluted.

Human waste management at base camp has improved, but there are concerns about leaks from large pits where garbage and human waste are disposed of.

Solving these issues could cost around $850,000 per year. Byers works with local groups to find new water sources due to climate change impacts like glacial lake build-up that can flood Sherpa areas.

Changing weather patterns are also affecting tourism. More clouds often close Lukla Airport. A new road is being built for 4x4 vehicles to ensure tourists keep coming, but this could cause soil erosion and landslides.

Everest shows the effects of climate change and over-tourism clearly, making it a good place to learn how to solve these issues.

A new survey from 33 countries shows that people often misunderstand key facts about their societies. 

In Britain, people think the richest 1% own 59% of wealth, but they really only have 23%. Americans believe 33% are immigrants when it is actually 14%.

Brazilians guess the average age in their country to be 56, but it’s 31. Russians think women make up 31% of politicians, but they’re only 14%.

British people think that 43% of young adults aged 25-34 still live at home with parents, when the real number is just 14%. In India, people guess internet access is 60%, while it’s really only 19%.

Why do people often get these facts wrong? It's partly because they struggle with basic math and can misunderstand questions. For example, most countries overestimate how many people don’t follow a religion: respondents think it’s 37% on average across the surveyed countries, but it is actually just 18%. People may be thinking of religious practice instead of census data.

People also make quick judgments based on easily available information rather than precise calculations. This can lead to big overestimates about rural populations in many countries. When answering questions like these, people use “fast” thinking instead of careful analysis, as explained by psychologist Daniel Kahneman.

Survey participants often generalize from their own situations and forget they might not be representative of the whole population. For instance, our survey was mostly online, which means that respondents were likely more educated and connected than average in developing countries.

We also have "emotional innumeracy" when estimating realities; we tend to overstate issues that worry us. In Britain, this explains why people think there are many wealthy people, young adults living at home, and immigrants. 

The survey shows some areas where people aren’t worried enough, like obesity rates. People in most countries underestimate how overweight their populations are. For example, in Saudi Arabia, 71% of the population is obese or overweight, but people think it’s only 28%.

The study also reveals interesting facts about different societies. The richest 1% in Russia own 70% of wealth, while in New Zealand they own just 18%. Half of Italians aged 25-34 still live with their parents, compared to only 4% in Norway.

In India, the average age is 27, but it’s 47 in Japan. Only 10% of politicians are women in Brazil, Hungary, and Japan, while Sweden has 44%.

When reality is so varied across countries, it's no surprise we often get these facts wrong.

The tiger in India, orangutan in Indonesia, and panda are animals that people know are in danger. These are beloved animals no one wants to lose. However, scientists are worried that other smaller animals like ladybugs may also be at risk. This could harm nature more than we think.

Scientists say we might now be in the Anthropocene, a time when humans have such big effects on Earth's environment that they can change it forever. In 2014, WWF found that animal numbers dropped by 52% over forty years. Freshwater animals decreased even more, falling by 76%.

Some insects like bees help grow our food by pollinating plants. Worms break down waste and bats control pests like mosquitoes. Without them, farming could lose over $22 billion in North America alone.

Dr Nick Isaac from the Centre for Ecology & Hydrology says common animals are declining just as fast as rare ones. We depend on these more than rare animals because they are everywhere. The drop in numbers of species is very bad and will affect humans a lot.

More than 1/4 to over 1/3 of birds, mammals, and amphibians used for food or medicine might disappear soon. In some places, people rely heavily on wild animals for food.

People are using up natural resources too quickly, causing damage like climate change and loss of habitats faster than before. It's not just big animals we need to worry about; small creatures like insects are also important.

Sir David Attenborough said in 2013 that humans are harming Earth a lot. But WWF says it is still possible to stop the problem from getting worse if everyone works together. We use more trees, fish, water, and carbon than nature can replace or absorb.

France made history when it appointed Helena Costa as the first female manager of a professional men's football team in the top two divisions of any European league. This happened at Clermont Foot 63, which is in second division and currently ranks 14th out of 20 teams.

Helena Costa, 36, was born in Portugal and has a master’s degree in sports science. She also holds a UEFA coaching license. Before this job, she coached male youth teams at Benfica, led the Qatar women's team to its first international win in 2012, and managed Iran’s national women's team until September 2013.

Costa was hired for two years by Clermont Foot 63 president Claude Michy. Some people think this is just to get more attention for a smaller club with an average home crowd of around 3,800 in the Auvergne region of France. 

France’s women's minister, Najat Vallaud-Belkacem, praised the decision as important for the future of professional football.

Carolina Morace, an Italian who was previously a woman coach of a men’s team, said that Costa being hired means she knows how to do her job well. However, in 1999, Morace resigned from her coaching position after only two games because of conflicts with the club owner.

Raymond Domenech, former manager of France's national team, believes women can manage men’s teams and should be given chances like anyone else.

Reactions to Costa’s appointment have been mixed. Some fans are hopeful for change while others doubt she will last long or earn respect from players. Véronique Soulier, president of the club’s supporters’ association, is optimistic that a woman in charge might help motivate the team and make them less demanding.

Costa's reputation suggests she won’t be easy to work with; she was once called "Mourinho in a skirt" after her time at Chelsea. She accepts this comparison as long as it means people see her determination to win.

Loneliness is becoming a big problem in Britain. According to the Office for National Statistics, Britain has more lonely people than any other European country. British people are less likely to have close friends or know their neighbors compared to people from other EU countries.

Research by Professor John Cacioppo at the University of Chicago found that loneliness can be very bad for older people's health. It’s twice as harmful as obesity and almost as dangerous as poverty when it comes to causing early death.

However, younger adults also face a big problem with loneliness. In 2010, the Mental Health Foundation discovered that young people aged 18-34 worry more about feeling lonely than older people over 55 years old. They are more likely to feel depressed because of loneliness.

Sam Challis from Mind, a mental health charity, says there is help for older people who feel lonely, but not enough support exists for younger adults after they turn 21. Loneliness can lead to stress, depression, paranoia, anxiety, addiction, and even suicide.

Dr Grant Blank at the Oxford Internet Institute notes that while social media helps us stay in touch with faraway friends, it can also replace face-to-face interactions. This can make people feel more lonely if they compare their lives to idealized versions shared online.

While meditation apps like Headspace are popular for mental health issues, they might not help loneliness as much because they encourage being alone. Sam Challis suggests addressing the reasons you stay home instead of meeting others first.

A study at the University of Michigan found that Facebook can lower life satisfaction but using technology to meet new people may be good. For Maddy Matthews, a 19-year-old student who is a new mother, the website Mumsnet has been helpful in feeling less lonely when she cannot see her friends often.

Helplines like Samaritans and Get Connected provide support for loneliness among young people. At work, it can help to talk with your employer about how you feel. John Binns experienced stress-related depression but found that being open helped him return to work more easily.

Office conversations can also help prevent feeling isolated at work. Rick Hughes from the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP) says forming connections with team members reduces isolation even when stressed.

Nicky Forsythe, a psychotherapist who runs Talk for Health, emphasizes the importance of regular social support like talking to empathetic listeners. For building skills such as empathy, counseling can help. Universities often offer these services too.

Loneliness is not just an issue for older people but affects younger adults severely. Addressing loneliness early in life could prevent it from becoming a bigger problem later on.

The creator of a new computer system used in hospital autopsies says this technique could end "perfect murders." The system is called 'Virtopsy' and it's now being used at some medical institutes across Europe. It was created by scientists at the University of Zurich. Instead of using a scalpel to cut open the body, doctors use computers to look inside the body in 3-D.

Michael Thali, who directs the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Zurich and helped create Virtopsy, says this system could change criminal investigations because it allows finding every piece of evidence.

Virtopsies use high-powered MRI, CT scans, and surface scans of dead bodies. These devices together are called a 'Virtobot.' This method can detect injuries like lesions, blows, air pockets, heart attacks, and even cancer—things that might not be found in a traditional autopsy.

Richard Dirndorfer, one of the creators of Virtopsy and an expert in DNA analysis for crime cases, thinks that, just like DNA analysis replaced blood group testing over time, Virtopsies could replace regular autopsies.

This new computer method helps doctors see inside dead bodies very closely. It has already found injuries not seen during traditional autopsies. The goal now is to use the new method alongside traditional ones.

Dominic Wichmann, a doctor at Hamburg’s University Hospital, says it will help forensic scientists plan their work better. Many criminologists from around the world have visited Switzerland to see how this new method works.

The TV show CSI has shown Virtopsies twice: once to prove a murder was done with a bullet through the cheek and another time to make sure a man’s body stayed intact so he could be frozen after death as requested.

Scientists worked on the project for decades. At first, they were in an unheated lab and seen as strange by others. Later, money from a wealthy eye doctor helped develop the technology. Some people thought it would hurt traditional autopsy skills, but younger scientists see it as something that can improve and maybe replace regular autopsies one day.

Lars Oesterhelweg, Deputy Director at Berlin's Charité Hospital using Virtopsy, said they still need to cut bodies open sometimes to check blood color, consistency of body fluids, or smells. He added that Virtopsy is especially helpful for re-examining cases where the cause of death was unclear, allowing third opinions and reopening investigations.

Doctors say families prefer this new method because it does not damage the body like a traditional autopsy would.

You can be Aagot, Arney or Ásfríður; Baldey, Bebba or Brá. Dögg, Dimmblá, Etna and Eybjört are good choices; also Frigg, Glódís, Hörn and Ingunn. Jórlaug works too, as do Obba, Sigurfljóð, Úranía and Vagna. But you cannot be called Harriet if you are a girl in Iceland.

“The whole situation,” said Tristan Cardew, with British understatement, “is really rather silly.” Alongside his Icelandic wife, Kristin, Cardew is fighting against the National Registry's decision in Reykjavik not to renew their daughter Harriet’s passport because her name isn’t recognized as an approved Icelandic name.

Since the registry doesn't recognize the name of Harriet's 12-year-old brother, Duncan either, the two children have used passports with names Stúlka and Drengur Cardew: Girl and Boy. “But this time,” said Cardew, a British cook who moved to Iceland in 2000, “the authorities want to follow the law strictly.” The law says no official documents will be given to people without approved Icelandic names.

Because of this, the family from Kópavogur might have missed their holiday in France until they got an emergency UK passport from the British embassy.

Names are very important in Iceland. With only around 320,000 people, phone books list subscribers by first name because most surnames just say that you are your father’s (or mother's) son or daughter. For example, Jón Einarsson’s children might be Ólafur Jónsson and Sigríður Jónsdóttir.

The law states that names of children born in Iceland must be on a recognized list within six months after birth unless both parents are not Icelandic. If the names aren't on a list of 1,853 female and 1,712 male names, parents need approval from the Icelandic Naming Committee.

Each year for about 5,000 children born in Iceland, the committee gets around 100 name applications and rejects half under a law aimed at preserving saga language. Names must have Icelandic endings, not conflict with the language's structure, and follow writing rules of Iceland’s alphabet.

This means names with letters like “c” are not allowed because they don’t exist in Iceland’s alphabet. Also, names that can't fit Icelandic grammatical cases are rejected too. “That was Harriet's problem,” said Cardew.

Iceland’s naming laws have faced criticism over the years. In 2013, Blær Bjarkardóttir Rúnarsdottir won a court case allowing her to be called by her name rather than "Girl," as not letting her use it was against the Icelandic constitution. Jón Gnarr, the former mayor of Reykjavik, said Iceland’s naming law is unfair and limits creativity.

The Cardews could fix Harriet's problem by giving her an Icelandic middle name. “But that would be too silly,” said Cardew. "Are they saying we aren't welcome here?"

Google has made maps of many places around the world but not the cold Arctic area. Now they are going to make maps for Iqaluit, a town in Nunavut, Canada, where about 7,000 people live. In July 2013, these maps will be shown on Google's Street View.

Aaron Brindle leads this project and says that he takes his good maps for granted but the north hasn’t had such detailed maps before. Instead of using a car with cameras like they do in other places, the team had to hike around Iqaluit’s snowy roads and unknown trails. They also walked part of a 15km road called the Road to Nowhere.

The mayor, John Graham, said that curious locals followed the mapping team everywhere. This project follows others led by explorers like Martin Frobisher in the past.

Google had trouble getting all the right information for their maps because the town has grown quickly due to a mining boom and some businesses use PO boxes instead of home addresses. About 30 local people helped fix these issues using laptops provided by Google.

This project helps promote Iqaluit as a place to visit or live, and makes planning easier. Before mapping Iqaluit, Google tested the process in Cambridge Bay, a smaller town nearby.

Brindle hopes that in the future they will make better maps for other northern areas too, but it's very expensive to move people and equipment around such large areas. He wants to see big changes in how Canada’s north is mapped over the next few years.

Governments in Europe hope to find ways to stop unemployment from getting worse, but in some parts of the EU, joblessness keeps rising and talking about solutions doesn’t help much.

In Italy, one mayor thinks he found an answer for his town's lack of jobs. Instead of solving the problem, it might be seen as giving up. Valter Piscedda, a left-center mayor from Elmas near Cagliari in Sardinia, plans to pay some residents to leave and find work elsewhere.

He told The Guardian that over the past year and a half, he has been helping young people who are frustrated with job hunting. Some want local help while others have given up and want to go abroad for experience.

To support those wanting to move, Elmas will provide €12,000 to pay for ten unemployed locals aged 18-50 for intensive English lessons, a cheap flight, and a search for work in Europe. Applicants must have lived there for three years, earn less than €15,000 per year, and not be university-educated.

Unemployment is high in Sardinia and parts of central Italy, with a jobless rate of 17.7% and over 54% of young people out of work as of the second quarter of 2014, according to Istat (National Institute of Statistics).

Piscedda insists this won't lead to a brain drain; he believes those who leave might return with more skills. The program is meant for those in need without other options.

Elmas previously offered financial incentives to businesses to hire young workers but had 120 applicants for only 20 positions.

The "Adesso Parto" (Now I’m leaving) program got mixed reactions from Elmas residents. Some think it's a good chance to learn and experience new cultures, while others question why the money isn’t used locally instead.

Piscedda says he deals with real problems daily and must help those without alternatives. He believes temporary work is not enough; the goal is to provide long-term solutions.

Natural factors like water and sand can make cities vulnerable or lead to their disappearance. If the planet got colder due to climate change, ice would be another factor. In 2013, an "ice tsunami" hit Ochre Beach in Canada when a wall of melting iceberg was blown onto shore by winds, destroying houses.

Rising sea levels are making cities like Venice vulnerable. A century ago, Venice flooded ten times per year; now its lowest point, Piazza San Marco, is below sea level and floods about 100 times annually. In addition to rising sea levels, the land in Venice sank by 20cm from 1950 to 1970 due to industrial activities around the city.

Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam is sinking at a rate of 2cm per year, but Jakarta is dropping even faster—between 10 to 20cm annually. Over three decades, Jakarta has sunk by about four meters, making its seawall less effective. The Indonesian capital pumps out so much groundwater that the land is drying and compacting, creating a bowl shape.

Miami faces problems due to being low-lying, increasing tropical storms, and porous limestone absorbing rising sea water. This leads to sewage issues and polluted freshwater. There's a chance Miami may become uninhabitable.

In the Maldives, populations on whole islands are considering leaving their homes. The capital, Male, built a ten-foot seawall costing $63 million but only stabilizing rising sea levels can save it long-term.

Rainfall also endangers cities like Detroit, where outdated sewage systems were overwhelmed by heavy rain in one morning. Detroit is struggling to improve its system due to economic issues and is vulnerable to water-borne pathogens.

In Africa, desertification is causing the Sahara Desert to expand at a rate of 30 miles per year, threatening Mauritania's settlements. Chinguetti has lost population from 20,000 in mid-twentieth century to just a few thousand due to sand piling up in streets and trading ceasing.

Rancho Mirage in California may be abandoned due to over-expansion and water shortages. The city uses more than 200 gallons of water per person daily, leading to drought-like conditions. A 25% cut in water use is unlikely to stabilize the resort.

Abandonment can cause cities to disintegrate quickly. For example, Hashima Island in Japan was a concrete city built for coal mining but abandoned when resources ran out; now sea spray causes its walls to collapse.

Forest fires are a growing threat in urban areas in America and Australia, potentially rendering cities uninhabitable. Long-term droughts make trees highly combustible.

Venice, Jakarta, Miami, and Malé face the greatest risks due to rising seas and sinking land, making them the world's most vulnerable metropolises.

It's called 'the hotel of mum and dad,' but few guesthouses offer such good deals. Because housing is very expensive, one in five young adults stays at home until they are 26 or older, and the same number do not pay anything for living there. A survey found that in different parts of the country, from just under 9% in the East Midlands to more than double that amount in London where house prices and rents are the highest, young adults live with their parents. The survey also showed that about 20% of these young people do not pay anything at all.

Young adults face low wages and very high rents, which makes it hard for them to buy a home or even save money for a down payment on a house. Research by the homeless charity Shelter found that half of tenants cannot save any money toward a down payment, while a quarter can only save £100 or less each month. Although mortgages are cheaper due to low interest rates, good deals still require large down payments.

Young adults return to their family homes to save money when parents can't offer them financial help. The survey found that 28% of adults live at home to save for a down payment, but 30% aren’t saving any money.

A person from the company doing the survey said: “Parents are letting young people stay longer than expected because high rents and the need to save for buying a house mean some kids have no choice.”

Michael Day, who is 30 and lives with his parents in Bristol, says he can't afford both high rent and saving for a down payment. Renting a one-bedroom home costs between £500 and £800 a month, while buying one would cost about £130,000.

Sue Green from Saga said that most parents are happy to let their children stay in the family home without paying rent because it can help them buy a house sooner. Some children contribute by buying groceries or doing chores around the house.

Angus Hanton from an organization called the Intergenerational Foundation believes older generations caused the housing crisis and young people shouldn't be blamed for staying at home. Young people have seen their average incomes drop about 20% since 2008, and high rents make it harder to save money.

Jenna Gavin is 29 and lives in Southport with her parents. She moved out briefly for university but returned because renting a one-bedroom flat would cost more than £420 a month before bills. Jenna works as a medical receptionist nearby and wants to stay in the area, but she can't afford to rent or buy.

Jenna tries to save money, but it's hard to build up enough funds for a down payment on a house. Her parents don’t charge her rent and want her to try to save money. Jenna helps by bringing food and doing chores around the home. She gets along well with her parents but hoped to live on her own by 30. “I don't see that happening as it's next year, but hopefully in a couple of years I’ll move out,” she said.

David Bowie, who died of cancer, kept surprising people until the end. His last album, Blackstar, came out on his 69th birthday in January 2016 and showed that he still made powerful music.

In the 1970s, Bowie led musical trends and pop fashion. He started as a mime entertainer and became known for glam-rock, then moved into "plastic soul," and later created new electronic music in Berlin. His ability to change sounds and images with intellectual curiosity is rare in pop history.

Bowie was born David Robert Jones in London. The family moved to Kent when he was young. He showed talent in singing and playing the recorder. Later, he studied art, music, and design. In 1961, his mother bought him a saxophone, which became important for his later music.

At age 15, David formed his first band, the Kon-rads. He went solo soon after and changed his name to Bowie to avoid confusion with Davy Jones of the Monkees.

His first album came out in June 1967. In July 1969, he released "Space Oddity," a song that became popular around the time of the Apollo 11 moon landing. 

In March 1970, Bowie married art student Angela Barnett. The Man Who Sold the World was his first album in late 1970 with daring and serious themes like immortality and mysticism.

The next year, he released Hunky Dory. Later that year came The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars, which made him famous as a sci-fi glam-rock star. His hit "Starman" and flashy stage costumes sparked fan excitement similar to Beatlemania.

Bowie’s album Aladdin Sane in 1973 had hits like “The Jean Genie.” By this time, he was also exploring funk and soul music on his album Young Americans from 1975. This gave him a US number one hit with "Fame," featuring John Lennon.

In 1976’s Station to Station, Bowie introduced the Thin White Duke persona. He had divorced Angela in 1980. In 1980 he released Scary Monsters (and Super Creeps), with its hit single “Ashes to Ashes.”

Bowie also acted on stage and in movies like Christiane F and Cat People. His album Let’s Dance in 1983 was a commercial success, with hits "Let's Dance," "China Girl," and "Modern Love." He played at Live Aid in 1985, where he performed well.

In April 1992, Bowie married the model Iman and they bought a home in New York. In 1993, his album Black Tie White Noise was popular. His daughter Alexandria was born in August 2000.

After the September 11 attacks in 2001, he performed at Concert for New York City. In 2004 during his Reality tour, Bowie had chest pains and needed emergency surgery to clear a blocked artery.

In 2006, he took time off from touring and recording. He received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2006 after being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1996.

His album The Next Day in 2013 was his first new material in a decade. It included the single “Where Are We Now?,” which gave him his first UK top 10 hit since 1993.

In 2014, he won the Best British Male at the Brit Awards, becoming the oldest winner ever. Bowie is survived by Iman, their daughter Alexandria, his stepdaughter Zulekha, and son Duncan from his first marriage.

At Addis Ababa airport, visitors see pictures of golden grains, tiny red seeds, and men around a big pancake. Billboards say, "Teff: the ultimate gluten-free crop!"

Ethiopia is one of the world's poorest countries but it is home to teff, a highly nutritious ancient grain now sold in health food shops and supermarkets in Europe and America.

Teff has tiny seeds as small as poppy seeds. It is high in calcium, iron, and protein with a good set of amino acids. As it does not have gluten, the grain can replace wheat flour for bread, pasta, waffles, and pizza bases. Teff's nutrition offers new profitable markets in the west.

In Ethiopia, teff is very important. Around 6.3 million farmers grow it, covering over 20% of all farmland. The ground seeds make injera, a spongy flatbread essential to Ethiopian food. This grain is key for many religious and cultural events. In Ethiopia and Eritrea, people eat around big pieces of injera, which also serves as utensils while sharing stews, showing friendship.

Outside of communities in the west, teff was not well-known but health and gluten-free markets are now making it popular again. It is called Ethiopia's "second gift to the world" after coffee.

Sophie Kebede, an entrepreneur from London who owns a UK company that specializes in this grain, said she was surprised by its nutritional value. She grew up eating injera.

Growing demand for ancient grains has not always been good for poor communities. In Bolivia and Peru, farmers have conflicts over land when selling their entire crops to meet western needs.

Ethiopia's growing middle class is driving up teff prices, making it hard for the poorest people to buy it. Most small farmers sell most of what they grow in cities. This has helped incomes but also affected nutrition as teff is the country’s most nutritious grain.

The government wants to double teff production by 2015. They think the grain can help school meals and emergency aid programs, reducing malnutrition among children and teens.

Though Ethiopia's economy is growing fast, it remains on the UN list of least-developed countries. About 20% of young children are malnourished or have stunted growth.

The government plans to increase teff yields by developing better types and planting techniques, and reducing losses after harvest.

Since 2006, Ethiopia has banned raw teff grain exports but allows injera and processed products shipments. They hope to produce enough for both domestic needs and strong export markets.

Mama Fresh is a family business selling injera to top restaurants in Addis Ababa and exporting it to Finland, Germany, Sweden, and the US mainly for diaspora communities. They plan to double exports to America in 2014 and start making teff-based pizzas, bread, and cookies.

David Hallam from the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization warns that export opportunities can be mixed blessings for poor countries.

Regassa Feyissa, an Ethiopian agricultural scientist, warns that increased teff production could hurt farmers by displacing other important crops. Efforts to boost production might benefit businesses more than small farmers.

Farmers in the US, Europe, Israel, and Australia have started growing teff because little is available internationally from Ethiopia.

Kebede prefers sourcing her grain from Ethiopian farms but gets it from southern Europe now. She believes Ethiopians should supply this sought-after grain.

David Cameron, Barack Obama, and Pamela Anderson have said no to the Ice Bucket Challenge. George W Bush, Benedict Cumberbatch, and Stephen Hawking have joined in. The challenge raised $100 million for a US motor neuron disease charity and £4.5 million for a British one, plus more money for charities in Hong Kong and Australia. But some people do not like it. They say famous people are just showing off their bodies or having fun without giving any money.

The Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) Association got criticized for paying top staff high salaries. The challenge started in the US in July. It first appeared on American TV on July 15. Now, the ALS Association is not trying to get a patent for “Ice Bucket Challenge” anymore because of criticism.

The charity WaterAid says people should use recycled water or sea water. Douglas Graham from the MND Association said they did not expect this but are very happy with the donations.

Pamela Anderson wrote that she cannot support the ALS Association’s work on animal testing. Some stars, like Matt Damon and Verne Troyer, found different ways to do the challenge because of environmental concerns.

Lincoln Humphries, an Australian TV host, said he would not do it and suggested donating money directly instead. The MND Association said they can handle more money for research and support for people with this disease.

The awareness from the challenge is very valuable too. On one day recently, their website got 330,000 visits, which usually happens in an entire year. Every penny will be used to help find a cure or treatment and care for people with MND.

Dan Sullivan, a 27-year-old venture capitalist from Silicon Valley, missed his breakfast with the Guardian because he got pulled over on his motorcycle. He admits that he is often late for dinner dates and forgets to give presents.

To solve these problems, he created a start-up called BetterBoyfriend.me. The service sends girlfriends or wives a present every month for about $70. Sullivan has been testing this program with around 350 boyfriends who pay him approximately $17,000 each month. Most of his members are from Harvard and other investors like those working at Apple, Google, and Facebook.

Each month, members can choose one out of seven possible gifts such as chocolate or a tea set, which is then sent to the girlfriend without any branding or labels.

Sullivan tests his ideas by buying ads on Facebook. BetterBoyfriend.me has become popular because it addresses a common issue that many people face.

Before starting BetterBoyfriend.me, Sullivan had another idea for a dog-sharing service but decided against it. He also created InvisibleBoyfriend, an app that lets users design a virtual boyfriend to deter unwanted advances or provide companionship.

Sullivan says he now acts as a relationship consultant for the boyfriends who use his service. Initially, some packages included receipts with his name on them, causing issues when girlfriends found out. About half of the women receiving the gifts know about Sullivan's involvement, and this often increases with age.

The founder has gotten to know the boyfriends well over time and even made deliveries to hospital delivery rooms. He learned that it was better to give gifts directly to the boyfriend instead of the girlfriend.

Sullivan emphasizes keeping his relationship focus on the boyfriend and not letting the girlfriend find out about BetterBoyfriend.me unless they want to.

Scientists have made a mirror that sends heat into space to cool buildings instead of using air-conditioning units. This new mirror could greatly reduce the energy needed for keeping places like offices and shops cool.

In the U.S., about 15% of the energy used by buildings is for air conditioning. The scientists think this mirror might stop the need for extra cooling in some cases.

Tests on a rooftop in Stanford, California showed that while black paint got up to 60 degrees Celsius hotter than normal temperature and bare aluminum reached 40 degrees Celsius higher, the mirror was actually cooler—up to 5 degrees Celsius below the air temperature.

Shanhui Fan, who led the development of the mirror at Stanford University, explained: “If you cover a big part of the roof with this mirror, it can save a lot of power. You can reduce the electricity used for air conditioning by a lot.”

Buildings get hot from many sources such as hot water boilers and cooking areas. In hot countries, warm air also enters through doors and windows, and sunlight heats buildings too.

The Stanford mirror reflects 97% of visible light and works as a thermal radiator to release heat as infrared light that goes right through the atmosphere into space. It is made up of thin layers, with silver on the bottom and alternating layers of silicon dioxide and hafnium oxide above it. The total thickness is around two micrometers or two thousandths of a millimeter.

The mirror can cool buildings by releasing heat directly to outer space, which acts as a big cooling source. In tests, the mirror had a cooling power of 40 watts per square meter at normal temperature.

Fan said that covering a three-story building with these mirrors could save about 100 megawatt-hours of electricity each year and cost between $20 to $70 per square meter.

The mirror can be used to cool water or fluid, which is then pumped around the building for cooling. However, Fan says it won't help slow global warming because roof space only covers a small part of Earth's surface. The main benefit is reducing electricity use.

Marin Soljačić from MIT said he’s excited about the mirror’s potential to reduce air conditioning needs and possibly eliminate them in some cases by using large surfaces like those on shopping malls for substantial cooling.

It might be like Trevor Baylis’s wind-up radio from before the internet – a cheap light powered by gravity that could end dangerous kerosene lamps in Africa and India.

Patrick Hunt, a British designer, tried to get funding for his invention but faced problems. He said it was hard because banks didn’t want to take risks on an untested idea.

So he used crowdfunding on Indiegogo, which had just opened in the UK. In five days, he raised £36,200 and within 40 days, over £400,000.

His LED light uses a dynamo that gets power from a slowly falling 10kg bag of rocks, providing half an hour of light when lifted to about 2 meters high.

Hunt plans to make the lights in China. He will test by delivering 1,000 lights to Africa before mass production.

Danae Ringelmann, who co-founded Indiegogo, believes crowdfunding is fair and shows if customers like an idea quickly.

Indiegogo charges a 4% fee for successful campaigns but doesn’t offer shares. Instead, people get perks based on how much they donate.

Crowdfunding has helped many businesses test their ideas without needing bank loans or venture capital funding. It lets entrepreneurs see if there’s interest in their product and get feedback before spending too much time or money.

JMW Turner, a famous British painter, will be shown on the new £20 note after a vote across Britain. It will be the first time an artist is on a British banknote. Mark Carney, who leads the Bank of England, asked people to suggest artists and cultural figures for this honor.

Turner won against 590 other choices suggested by 30,000 people. A group of experts then picked five final names: Barbara Hepworth, Charlie Chaplin, Josiah Wedgwood, William Hogarth, and Turner. They chose these based on their important work in art and influence on British society.

The announcement happened at the Turner Contemporary gallery in Margate, where Turner used to stay when he visited. Mark Carney and artist Tracey Emin made this announcement together. Carney said it was very important for people to choose who would be on the banknote because money should also have cultural meaning.

Turner is seen as one of the most important British artists ever. His work has a big effect today. The new £20 note will show Turner’s self-portrait and his famous painting, "The Fighting Temeraire." It will also include a quote from him: “light is therefore colour” and his signature.

This new note replaces the one with Adam Smith on it and will be used by 2020. This is the first time people could vote to decide who goes on British money.

Police and intelligence groups have used lie detectors, also known as polygraphs, for nearly 100 years. They help catch criminals and find spies. Movies often show guilty people sweating while connected to the machine.

However, researchers from Britain and the Netherlands have developed a new method that could replace polygraphs within ten years. This new approach looks at full-body movements to spot signs of lying. It has been successful in tests over 70% of the time.

Polygraphs are commonly used in the U.S. for criminal cases and security checks for FBI and CIA staff, but they are less popular in Europe. Many scientists and legal experts doubt their reliability. The new method performs better in experiments.

The idea is that people who lie tend to fidget more. A special suit with 17 sensors measures movement up to 120 times per second in three dimensions for 23 joints. This helps find signs of guilt based on body movements.

Professor Ross Anderson from Cambridge University says interviewers can only guess if someone is lying about 55 out of 100 times, and polygraphs are slightly better at around 60%. However, they can be misused during interviews. People often feel anxious when facing a polygraph test.

The new method has a success rate over 70%, with some tests reaching more than 80%. Anderson believes the technique is reliable because guilty people move their bodies differently.

Anderson also notes that torture by agencies like the CIA does not work well for getting accurate information. The research paper was written by Dr. Sophie van der Zee from Cambridge University, Professor Ronald Poppe from Utrecht University, Professor Paul Taylor from Lancaster University, and Anderson himself.

Polygraphs were invented in 1921 and measure changes in pulse, blood pressure, sweating, and breathing to check if someone is lying. However, the US Supreme Court ruled in 1998 that there was no agreement on the polygraph's reliability, a finding supported by the US National Academy of Scientists in 2003.

In their experiment, Anderson and colleagues tested 180 students and employees at Lancaster University. Half were told to tell the truth while the other half lied. Participants were paid £7.50 for each 70-minute test session that included two different scenarios.

In one scenario, some participants played a computer game called Never End, while others pretended they did when they had only read notes about it. In another, people either brought a lost wallet with £5 to a box or hid it and lied about finding it.

Overall, the researchers correctly identified 82.2% of the interviewees as truthful or deceptive by analyzing their limb movements. Anderson explains that while liars often wave their arms more (detectable around 60% of the time), the real success comes from measuring total body motion, which is over 70%. This can be improved further with better questioning.

The body movement method isn't affected much by cultural background, anxiety, or how hard someone is thinking. However, using full-body suits costs about £30,000 and can be uncomfortable. Anderson's team is exploring cheaper options like motion-sensing technology from video games.

Anderson says that while CIA agents could learn to stop moving their bodies to avoid detection, freezing their movements would itself be a sign of lying.

Rebecka Singerer got tired of being told that beer was too dark or strong for her and decided she could drink whatever she wanted. Now, as a childminder in Gothenburg, she joined FemAle, a group aiming to create Sweden’s first beer made by women.

The group created We Can Do It, a pale ale sold across Sweden. The label is inspired by Rosie the Riveter, an icon of female empowerment from World War II. Elin Carlsson, a 25-year-old car painter at Volvo and the founder of FemAle, says their beer is for everyone and not just women.

FemAle faces long-standing biases in the beer world. Big brewers like Carlsberg have tried to appeal to women with lighter or flavored beers that did not succeed. FemAle’s strategy includes tastings where women can try different flavors and learn about beer, encouraging more women to enjoy it.

The idea for FemAle came from the women meeting at beer festivals. Felicia Nordström, a bar worker, started We Can Do It after getting tired of beer experts questioning her knowledge. She worked with FemAle and Ocean, an independent micro-brewery, to create the recipe and brew 1,600 liters.

Thomas Bingebo, the head brewer at Ocean, says their beer is not specifically for women but is their hoppiest brew. The first batch sold out quickly, and other breweries are interested in collaborating with FemAle on new beers.

We Can Do It uses Maris Otter, Amber, and wheat malt, and has Galaxy and Cascade hops. Its bitterness level (IBU) is 65, and its alcohol content is 4.6%.

Elin Carlsson believes women choose wine because they do not know much about beer or what to order. FemAle aims to change that by introducing new flavors.

Singerer used not to like stout but now enjoys Guinness and even stronger stouts. She says the group is part of a growing interest in craft beers in Sweden, replacing traditional strong lagers with more diverse choices.

Emma Henriksson, a 22-year-old member working at a garden equipment company, points out that every woman interested in beer can enjoy it differently. Singerer adds that every pub wants to attract women and FemAle has found the way to do this effectively.

Walking onto the stage, Donald Trump, who is trying to become the Republican presidential nominee, said something unexpected for someone doing so well in polls. "Unless we win, it doesn't mean a thing," he told a big crowd of 11,000 people in South Carolina. He also wanted to pick the election date and have it soon.

Trump has some doubts but usually speaks confidently about winning. His main idea is that he is a “winner.”

Trump’s campaign surprises many experts, especially after several controversies where his statements caused trouble. For example:

1. He questioned if John McCain was truly a hero because he got captured during the Vietnam War.
2. During a debate, he insulted Megyn Kelly from Fox News for asking him tough questions.
3. Trump has also said bad things about Mexican immigrants and claimed that Black Lives Matter protesters deserved rough treatment.
4. He made fun of a journalist’s disability and falsely accused Muslim Americans of cheering during the 9/11 attacks.

Trump believes many incidents were exaggerated by the media, but he refuses to take back what he said.

His rivals worry his supporters might get tired of him attacking minorities. A recent poll shows his support among Republicans has dropped by 12 points but still stands at 31%.

Critics like Bobby Jindal say Trump is not a typical conservative or liberal; instead, he believes only in himself.

Liz Mair, who organizes against Trump, thinks his comments are designed to appeal to his core supporters. She urges people to actively fight him rather than just hope he fails.

Trump’s main issues – immigration reform, free trade deals, and Obama's national security policy – have become key topics of the election. His policies on deporting undocumented immigrants and building a wall between Mexico and the US have hurt Jeb Bush’s campaign.

Polls show that currently among Americans who are Republicans, Trump has 25-30% support. It will be hard for another candidate to win over his supporters without losing their own.

Some voters say they definitely would not support Trump. Steve Deace says Trump's actions create a loyal following but limit growth beyond that group.

Frank Luntz believes Trump speaks for people who feel unheard and like him because he is outspoken, even if it’s outrageous.

Supporters appreciate Trump’s confidence and believe he can fix the country.

A long time ago, in 1977, people went to watch movies about a galaxy far away where spaceships fought each other and robots met Wookiees. The spaceship called Millennium Falcon could travel very fast.

In 2015, the Star Wars movies are still popular. There will be new films about Han Solo and Darth Vader.
