Paul Dergarabedian from Rentrak said that people all over the world are excited to see new Star Wars posters and trailers.

Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012 for $4 billion. They planned three more episodes (VII, VIII, IX) and spin-off movies. One of these is a story about how Han Solo became famous, coming out in May 2018.

Episode VII came out in December 2015, and it was called Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Episode VIII was due in 2017, and another movie, Rogue One, came out in 2016 to show how rebels got plans for the Death Star.

Disney also bought Marvel Studios in 2009. They use smart marketing by making all six original Star Wars movies available on streaming services.

The "Expanded Universe" includes books, comics, games, and other products about Star Wars that have been popular since the internet became widespread.

Michael Rosser from Screen International said that the new films will connect with the first ones in a way that the prequels (films made between 1999-2005) did not. The prequels earned $2.5 billion, even though many people did not like them much.

Rosser thinks movie studios want to keep making good quality films and get more people into theaters because watching at home is less exciting.

Dergarabedian expects Episode VII to make over a billion dollars worldwide when it comes out in December 2015. Star Wars remains the most popular movie brand.

In 2010, the old city in Srinagar was dangerous. Police would only enter wearing body armor because violent separatists were fighting for an independent Kashmir. This fighting led to over 100 deaths.

Now things have changed. Tourists can enjoy mutton tikka and rogan josh in those same streets. The Nowhatta mosque, where young people used to gather to throw stones at security forces, is now part of a walking tour focused on heritage and markets. Houseboats by Dal Lake are booked months ahead, and visitors can take photos in the beautiful gardens around the lake. Ski resorts nearby were busy with Russian tourists until the snow melted.

In 2002, only about 27,000 tourists visited Kashmir Valley due to fear of anti-Indian violence that killed up to 70,000 people. In 2012, almost one million tourists came, including more than 23,000 from outside India. However, fewer than 150 British visitors were there because the UK Foreign Office warns against travel due to security issues.

Omar Abdullah, Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir, wants the UK to change its warning but has not succeeded. “It’s frustrating,” he said. Insurance becomes invalid for travelers visiting under these warnings. The last known case of foreign tourists being killed was in 1995 when six Westerners, including two Britons, were kidnapped by a militant group.

Abdullah argues that British citizens have been killed in other countries without travel restrictions being imposed. He states there’s no reason to single out Jammu and Kashmir as unsafe. Germany relaxed its guidelines for tourists visiting the region in 2011 after disturbances died down in 2010.

Syed Ali Shah Geelani, a leader of a pro-independence party, also supports tourism, saying visitors are welcome. Some worry about ethical issues but locals support tourism to boost the economy.

Better infrastructure like roads and electricity is needed, along with more evening activities for tourists since there’s only one cinema in Srinagar. A local Islamic group issued a dress code for foreign tourists, which Abdullah sees as asking tourists to be sensitive to cultural norms.

Abdullah pushes tourism because Jammu and Kashmir's finances are poor after years of turmoil. The state receives £72 million in taxes but pays £155 million in salaries to public employees. Tourism is seen as a way to bring money into the region.

For now, Abdullah feels satisfied that people can come, enjoy their time, and leave safely.

James Hamblin, who works at The Atlantic magazine, did not shower to see how it affects his body. He found out that washing too much can make your skin work harder to stay healthy. Showering with hot water and soap takes away natural oils and good bacteria from the skin, which can dry it out. This might even cause you to smell more after repopulating bad-smelling bacteria.

When people stop showering and using soap often, their skin goes through a change first but then gets better. The oil in your skin balances, and healthy bacteria grow. Less frequent showers can help acne and eczema, according to dermatologists.

Taking fewer showers also saves water and is good for the environment. An average shower uses 65 liters of water and lasts seven minutes. Using less soap means less waste from bottles too.

If you worry about smelling bad or feeling dirty, remember that using deodorant can help with smell issues. Also, washing your hands with soap is still important to stop spreading germs.

You don’t have to stop showering completely like Hamblin did, but trying to skip a few showers and use less soap might be good for you and the environment.

Since he was diagnosed with HIV at age 48, Moses King has struggled to get enough food for his family of six children in Liberia. Although he could grow vegetables and buy rice, expensive protein sources like meat and fish were hard to come by. This led to nutritional problems because he needed more protein to stay healthy.

Pate K Chon, an HIV counselor, had a solution after seeing a documentary about fish farming in Thailand. She wanted to start a similar project in Liberia to help people with HIV get both work and protein. In 2012, she met John Sheehy who helped build the fish farm near Monrovia.

The project is now called Grow2Feed Liberia Fish Farm and has 12 tanks that will each hold 5,000 fish. The farm can produce up to 200,000 fish a year for about 1,200 HIV-positive people in the community. Waste from the fish tanks also helps irrigate crops, providing more food and income.

HIV is still stigmatized in Liberia, where 1.5% of the population has it, mostly women and girls. Good nutrition is very important for those with HIV because they need more protein to stay healthy while taking their medicine. This farm provides both work and a source of fish that people can eat or sell.

The project caught the attention of the Liberian government and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. Fish farming has great potential in Africa since much of the fish sold is imported from China and is not high quality. Sheehy hopes to spread this model throughout Liberia and other regions, always keeping it non-profit and focused on helping those in need.

For 85 years, Pluto was just a grey dot on school maps of our solar system. But on July 15th, we got our first close look at it, showing us big mountains made from ice that rival the size of the Alps or Rockies.

The New Horizons spacecraft took these amazing pictures and sent them back to Earth from about 4 billion miles away after a nearly ten-year journey. Alan Stern, who led the mission, said the images were better than expected: "New Horizons is giving us great data already."

One big surprise was finding mountains on Pluto in the Kuiper Belt area, where many icy objects float around. John Spencer, part of the team, found these mountains to be about 11,000 feet tall and hundreds of miles wide.

The pictures showed that Pluto’s surface looks very smooth with no craters, meaning it might still have some geological activity like ice geysers or volcanoes called cryovolcanoes.

During the NASA press conference, they showed off beautiful images of the sun and eight planets before revealing Pluto. Dwayne Brown from NASA said, "We’ve brought what was a blur into focus."

Stern believes there’s more to learn about Pluto in the next year. They found that while the mountains are made mostly from water ice, the surface also has thin layers of methane and nitrogen ices.

The mountain formation on Pluto happened very recently, within the last 100 million years, suggesting active geological activity still happening on its surface. The images show for the first time ice mountains outside giant planet moons.

Pluto’s smooth surfaces may be due to internal heat or snow covering up old craters. These pictures are so detailed that if the spacecraft were flying over London, you could see Heathrow airport's runways clearly.

It takes hours for New Horizons to send back a picture from Pluto because it is 5 billion kilometers away and will take sixteen months to send all its data collected during the fly-by.

Scientists decided to name the heart-shaped feature on Pluto "Tombaugh Regio" in honor of Clyde Tombaugh, who found Pluto in 1930. The new Charon image shows a complex surface with deep canyons and cliffs.

Charon’s surface is also varied and has been affected by geological activity, as seen in the big canyon estimated to be between seven and nine kilometers deep.

Cathy Olkin from the team said, "Charon just blew our socks off," showing how excited scientists were about these findings. 

Pluto is made mostly of rock with a lot of ice on top and has temperatures around minus 230 degrees Celsius. As New Horizons moves into the Kuiper Belt, it hopes to uncover clues about the early solar system.

In August 2015, mission scientists chose which object to visit next in the Pluto system, including moons Nix, Hydra, Styx, and Kerberos. The new image of Hydra shows its irregular shape with estimated dimensions of 43 by 33 kilometers and likely has a water ice coating on its surface.

John Grunsfeld from NASA said, “New Horizons is showing us why research matters, and the mission’s images surpassed expectations.”

Future pictures will give more clues about these moons' formation billions of years ago.

In the journal Nature, Roger McKinlay, who used to be president of the Royal Institute of Navigation, says that depending too much on GPS technology could hurt our natural ability to navigate. He warns that if we don't use these skills, they will get weaker as we rely more on smart devices.

McKinlay thinks a lot of money will need to be spent before navigation systems are good enough for autonomous vehicles to become widespread. Until then, he believes there should be better research into different ways of navigating and teaching children how to do it without technology. “Schools should teach map reading as a life skill,” he said.

Around 66% of UK adults owned smartphones in 2015, up from 39% in 2012. McKinlay thinks we shouldn't depend entirely on devices for navigation because "navigation is a use-it-or-lose-it skill."

Research led by Dr Hugo Spiers at University College London found that retired taxi drivers did worse on navigation tests compared to those still working as taxi drivers, showing that not using these skills can make them weaker.

Spiers also warns about the danger of relying too much on GPS. He mentions a driver who died in Spain because their satnav led them into a reservoir. "There is a real risk when you rely on a satnav," Spiers said.

Spiers notes that how we use navigational technology can affect our own skills. For example, using audio instructions takes less thinking than using smartphone apps to look at maps and plan routes.

McKinlay believes navigation technologies still have a long way to go before they are advanced enough for futuristic ideas like driverless cars and smart cities. He thinks GPS is not yet good enough for critical applications such as landing aircraft safely.

Spiers suggests that artificial intelligence might improve navigational aids, but McKinlay remains doubtful. He hopes future technology will be able to understand what a person wants or needs while navigating.

McKinlay emphasizes the importance of humans being able to control their navigation. "Do you want people to be shocked and unable to do anything when GPS fails?" he asked. "Technology is just a tool, not magic."

Starting a new year can make you feel unhappy about work because it feels like forever until the next holiday and it’s dark when you start and end your day. If you dislike your job, you might want to change it.

Before looking for a new job, think carefully. Here are five unusual jobs people do:

1. **Dog-food Taster**
   - Task: Taste dog food to check its quality.
   - Details: Smell and taste fresh batches of dog or cat food.
   - Salary: £20,000 entry-level; £50,000 for experienced managers.
   - Worst Part: Meeting deadlines. The meat used is safe for humans too, but some products smell very bad.
   - Satisfaction: No two days are the same, and helping pets be happier makes it rewarding.

2. **Hygiene Technician**
   - Task: Clean areas exposed to dangerous materials from accidents or crimes.
   - Details: Clean up after suicides, crime scenes, and hoarders’ houses.
   - Salary: £14,500 entry-level; up to £22,000 for top positions.
   - Worst Part: Emotional strain of cleaning up suicides.
   - Satisfaction: The job is varied and helps keep people safe.

3. **Biogas Engineer**
   - Task: Set up biogas plants using waste in developing countries.
   - Details: Connect toilets to digesters filled with human waste, animal dung, etc., to produce gas for cooking and lighting.
   - Salary: £10,000 entry-level; £30,000 for chief technical officer.
   - Worst Part: Seeing people struggle financially and dealing with the smell of decomposing waste.
   - Satisfaction: Helps communities increase income, improve hygiene, and allows girls to attend school.

4. **Eel Ecologist**
   - Task: Help conserve endangered European eels.
   - Details: Measure and weigh adult eels up to 2kg in rivers and marshes.
   - Worst Part: Dealing with the tricky nature of eels and learning about environmental damage.
   - Satisfaction: Working outdoors and helping river systems.

5. **Shopping Channel Presenter**
   - Task: Sell products live on TV, demonstrating them while appearing enthusiastic.
   - Details: Prepare a lot beforehand to know all product details.
   - Salary: £30,000 trainee; over £55,000 for experienced presenters.
   - Worst Part: Unusual work hours like late nights and weekends.
   - Satisfaction: Enjoying the excitement of live presenting and seeing viewers order products.

Google showed a new car that doesn’t need a driver to control it. This car is electric and can go up to 25 miles per hour. It does not have any pedals or steering wheel, only two seats and one big red STOP button. To use the car, you just press a button on your phone to pick you up and tell where you want to go.

Google made about 100 of these cars for testing around their offices in California. The company’s co-founder, Sergey Brin, said this car will help people who have trouble using public transportation now.

Sitting inside the car is relaxing because the computer does all the driving for you. Google says it will be safer for pedestrians because its front is made with foam to absorb impact and it has a plastic windshield.

The cars were built by an unnamed company in Detroit, and they are not available yet. They use very detailed maps that need to be created ahead of time so the car can drive safely on them. Right now, only 2,000 miles out of more than 170,000 miles of California’s roads have these detailed maps.

Google hopes to share this technology with other car companies in the future. However, taxi drivers worry that driverless cars might take away their jobs. There are about 22,000 black cabs and around 100,000 people who drive taxis for hire in the UK.

Chris Urmson from Google said it’s better to have a simple emergency stop button instead of steering wheels or brakes because there is no guarantee a person could take over safely during an emergency. 

The self-driving cars have driven about 700,000 miles without causing any accidents themselves. This project aims to make roads safer and give more mobility options for people.

Google’s driverless car project has been in development for over ten years by team members before they joined the company.

Valdevaqueros is a beautiful, untouched beach in southern Spain where kitesurfers fly over the waves. The beach has only an access road lined with camper vans from different countries filled with windsurfers and kitesurfers attracted by strong winds.

For many years, Valdevaqueros was very different from the concrete-lined beaches of Torremolinos and Marbella nearby. But on May 29, the local council in Tarifa approved plans to build a large tourist complex right next to the beach. The project includes 1,400 hotel rooms and 350 flats.

Environmental groups say this will harm the habitats of protected animals. However, most city officials support it because they think it will create jobs. In Tarifa, which has 18,000 people, 2,600 are unemployed due to Spain's severe economic crisis.

Sebastián Galindo, an opposition councillor from the Socialist Party who still supports the project, said traditional sources of income like fishing are disappearing as fish stocks decrease and fleets reduce. He believes sustainable tourism is Tarifa’s only solution.

The new complex would be 800 meters from the coast, which meets a law that requires buildings to be at least 200 meters away from the beach to prevent unsightly developments similar to those built in the 1960s and 1970s during the rise of mass tourism.

Some oppose more housing because Spain already has one million empty homes. The central government suggested selling properties worth at least €160,000 to foreigners who would get residency permits. Opponents say this favors wealthy people over migrant workers from countries like Morocco, whose coast is just 14 kilometers away and visible from Tarifa.

Surfers worry that new buildings will weaken the strong local wind, which brings many visitors. A surfer named Henning Mayer thinks construction might not happen because it didn't in the past.

Tarifa is a key crossing between Africa and Europe where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic. Environmentalists say this area is important for migrating animals too.

A campaign to save Valdevaqueros started after the council approved the project. It has support from groups like Greenpeace, Birdlife Spain, and the World Wide Fund for Nature. The complex could affect an ancient Roman town called Baelo Claudia and might cover unknown Roman ruins.

The Andalusian College of Geographers says parts of the new resort will overlap with a national park and two wildlife conservation areas, including places where endangered bats live. This project ignores European environmental rules.

Tarifa faces water shortages in summer, and previous plans for other developments were stopped due to lack of water. Many locals prefer building closer to Tarifa's old center instead of far away on green fields near the beach.

Biologist Aitor Galán says this area is one of only two seaside vulture breeding grounds in Europe and should be protected. Building a resort here would destroy it, turning Valdevaqueros into another crowded tourist spot like Benidorm. The beauty of wildlife and wind draws people to Tarifa now, but developers use the current economic crisis to justify such changes.

Scientists have made a map of the brain called an "atlas." This atlas shows where different words and their meanings are located in the brain. The map looks like a colorful quilt spread over the brain.

Jack Gallant, a scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, said they wanted to make a big map showing how one part of language—word meanings—is stored in the brain.

Not just one spot holds a single word or idea; several spots are involved. Also, each word is connected with many different spots across the brain. Together, these spots form networks that show what words mean: words like "life," "love," "death," and "taxes" each have their own network.

Alexander Huth, who led the study, said this method might help figure out which words a person hears, reads, or thinks about by looking at brain activity. This could be useful for people with diseases that stop them from speaking.

To make this map, they watched what happened in people's brains when they listened to stories on The Moth Radio Hour, a popular radio show. They then compared the stories' words with the brain activity data to see which areas of the brain were active during different kinds of words.

Huth picked these stories because they are short and interesting. This way, he was sure people would focus while listening. Seven people listened for two hours each, hearing about 25,000 words, including more than 3,000 different ones.

The atlas shows that similar words activate the same areas of the brain. For example, the left side of the brain near the ear has spots for words like "victim," "killed," and "murdered." The right side of the brain near the top is activated by family terms such as "wife" or "husband."

Each word has more than one spot in the brain because most words have many meanings. For example, the word "top" lights up spots connected with clothing, numbers, buildings, and places.

People can explore this map on an interactive website. The maps were similar for all seven participants, suggesting their brains organize language similarly. However, only five men and two women who speak English natively were scanned. People from other backgrounds might have different brain atlases.

Scientists now plan to use the atlas to study how the brain handles various concepts like numbers or religion. They are also working on new maps for other parts of language, but making a map for story structure has been difficult so far.

Uri Hasson, another scientist, said this work is important because it shows how the brain works in real-life situations. He thinks they can make better maps and eventually figure out what words people think by looking at their brains. This could have big ethical issues, but could also help check if political messages are understood by the public.

Lorraine Tyler, a scientist from Cambridge University, said this research is groundbreaking but still has much to discover about how word meanings work in the brain.

A Canadian man named Jordan Axani became famous after offering a free trip around the world to any woman named Elizabeth Gallagher. This was because his ex-girlfriend's name was Elizabeth Gallagher, but they broke up and he could not change the names on the tickets.

In 2014, Axani posted about this offer on Reddit. A student from Nova Scotia named Quinn Gallagher replied, and Jordan chose her to go on the trip. Quinn already had a serious boyfriend, so there were no chances for romance between them.

Jordan and Quinn traveled together for three weeks, visiting cities like Milan, Venice, Vienna, Prague, Khao Lak in Thailand, and Hong Kong. At first, they found it hard to get along but eventually became close friends, like brother and sister.

After the trip ended on January 12 at 3 am when they returned to Toronto, Jordan said their relationship was strictly friendly with no romantic future. He went straight from the airport to a board meeting for his charity, A Ticket Forward, which he started after his Reddit post became popular. The charity plans to offer free trips around the world to people who survived abuse, cancer, and war.

Jordan also mentioned that there is interest in turning his story into a TV show or film, though nothing has been confirmed yet.

As for his personal life, Jordan said he is not looking for new relationships right now but remains open to what life brings.

US researchers say a nasal spray with the 'Love hormone' oxytocin may help children with autism handle social situations better. Scans show that one dose of this chemical improves how the brain reacts to facial expressions, which could make social interactions feel more natural and rewarding.

Kevin Pelphrey from Yale University suggests that using oxytocin regularly might make behavioral therapies for autism more effective. He expects it would lead to "more appropriate social responding," including increased interest in interacting with others and better conversation skills.

Autism affects over one in 100 people, causing difficulties in social interaction and communication. There is currently no established treatment for these issues caused by autism. Scientists at Yale are studying oxytocin as a possible treatment because it helps with bonding and trust.

Results from studies on oxytocin have been mixed, but Pelphrey believes it can help the brain learn from social interactions when used alongside therapies that encourage more social engagement. 

The researchers scanned the brains of 17 youths aged eight to sixteen with autism while they looked at images of cars or faces showing different emotions. The scans were done after inhaling a placebo or oxytocin through a nasal spray.

After using oxytocin, the brain's reward circuitry worked more normally, being more active when looking at faces and less active when viewing cars. This study appears in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in the United States.

Pelphrey warns against using oxytocin as treatment for social difficulties in autism until further research is done and advises not to buy it from online suppliers. 

Simon Baron-Cohen, director of Autism Research Centre at Cambridge University, says this study shows changes in brain activity related to social cognition but notes that oxytocin did not change performance on tasks measuring social skills.

Uta Frith, who studies autism at University College London, adds that while the study suggests faces become more interesting due to greater activity in reward evaluation areas of the brain, there is no effect seen in actual behavior. Demonstrating an effect on behavior will be necessary for any nasal spray treatment to have value.

Cathal Redmond was taking photos with his new underwater camera off the Greek coast. He thought the pictures would be great, but when he looked at them later, they were brown and unclear. He blamed this on not having enough time to set up the shots while holding his breath.

Redmond decided to solve this problem by inventing the Express Dive – a device you put in your mouth that lets you stay underwater for two minutes. It is meant to be easier than scuba diving, which requires heavy and expensive equipment. The prototype looks like a mix of a scuba mouthpiece and a water bottle.

Redmond, 27, loves being able to breathe underwater but dislikes the extra gear needed for scuba diving. He says, “I wanted people to do more in the water without holding their breath.” In 2006, he took a scuba-diving course and found it hard to get used to all the equipment.

During his final year at the University of Limerick studying product design, Redmond created the Express Dive. It has two main parts: a fan that sucks in air when above water, compresses it through valves, and stores it in a tank. The tank lights up green when full. As you dive, air comes out through the mouthpiece. A display shows how much air is left by changing from green to red.

The device can take enough air for two minutes of diving and refills in about the same time. Redmond shielded the electrics with waterproof casing and used a wireless charging system similar to those for phones.

Redmond says using it feels like breathing through a snorkel, but underwater. The prototype is made from foam, aluminium, and silicone and has been tested partly. He believes two minutes of air makes a big difference since most people can only hold their breath for about 40 seconds. Redmond got £5,000 to develop the project further after coming second in an international award. The device might cost around £280 and weigh between 1kg and 3kg.

On a normal day, Starbucks outlets are busy with social activities like business meetings and reading groups. But now, a group called UK Uncut plans to turn many of these coffee shops into places for children and homeless people to highlight that Starbucks avoids paying taxes.

This plan comes as a Starbucks executive must answer questions from the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee about why the company did not pay any corporation tax in the UK over the past three years, despite saying they were doing well in Britain. The Chief Financial Officer of Starbucks, Troy Alstead, will try to improve the company’s image which has been damaged by this controversy.

Some MPs said officials from HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) have friendly relationships with big businesses. Conservative MP Richard Bacon said these arrangements do not smell good.

UK Uncut wants to connect government spending cuts, especially those affecting women, with tax avoidance by large multinational companies. They claim that £32 billion was lost due to tax avoidance in 2011 and say the government could fund important services if they stopped this from happening.

Anna Walker, a UK Uncut campaigner, stated that they chose Starbucks as their target because it is found on almost every street in Britain, making it easy for people to take action locally. They plan to highlight cuts by transforming Starbucks into services like shelters and daycare centers.

Several international companies have been criticized for not paying corporation tax despite having big operations in the UK. According to a YouGov poll, Starbucks has had the worst impact on its image from this criticism. However, Starbucks says they always pay taxes correctly and have paid more than £160 million in various taxes over the last three years.

Margaret Hodge, who leads the Public Accounts Committee, said Apple, eBay, Facebook, Google, and Starbucks avoided almost £900 million in tax. Prime Minister David Cameron agreed that HMRC needs to look into it carefully to ensure these businesses pay fair taxes while encouraging them to invest in the UK.

A spokesperson for Starbucks stated they follow all tax laws and rules in every country they operate in, including the UK, where they spend a lot of money on local suppliers and create jobs and apprenticeships. They hope UK Uncut will respect their staff and customers and recognize the value they add to the economy by paying what they believe is their fair share of taxes.

The government is getting ready for many legal cases from people who say they were mistreated and put in prison during the last days of the British Empire. This comes after a London court said three Kenyans can sue the British government because they were detained and tortured during the Mau Mau rebellion.

The court refused to accept that it is too late for these cases since the rebellion happened over 50 years ago. In 2011, the same judge ruled that the claimants should sue the British government, not the Kenyan one, even though Kenya gained independence in 1963.

Human rights activists think more than 5,000 out of the 70,000 people detained by the British authorities during this time are still alive and might bring claims against Britain. This ruling could also allow victims from other former colonies to sue for damages.

The Foreign Office said they would appeal because usually you have to file a civil case within three to six years. They argued it was too late now since many key people are dead.

Three elderly Kenyans, Paulo Muoka Nzili (85), Wambugu Wa Nyingi (84), and Jane Muthoni Mara (73), won the legal battle after three years of fighting in court. Their lawyers say they suffered brutal acts including castration, beatings, and sexual assault.

In Nairobi, Kenya, news of their victory brought joy to them and their supporters. They want compensation so they can forgive the British government.

The judge said there was evidence of systematic torture and that a fair trial is possible now because many documents were found in 2011 from a secret colonial archive.

British lawyers admitted all three Kenyans were tortured by the colonial authorities, but tried to avoid legal responsibility using technical defenses. This case could encourage other victims from places like Malaya, Yemen, Cyprus, and Palestine to sue as well.

There are also veterans of the Eoka insurgency in Cyprus who might bring claims. In Malaysia, relatives of 24 rubber plantation workers killed by British troops are fighting for a public inquiry. Former prisoners from Aden may have claims too, but it could be hard to contact them since Aden is now part of Yemen.

This case has big legal implications and could change how we understand British history during the colonial period.

Getting enough sleep used to be seen as unimportant and even a sign of laziness. People believed that working all the time was better than sleeping. Now, Arianna Huffington says getting good sleep is important for your health in her book "The Sleep Revolution." Her ideas are becoming popular.

Many new businesses now offer ways to help people sleep better. High-end hotels have special programs to improve sleep. At home, you can buy devices like a mattress cover that tracks how well you sleep or a mask that helps you nap more efficiently.

Sleep is also changing in workplaces. Companies are adding rooms where workers can take naps. Huffington thinks these nap rooms will soon be as common as meeting rooms.

The idea of getting enough sleep fits with the lifestyle of people who value healthy living and buy expensive health products like green juice or fitness classes. Wearable technology makes it possible to track how well you sleep, which some people find important.

Huffington says that sleeping eight hours a day can help you perform better at work. She has many assistants to handle her daily tasks so she can get enough rest. Most of these assistants leave after about one year because the job is very hard and pays low wages.

Research shows poorer people often sleep less well than wealthier people. People who worry about their safety or don't have enough food, or those working unusual hours, may not sleep well. African Americans tend to get less good quality sleep compared to white Americans due partly to stress from discrimination.

Wealthy white women usually get the best and most sleep in America. This might be Huffington’s target audience for her book on sleep.

While more people think sleep is important now, this could change soon. The military is researching ways to allow humans to function well with less sleep using drugs that reduce the effects of not sleeping enough.

In the future, people may find a way to avoid needing as much sleep or remove the need for sleep entirely. This would mean only poor people might have to spend so much time sleeping.

They call him the Robin Hood of banks. Enric Duran took out 68 loans from 39 Spanish banks without planning to pay them back. He used nearly half a million euros to support projects that promoted alternatives to capitalism.

After hiding for 14 months, Duran is still proud of what he did. “I’m happy with my actions,” he said in an interview from an undisclosed location. The money helped create opportunities and build a strong network for these initiatives.

From 2006 to 2008, Duran took out loans under false names. He started by applying with his real information but was denied. Later, he used the name of a fake TV production company to get €492,000.

In 2009, he was arrested in Spain and spent two months in prison before being bailed for €50,000. In February 2013, facing up to eight years in prison, he fled rather than stand trial. He doesn’t believe the judicial system is legitimate.

Duran’s actions helped push anti-capitalist movements into the spotlight during Spain's economic crisis. Today, these movements are supported by thousands of Spaniards, as shown by groups like the Indignados.

Now, Duran wants to promote restorative justice in Spain's legal system and share insights on banking practices with bank workers and the general public.

A group of experts and charities say fake allergy tests are making many people think they need treatments or special diets when they don't. This can lead to not eating enough nutrients, which is bad for health. Allergies and problems with certain foods are becoming more common, but mixing up these two issues often causes trouble.

Tracey Brown from Sense About Science said that the confusion between myths and real science is causing big problems. Some people get treatments they don't need while others who really do need help aren't getting it.

Moira Austin of the Anaphylaxis Campaign warned that when too many people claim to have allergies, restaurants might not take proper care with those who actually do. This can be very dangerous and has led to deaths.

The guide made by Sense About Science says most home allergy tests you find online or in shops are not based on good science. For example, some tests look for a type of antibody called IgG, but having more of this doesn’t mean someone is allergic. Another test uses acupressure and tries to measure electrical resistance through the skin when holding food. The guide says these and hair tests don't work because hair isn't part of how allergies happen.

Paul Seddon, a doctor who treats children with allergies, said he often sees kids put on very strict diets based on these fake tests. This can be hard for families and stops children from eating normally or going to parties.

Adam Fox, another allergy doctor in London, says it's tough to fix when parents have already tried lots of different foods that don't really need to be avoided. Children then miss out on important nutrients because of diets based on incorrect tests.

The guide also explains that allergies are becoming more common, especially for children with allergic rhinitis and eczema. These diagnoses have tripled in the last 30 years, so people think their health problems might be from allergies. However, many beliefs about what causes allergies, like food coloring or fast food, aren’t true according to science.

In New Orleans, you can no longer smoke inside bars. This is different from other cities because New Orleans promotes a fun atmosphere that attracts tourists. An indoor smoking ban will have special effects on the city’s unique culture.

Since Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the New Orleans city government has tried to control noise and bar activity more strictly. They also fight for a new “noise ordinance” which affects music.

William Walker, who owns a bar, says he dislikes the anti-smoking law because it forces smokers outside, increasing tension already present.

Many of New Orleans’s best bars are in quiet neighborhoods, but some people find this unacceptable now. Martha Wood lives near a loud bar with live music and supports the noise ordinance, though she does not complain about the noise from her neighbor. Her bar is one that can no longer allow drinks to go due to past noise issues.

The Maple Leaf club stopped smoking voluntarily in 2014 as did another club where artists asked for smoke-free nights. Zalia BeVille, who manages All Ways Lounge, agrees with the performance venues showing consideration to performers. All Ways Lounge went smoke-free in 2013 because singers and horn players requested it.

Geoff Douville, owner of Lost Love Lounge, likes the ban as he felt forced by smokers before. He says that without a city-wide rule, people would just go to another bar that allows smoking.

Neil Timms owns an English pub and fears losing money like when England banned smoking in 2007. To avoid this fate, he is building a patio outside for smokers.

Councilwoman LaToya Cantrell introduced the ban because she believes it can protect workers who are part of New Orleans's hospitality industry that drives Louisiana’s economy. She thinks communication and partnerships between communities and businesses can solve noise concerns.

Bar customers are encouraged to report illegal smoking by filling out forms or calling 311 with time-stamped photographs. Neil Timms complies with the ban because he doesn’t want someone getting hurt over a photo of an illegal smoker.

Geoff Douville, though, is not worried about the complaints and shares Cantrell’s hope for a positive outcome.

A Spanish degree helped me get a job as a journalist with an international news agency in Mexico City, but it didn't stop me from making mistakes when I first started. After traveling by bus from New York to the Mexican capital, my job interview tested my language skills. My work involved covering political events during the day and coordinating coverage of Central American conflicts at night. Sometimes, I had to report on disasters like fires or explosions.

As a reporter, I struggled with numbers in Spanish just as much as in English. Misunderstandings led me to call wrong phone numbers, often waking Mexican grandmothers instead of the police. In my stories, I sometimes overestimated casualties. For instance, an initial report said 83 people were killed in a fire, but later it was only 38. Another time, what started as 12 injured turned out to be just two. Finally, an editor from Washington called me and yelled, "Has no one ever told you that the number of dead can’t go down?"

Numbers in different languages can be confusing due to differences in numbering systems. For example, in German, 2:30 PM is said as "half three" (halb drei), and 21 becomes “one and twenty” (einundzwanzig). Some experts think there’s a connection between dyscalculia – trouble with math – and difficulty learning numbers in foreign languages.

Many people who are good at speaking a second language still have trouble with numbers. In my experience, I had problems with numbers even when I was fluent in other aspects of the language. This issue followed me from Mexico to Germany and Portugal.

Despite these challenges, once I had an unexpected success. When the American consul in Veracruz was held hostage, I tried calling to get information but dialed a different number. Instead, I ended up chatting for 15 minutes with the gunman. Even though I couldn’t persuade him to stop, my reputation as a new reporter improved that night.

Nobody knows if the economic crisis in Greece came first or a drug called shisha. Shisha is now known as the “cocaine of the poor.” It is dangerous and can be bought for €2 or less, making it very popular in Greece, which has been hit hard by financial problems.

Maria, a former heroin addict, says that shisha is one of the worst drugs because it burns your insides, makes you aggressive, and can drive you mad. However, it is cheap and easy to get, so many people use it.

This drug crisis has put more pressure on Athens’s health services, which are already struggling due to budget cuts. Shisha, a type of crystal meth mixed with dangerous substances like battery acid and engine oil, is widely used by homeless Greeks who have been forced onto the streets because of poverty and hopelessness.

Konstantinos, another drug addict, adds that shisha makes you want to kill without understanding your actions and has led to many deaths. For Charalampos Poulopoulos, head of Kethea, Greece’s top anti-drug center, shisha represents the effects of a crisis that has caused record levels of poverty and unemployment.

Shisha is called an “austerity drug” because it was created for those who can no longer afford expensive drugs like heroin or cocaine. It can be sniffed, injected, and made in home labs without specialized knowledge, making it extremely dangerous.

In Greece, years of recession have led to higher rates of depression, drug abuse, alcoholism, crime, and prostitution. Many women agree to unprotected sex to make more money for buying drugs like shisha. In 2012, two sex workers gave birth on the streets of Athens.

Suicides and HIV infections are also rising among drug users in Greece, where youth unemployment is the highest in the EU at 64%. The crisis has made people feel pessimistic and self-destructive because they cannot find work. Shisha use is particularly common in Athens, which has been hit hardest by economic problems.

The Greek government tries to solve this issue by removing drug users from city centers through police operations that clear streets of homeless people. However, these actions only push the problem further into the hands of drug dealers who offer protection to those marginalized by society.

Kethea and similar state-funded organizations are facing budget cuts despite studies showing that every euro invested in them saves about €6 in criminal justice and healthcare costs. Since 2009, Kethea has lost 70 out of its 500 staff members due to these cuts.

On the streets of Athens, there is a growing fear that austerity measures not only do not work but also lead to deaths.

The UN says that reducing food waste by just 25% worldwide could provide enough food to feed all malnourished people. Every year, about 1.3 billion tons of food is wasted, which is a third of what's produced. This includes 45% of fruits and vegetables, 35% of fish and seafood, 30% of cereals, and 20% each of dairy products and meat. About 795 million people suffer from severe hunger.

Efforts to reduce food waste, like a new law in France that forces supermarkets to give unsold food to charities, have shown how big the problem is. The UN says this is one of the key challenges for achieving food security. By 2050, food production needs to be 60% higher than it was in 2005 to feed a growing world population.

Reducing wasted food would make it easier to meet future food demands without putting more strain on resources. Food loss and waste happen differently around the world. In developing countries, food is often unintentionally lost due to poor equipment or transportation issues. In wealthy countries, there's less unintentional food loss but more intentional wastage by consumers who buy too much and throw it away.

In developed countries, between 30% and 40% of purchased food is thrown away. In poorer countries, only 5% to 16% of food gets wasted. A report from 2011 found that in Europe and North America, each person wastes about 95 to 115kg of edible food a year, while people in sub-Saharan Africa and south/south-east Asia waste just 6 to 11kg.

Robert van Otterdijk of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization says food waste is mostly found in countries where people can afford to throw away food. He notes that industrialized countries waste about 222 million tons of food per year, nearly matching sub-Saharan Africa’s total net food production (about 230 million tons). However, developing countries suffer from high levels of food loss due to poor management and infrastructure.

Food loss and waste also have a big environmental impact. The carbon footprint of wasted food is about 3.3 billion tons of CO2 each year. That makes food waste the third biggest source of greenhouse gases after the US and China. Around 1.4 billion hectares, or almost 30% of all agricultural land, are used to grow food that gets wasted. More water is also used for wasted food than any single country uses for agriculture.

Van Otterdijk says the issue of climate change is tied to how we produce and consume more than what Earth can provide. Since one-third of food production goes to waste, this puts a huge strain on natural resources like land, water, energy, and contributes to greenhouse gas emissions.

The biggest offenders in food waste are countries like the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand where 39% of purchased food is wasted by consumers, followed by Europe with about 31%. In the UK alone, 15 million tons of food are lost or wasted each year. British households throw away 4.2 million tons of edible food annually, meaning that 11.7% of all purchased food is avoidably wasted, costing families around £700 a year.

Commonly wasted foods in the UK include bread, vegetables, fruit, and milk. Bread waste is highest by weight (414,000 tonnes), while lettuce and leafy salads are most wasted by percentage (38%). Poultry meat has the highest wastage rate both in terms of percentage (13%) and weight, and melons have the highest wastage among fruits at more than 25%.

The UK has made progress over ten years. Between 2007 and 2012, avoidable food waste dropped by 21%, from 5.3 million to 4.2 million tons due to greater awareness. Less wasted food is also ending up in landfills: only 14% was recycled or composted in 2000-2001 but this increased to 43% by 2011-2012.

Van Otterdijk says there’s an encouraging interest in reducing food waste. He hopes with continued effort from public and private sectors, global results will be seen after ten years.

Sometimes life isn't fair. Mark Zuckerberg created Facebook and is now worth about $48 billion. James Goodfellow invented the cash machine used by millions every day but didn’t get rich from it. He only earned £10 from his invention and hasn't made any more money since.

Goodfellow feels upset when he sees bankers getting large bonuses, wondering what they did to earn so much more than him.

He also feels annoyed that he isn’t seen as a good role model for inventors and engineers. His groundbreaking invention generated billions of pounds but didn’t make him rich. “Why would anyone want to follow in my footsteps?” he asks.

For years, there has been debate over who invented the ATM. In 2005, John Shepherd-Barron received an honor as the "inventor of the automatic cash dispenser." However, the UK government now says it was Goodfellow who invented the ATM, giving him a place in history.

In the mid-1960s, Goodfellow worked on developing a way for customers to withdraw cash from banks on Saturdays. He created a machine that would issue cash based on a personal identification number (PIN) and a card with holes punched in it.

Goodfellow’s patent described a system using a card reader and buttons mounted on the bank wall. When a customer wanted money, they inserted their card and pressed buttons according to their PIN.

The first Goodfellow ATM was installed in 1967. At around the same time, Shepherd-Barron made a similar machine that used cheques with carbon-14, a mildly radioactive substance, instead of cards. His machine opened on June 27, 1967, while Goodfellow’s opened one month later.

Goodfellow was upset when Shepherd-Barron received an honor for inventing the ATM in 2005. He believes his invention is important because he made it work, just like the Wright brothers who invented flight.

Today, there are about 3 million ATMs worldwide, with a prediction to reach 4 million by 2020. Goodfellow accepts that while he didn’t invent the idea of cash-issuing machines, his invention made them possible.

Goodfellow’s achievement is now recognized in a guidebook called "Life in the United Kingdom." The book mentions him as one of Britain's great inventors from the 1960s. Goodfellow says that even though he didn’t change his life with the £10, he was happy doing his job.

Dr Ben Brabon from Edgehill University talks about how some people take MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses) because they are free. His course on vampire fiction is one of only two accredited MOOCs in the UK. Dr Brabon does not look down on these people; he just explains why some join.

MOOCs let many people, even thousands, learn from online courses for free. Investors put money into making these courses more interactive and sophisticated. They want to find a way to make money from MOOCs but so far, universities pay the cost of creating them. By studying how people use MOOCs, investors hope to get returns on their investments.

The challenge is figuring out who benefits most from MOOCs. Are they for international students, learners in developing countries, employees looking to learn more about their jobs, or just hobbyists interested in a topic?

Dr Brabon notes that many people start but do not finish these courses. For his vampire fiction course, 1,000 people signed up, but only 31 finished it. Most of those who completed the course had already earned degrees.

David Kernohan from Jisc says online learning needs advanced skills and offers little individual support. He believes MOOCs could be good for continuing education but might not appeal to everyone without high-level qualifications. 

As fewer people attend university part-time due to rising costs, free courses like MOOCs could provide a new path for higher education. However, he thinks using MOOCs alone for an entire degree is unlikely. Instead, combining campus experience with MOOC learning or creating global degrees with online courses might be possible.

Right now, completing a MOOC does not give much to show potential employers since there is no guarantee of course quality or assessment standards. Dr Brabon works on developing agreed standards and marking for MOOCs.

Some think MOOCs will help share first-world teaching with less developed countries, while others worry universities might use them to attract international students who pay tuition fees. Mike Sharples believes MOOCs are mainly about sharing university talent and getting student feedback worldwide, though they can also be used for recruiting students into master’s programs.

Matthew Poyiadgi warns that British universities may need a presence in countries like China or risk falling behind. Apple's brand and logo are the most valuable in the world, worth about $119 billion. This is more than the total yearly economic output of countries like Morocco, Ecuador, or Oman.

According to the Interbrand Best Global Brands report, Apple's brand value has gone up by 21% in one year. Apple, known for its bitten apple logo, leads the increase in value among tech companies. This has caused traditional brands like Coca-Cola, McDonald’s, and Gillette to fall in ranking.

Google's brand value went up by 15% to $107 billion, placing it second. Coca-Cola is third with a 3% increase to $81.5 billion, followed by IBM at $72.2 billion and Microsoft at $45.5 billion.

Facebook had the biggest increase, with an 86% rise to $14.3 billion, putting it in 29th place, ahead of companies like Volkswagen, Kellogg’s, and Ford.

Jez Frampton, CEO of Interbrand, said that brands like Apple have grown stronger because of digital and mobile technology.

Apple was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs in his garage. Its logo, made by Rob Janoff in 1977, has a bite to avoid looking like a cherry. Janoff said the logo represents desire and knowledge.

Graham Hayles, Interbrand’s chief marketing officer, noted that Apple’s brand accounts for about one-fifth of the company’s total value. He said that a strong brand helps a company make more money.

While many tech companies improved in rankings, some fell. Nokia dropped 41 spots to 98th place, and Nintendo fell 33 spots to 100th place.

Huawei, a Chinese company, entered the top 100 for the first time, ranking 94th with a brand value of $4.3 billion. However, the U.S. and Australia have partly banned Huawei due to concerns about cyber espionage.

Most top brands are American. The highest-ranked non-American brands are Samsung (South Korea), Toyota (Japan), and Mercedes-Benz (Germany).

Fashion brands in the top 100 include Boss, Prada, and Ralph Lauren. Louis Vuitton is the top fashion brand, ranked 19th with a value of $23 billion. H&M is 21st with a value of $21 billion.

Nike is 22nd with a brand value of almost $20 billion, while Adidas is 59th with a value of $7 billion.

Frampton said that customers can now easily share opinions about brands on social media like Twitter. Companies need to respond quickly to maintain good reputations.

Hayles added that customers want fast responses, 24/7 access, personalized options, and high levels of customization.

On a hill near Kielder Water in Northumberland, people gather at a wooden building called Kielder Observatory. This place is part of Britain's new astrotourism industry. Many people want to spend a night there to look at the stars, but only a few can go inside.

Inside the observatory, under low light, Gary Fildes, the founder and main astronomer, talks to his team. They plan to use powerful telescopes to watch Jupiter, Venus, and other stars like Capella and Betelgeuse. They might also see the International Space Station.

Gary Fildes leads the UK's growing astrotourism industry. In 2013, Northumberland became the only Dark Sky Park in England. Only 5% of the UK can see over 31 stars on a clear night. The International Dark-Sky Association gives Dark Sky Park status to places with very little light pollution. It is so dark in Northumberland that Venus can cast shadows.

Duncan Wise worked to get the Dark Sky status for Northumberland. He and others collected light readings and planned how to control new lighting in the area. Now, many of the 1.5 million visitors to Northumberland know about the Dark Sky Park. Hotels give guests night-vision flashlights and set out chairs for nighttime viewing.

Wise thinks Northumberland needs more observatories. A new 14-meter landscape center will include an observatory when it opens in a few years. Fildes wants to build Britain's first astrovillage with a large observatory, a planetarium, and a hotel. He hopes to attract 100,000 visitors a year.

Northumberland faces competition from other Dark Sky Parks like Galloway Forest Park in Scotland and Exmoor in England. These places offer stargazing tours and safaris. However, the UK still has a long way to go compared to northern Chile, which has many tourist observatories and clear skies.

People are interested in stargazing partly because of TV shows hosted by scientists like Brian Cox. Apps like Stellarium also help by turning phones into small planetariums. Fildes believes people are starting to value the beauty of the night sky.

Benjamin Carle tried to live using only French-made products for ten months. He did this as part of a TV show. In 2013, the Minister for Economic Renewal, Arnaud Montebourg, told people to buy French products to help French factories. Carle wanted to see if it was possible to follow this advice.

Before the experiment, only 4.5% of the things in Carle's home were made in France. He had to get rid of many items like his smartphone, TV, fridge, glasses, and coffee. His goal was to spend 1,800 euros a month, which is more than the minimum wage in France.

Carle had to replace his clothes with French-made ones. He bought French underpants for 26 euros, socks for 9 euros, a polo shirt for 75 euros, and espadrilles for 26 euros. He couldn't find French jeans.

He also had to find French food and drinks. He cooked with French-grown fruits and vegetables. He used a French toothbrush and washed his clothes by hand until he found a French washing machine.

Going out was hard because he couldn’t watch American movies or drink Belgian beer. At home, he listened to French music and read French books. He bought a French moped because he couldn’t use his British bike or a French car.

At the end of the experiment, Carle borrowed money to buy new things. An auditor said he was 96.9% French-made. The minister gave him a medal.

Carle thinks it’s not practical to live 100% French-made, especially with new technology. He wants people to think more about where they buy things from. Supporting local industries can help keep jobs and improve working conditions.

Two moms in South Africa found out they were raising each other's daughters because the babies were switched at birth in a hospital in 2010. One mom wants her biological child back, but the other mom refuses to give up the child she raised.

Henk Strydom, a lawyer for one of the moms, says this mistake is very sad and probably won't end happily. Both moms had their babies on the same day at Tambo Memorial Hospital in Boksburg, near Johannesburg, and no one noticed the mix-up.

In 2013, one mom, who is 33 and doesn't have a job, tried to get money from her ex-boyfriend for her daughter. He said he wasn't the dad. A DNA test showed the baby wasn't his or hers. This made her very upset.

She then met the other mom, and since December 2013, they've gone to counseling together, set up by the hospital. They met their real daughters there.

One mom sees similarities between her and her biological daughter. She finds it hard to take care of a child that isn't hers while her child is with someone else. She asked the children's court for custody of her biological child, but the other mom won't give her child back.

The High Court in Pretoria asked the University of Pretoria's Centre for Child Law to look into what's best for the kids. They will talk to the moms, dads, and anyone close to the girls. The children and moms will also have medical tests and might see a psychologist.

Karabo Ngidi, a lawyer from the center, says what happens should be best for the children. Biology matters, but it's not everything. Zulu traditions and customs will also play a role. It's still possible the ex-boyfriend of the mom suing could be the biological father of the switched girl.

This isn't the first time babies were switched in South Africa. In 1995, two moms got money after their sons were switched in 1989. In 2009, in Oregon, USA, Dee Ann Angell and Kay Rene Reed found out they were switched at birth in 1953. In 2013, in Japan, a man switched at birth got money after growing up poor while his siblings went to private schools.

Bruce Laing, a psychologist in Johannesburg, says switching babies can cause big problems and trauma. Parents might always wonder "What if?"

Seeing Clouds Up Close

One fun part of flying is looking at clouds. Even though clouds look light, they hold a lot of water—about 500 tons in a small cloud. Water is heavier than air, so why don't clouds fall? They do, but very slowly. It takes about a year for an average cloud to fall just one meter.

Cloud Types

Most people just say clouds are fluffy or dark, but weather experts know over 50 types. They use numbers 1 to 9 to group them. Cloud nine is the big, tall cumulonimbus. Being "on cloud nine" means feeling really happy.

Rainbows from Above

A plane is a great spot to see a rainbow. Rainbows form when sunlight hits raindrops. On Earth, we see a half-circle, but from a plane, it's a full circle.

Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight has all colors, but when it passes through air, blue light spreads more than other colors. This makes the sky look blue.

Life in the Air

Besides clouds and other planes, there isn't much to see outside a flying plane. But the air has lots of bacteria—up to 1,800 types over cities—and they can go as high as twice the height of a plane.

Turbulence

Turbulence can scare even experienced fliers. It can cause bumpy rides or sudden drops. No modern airliner has crashed due to turbulence, but injuries can happen if people aren't seated or if luggage falls.

Radiation During Flight

When body scanners were introduced, there were worries about radiation. But the scanners give off the same amount of radiation as one minute of flight. Cosmic rays from space also hit Earth, and they're stronger at higher altitudes.

Jet Lag

Long flights across time zones cause jet lag. To reduce it, eat bland food for 24 hours before travel, drink lots of water, and follow your destination's time schedule once you board.

Supersonic Flights

Some flights can go faster than sound. Jet streams in the upper atmosphere can move at 250 mph. If a plane moving at 550 mph enters a jet stream, it can fly at 800 mph, faster than sound.

Time Travel While Flying

Flights involve tiny amounts of time travel due to time zones and special relativity. Crossing the Atlantic weekly for 40 years would only move you 1/1,000th of a second into the future.

Tea and Coffee on Planes

Tea might not taste great on planes because water can't reach 100°C. It only gets to 90°C. Choose coffee instead.

Noise and Taste

Airline food can seem bland partly because planes are noisy, and noise can affect how food tastes.

Finding Missing Planes

It's hard to find a missing plane like Malaysian flight MH370. Planes don't send their location in real-time, unlike ships which have had tracking since the 1980s.

Ash and Airplanes

Volcanic ash can cancel flights. Ash melts in engines and damages them. Ignoring ash clouds is dangerous.

How Wings Work

Wings keep planes in the air using Newton's Third Law. The wing pushes air down, and the air pushes the wing up.

In October 2012, the Taliban sent a gunman to shoot Malala Yousafzai as she rode home on a bus after school. They wanted to stop her from speaking about girls' rights to education.

Nine months later, after many surgeries, Malala spoke at the United Nations on her 16th birthday. She said the Taliban failed to silence her.

Instead of celebrating with a cake, Malala sat in a big room at the United Nations. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called her a hero. Former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown wished her a happy 16th birthday.

Malala became famous when she wrote a blog for the BBC about getting an education under the Taliban. At age 11, she met Richard Holbrooke to ask for help. At 14, she was nominated for the International Children's Peace Prize. At 15, she was the youngest person ever nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.

After the Taliban attacked her, Malala had several surgeries, including a titanium plate on her forehead and a device to help her hear. Now living in Birmingham, she goes to school every day.

At the UN, Malala said she was not seeking revenge. She even said she would not shoot the man who hurt her, even if she could. She wore a shawl that belonged to Benazir Bhutto, a former Pakistani leader who was killed by extremists.

Malala said the Taliban fear education and women. She talked about attacks on schools and teachers. She explained that Islam supports education and equality, not violence.

Her speech inspired millions to sign a petition asking for education for all children. Malala said she didn't know how to start her speech, but she did not need to worry.

What surprised researchers was not how difficult the challenge was, but how much people tried to avoid it. The task was simple: sit in a chair and think.

Some people found this so hard that they chose to give themselves mild electric shocks to break the boredom. Two-thirds of men shocked themselves during a 15-minute thinking session. For women, one in four did the same. Scientists think men usually seek more excitement than women.

Psychologists from Virginia and Harvard Universities wanted to understand why most people find it hard to just sit and think. Across over 11 studies, they found that people disliked being left alone with their thoughts, no matter their age, education, income, or use of smartphones and social media.

In the first tests, students were put in a room alone, without phones, books, or writing materials. They had to sit and think for six to fifteen minutes. When asked afterward, the students said they did not enjoy the experience. They had trouble focusing and their minds wandered.

Researchers repeated the experiment at home with similar results. People found it even harder and often broke the rules by moving around or using their phones.

To see if the results were the same for non-students, the team tested over 100 people aged 18 to 77 from a church and a farmers market. These people also did not like being left alone with their thoughts.

The most surprising part came next. Students were given the choice to give themselves a mild electric shock. Earlier, they said they would pay to avoid these shocks. Surprisingly, 12 out of 18 men and 6 out of 24 women shocked themselves. This shows that being alone with their thoughts was so hard that they chose to shock themselves, even though they had said they would pay to avoid it.

Jessica Andrews-Hanna from the University of Colorado noted that while some might shock themselves to liven up a boring lecture, more research is needed to understand why people in the study chose to shock themselves.

The researchers were surprised by what people did to avoid a simple task. The task was to sit in a chair and think.

Some people thought it was so bad that they gave themselves small electric shocks to stop feeling bored.

Organic food has more antioxidants that are good for health and fewer toxic metals and pesticides compared to regular food, according to a big study. The study was done by a team led by Professor Carlo Leifert. They found that organic food has up to 69% more antioxidants than regular food. Eating organic fruits and vegetables can be like adding one or two more servings of the five recommended daily portions of fruits and vegetables.

The study looked at 343 studies worldwide comparing organic and regular fruits, vegetables, and cereals. It shows that farming methods do affect the quality of food we eat. Many antioxidants in organic food have been linked to reducing risks of heart disease, brain diseases, and some cancers.

The study also found that regular crops had higher levels of cadmium, a harmful metal, and pesticide residues were four times more common in regular crops than in organic ones. However, the levels of cadmium and pesticides in regular crops were still below safety limits.

Some experts, like Professor Tom Sanders, say the differences might just be due to natural variations and may not be very important for nutrition. He also noted that organic cereals have less protein than regular crops.

People buy organic food mainly because they think it's healthier and want to avoid chemicals. Others buy it because they care about the environment and animal welfare, and some just like the taste.

The study supports what many people believe about organic food. In other parts of Europe, there is more support for organic food and farming.

Emmanuel Limal, a 43-year-old actor from France living in Copenhagen, often used online dating sites to find a partner to start a family with. However, he was disappointed because most women he met were not interested in having children or did not mention it. 

Limal has a six-year-old daughter from a past relationship and comes from a large family. His father is one of eleven siblings. He wanted to have more children but couldn't find someone who shared his desire. He felt it was hard to talk about wanting kids on dates because it was seen as a taboo topic.

One day, he saw a profile of a 38-year-old woman who admitted she wanted children. This inspired him to create a dating site called Babyklar.nu, which means "baby-ready now" in English. The site asks users if they are okay with someone who already has children and if they want another baby, but does not ask how many children they want.

Since launching in June, the site has been popular, with 50 sign-ups an hour. More men than women have joined (53% to 47%). Some users commented that it was nice to openly discuss their desire for children.

In Denmark, the birth rate is low, with only 1.7 children per family, which is not enough to keep the population stable. Emmanuel hopes his site will help people who want to start a family find each other.

There are plans to launch the site in France and the UK later in 2013. Emmanuel believes that because Danes often have children before marriage, relationships can progress quickly. Also, since Denmark is a small country, people from different areas can easily date without much travel.

Emmanuel has also found a partner who wants to have a baby, and they are considering starting a family together.

Scientists have started to look at and map the tiny living things called bacteria in the New York City subway system. Dr. Christopher Mason from Weill Cornell Medical College led a team that studied the subway for 18 months. They looked at turnstiles, seats, ticket booths, and stations.

They found some worrying bacteria like those that cause meningitis, anthrax, and bubonic plague. However, the team says there is very little of these dangerous bacteria, and no one has gotten sick from them in New York for years.

Most of the bacteria found are harmless or even helpful. Some bacteria found match those used to make cheese and kimchi. For example, bacteria from different types of cheese were found all over the subway, while Swiss cheese bacteria were mostly in midtown Manhattan and the financial district. Kimchi bacteria were seen in the financial district and Bay Ridge.

Bacteria that can cause illnesses like diarrhea, nausea, and skin infections were also found. But these bacteria are not causing sickness in the city.

The team took over 1,000 samples from all 466 open subway stations. They found 15,152 different species, almost half of which were bacteria.

Dr. Mason says people should not worry about getting sick from the subway. He suggests washing hands and staying healthy as usual. He feels safer using the subway now.

Stations with more people, like Grand Central and Times Square, had more kinds of bacteria. The Bronx had the most variety of bacteria, while Staten Island had the least.

The team plans to study other cities like Paris, São Paulo, and Shanghai, and continue studying New York to see how the bacteria change with the seasons. This research could help health officials prevent and track diseases.

The team hopes this research will help keep people healthy by tracking and preventing diseases. They plan to study subways in other cities too. Dr. Mason now feels safer riding the subway.

Nelson Mandela, a great leader who fought for freedom in Africa, has died at 95 years old.

South Africa's first black president passed away at home in Johannesburg with his family nearby after being sick for many years.

President Jacob Zuma told the country that Mandela died peacefully at 8:50 pm local time. Zuma said, "Our nation has lost its greatest son."

Many people around the world honored Mandela. President Barack Obama called him Madiba, his clan name, and praised his strength and sacrifice. UK Prime Minister David Cameron said Mandela was a hero.

FW de Klerk, the former South African president who freed Mandela, said Mandela was a great unifier.

In South Africa, people gathered in the streets to celebrate Mandela’s life. They sang and danced, especially in Soweto near Mandela’s old home.

Mandela was born on July 18, 1918, and was given the name Nelson by his schoolteacher. He joined the African National Congress (ANC) in 1943 and helped start its youth league. In 1952, he opened South Africa’s first black law firm with Oliver Tambo.

After the ANC was banned in 1960, Mandela went into hiding. Following the Sharpeville massacre, where 69 black protesters were killed by police, Mandela decided to fight back with weapons. He was caught and sentenced to life in prison for trying to overthrow the government.

In 1990, FW de Klerk freed Mandela, and the world celebrated. Mandela led the ANC to win South Africa’s first multiracial election in 1994 and then left office after one term.

Mandela was known for his charm, love of boxing, and interest in women. He was married three times and had six children, 17 grandchildren, and 14 great-grandchildren.

People in South Africa and around the world were very sad. Barack Obama, the U.S. president, called Mandela "Madiba." Obama said Mandela changed South Africa and inspired everyone.

People were angry after earlier protests where police used rubber bullets, tear gas, and beatings over small bus fare hikes.

These protests happened as the Confederations Cup started. People were unhappy about high costs, poor public services, spending on sports events, bad healthcare, and issues with inequality and corruption. Most protests were peaceful, but there were clashes with police, burning cars, and broken windows.

In one case, a large group set fires and damaged a government building, writing messages like "Revolution" and "Hate police." Reasons for protesting varied. One person said they hated the government, while another, an unemployed architect, felt something was wrong with the country.

In Brasília, some protesters entered the national congress area. In Belo Horizonte, police clashed with those trying to enter a stadium. In Porto Alegre, a bus was set on fire, and in Curitiba, protesters tried to enter the governor's office. São Paulo had large peaceful gatherings.

Most protesters were young, and for many, it was their first big rally. Some compared these protests to ones in Turkey. Protesters wore Guy Fawkes masks, linked to Anonymous and Occupy Wall Street.

The protests are called the Vinegar Revolution, the 20-Cent Revolution, and the Free Pass Movement. Some felt the protests were unusual but liberating. President Dilma Rousseff supports peaceful protests but faced booing at the Confederations Cup opening. She faces challenges ahead, especially with the World Cup and a presidential election in 2014.

Amsterdam is known for being very free, but recently, the city's mayor, Eberhard van der Laan, said that coffee shops selling marijuana will stay open even though there is a new national law against it. This is good news for tourists.

However, the city has a new plan that might change how people see Amsterdam. The plan is to move some families who cause problems to special places made from shipping containers. These places are called "scum villages." The mayor says this plan is to help protect people who are being hurt or bullied.

Bartho Boer, who speaks for the mayor, says the plan is not against the city’s free values. He explains that the plan is for families who are very violent and scary, not just for neighbors who play music too loud. The families will live in these containers for up to six months. The containers have showers and kitchens and have been used before as student housing.

Boer says these families will get help from doctors, social workers, and parole officers while they live in the containers. After six months, they will find new homes. The city expects to move about ten families each year starting in 2013.

Some people think this plan is like what happened in the 19th century when troublemakers were moved to villages that became very poor. But Boer says the city has learned from the past and will not put more than one family in the same area.
